title: Warnock, Ossoff Secure Over $12 Million in Federal Funding to Repair Roadways Damaged by Natural Disasters
text:
Senators Reverend Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff successfully secured over $12 million in federal funding from the Department of Transportation to repair and reconstruct roads damaged by natural disasters across Georgia

The funding is provided through the Federal Highway Administration Emergency Relief Program

The funding will support critical roadway repairs across Georgia, including in the Chattahoochee and Oconee National Forests, following damage caused by Hurricane Helene, Hurricane Rafael, and severe ice storms

Washington D.C. — U.S. Senators Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA) and Jon Ossoff (D-GA) secured over $12 million in federal funding to repair and reconstruct roads damaged by natural disasters across Georgia. The funding, provided through the U.S. Department of Transportation’s (DOT) Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) Emergency Relief Program, will support roadway repairs across Georgia, including in the Chattahoochee and Oconee National Forests, following damage caused by Hurricane Helene, Hurricane Rafael, and severe ice storms.

“Communities across our state have been through a lot in the wake of these devastating storms, and for many, the work of rebuilding is far from over,” said Senator Warnock. “This federal funding will help repair roads damaged by these storms and make sure Georgians can safely get where they need to go.”

“Bringing Republicans and Democrats together, we are delivering these resources to help improve Georgia’s roads and highways that were impacted after Hurricane Helene and other storms,” said Senator Ossoff.

The funding includes $8.9 million to repair roadways and drainage structures in the Chattahoochee and Oconee National Forests that were heavily damaged during severe ice storms earlier this year. The funding package also includes $2.3 million to address widespread damage to traffic signals, roadways, signs and sign structures that were impacted by Hurricane Helene. Nearly $841,000 will support communities in South and East Georgia where Hurricane Rafael caused several rivers to overflow their banks, flooding roadways, damaging culverts and causing washouts.

title: ICYMI: Padilla, Schumer, and Senate Democrats’ Election Protection Task Force Release Report on Vote Counting Process for the November Election
text:
Senate Democrats’ Report Debunks White House and Election Deniers’ Baseless Attacks on Election Results

CALIFORNIA — In case you missed it, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Rules Committee with oversight over federal elections, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), and Senators Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) released a Senate Democrats’ Election Protection Task Force report encouraging voters to cast their ballot early and outlining for the American people what to expect on Election Day, Election Night, and beyond in terms of timelines for counting and announcing election results in several states with 2026 Senate elections.

More than 56 million people have already cast their ballots with tens of millions more expected to vote on Election Day. The Senate Democrats’ report explains it is possible that in some states – especially rural states, states with highly populated urban areas, and states where voters rely heavily on vote by mail – the outcome of the election may not be known on Election Night, which is normal and not a sign of irregularities. While some states allow ballots to be counted as they come in, others do not and can only begin counting after the polls close. The report also explains that two states with Senate elections in 2026 – Alaska and Maine – have ranked choice voting.

As in Donald Trump’s attacks on the outcome of the 2020 presidential election, the Trump Administration and White House officials have already repeatedly made efforts to undermine state and local election administration by spreading misinformation about the timing of counting of votes in the midterm elections.

The Senate Democrats’ Task Force report builds on the 2024 version of the report that focused on presidential battleground states and is updated to cover 15 states with Senate contests in the 2026 midterm election: Alaska, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, and Virginia. The report covers the early vote period, when polls close, deadlines for results, and timelines for sending, receiving, and processing mail-in and absentee ballots.

“The Trump Administration has been working to undermine Americans’ faith in our elections, but I know firsthand from running California’s elections and working with election officials around the country that American elections are safe and secure,” said Senator Padilla. “As we have seen in past cycles, and again in California’s May primary, the White House and their election denier allies will try to weaponize the timing of results to sow mistrust in the outcome based on changing unofficial vote totals. Our message to the American people is to tune out the noise, make your voice heard, and take pride in our democratic process. Vote early when possible. And be patient while every eligible vote is counted and certified as required by law.”

“Trump’s efforts to rig the midterms are the last gasps of a desperate and failing president,” said Leader Schumer. “His attacks on our election integrity are not just an attempt to avoid accountability from Americans fed up with his surging inflation and rampant corruption, they are also an assault on our nation’s democracy. Our Constitution is clear. Voters decide elections—not the president. Senate Democrats are fighting like hell to ensure they stay that way. Americans have the right to have their voices heard.”

“The right to vote is fundamental to our democracy, and must be protected. That means upholding the integrity of the election process and pushing back on efforts to undermine the freedom to vote. As this report lays out, state and local election officials are prepared to ensure American voters’ voices are heard at the ballot box,” said Senator Klobuchar.

“Americans just aren’t buying Trump’s excuses anymore on the corruption and the Iran war and this election is our opportunity to take back our democracy,” said Senator Murphy. “Millions have already voted to reject Trump’s assault on our freedoms and our communities – and there’s still time for everyone to make their voice heard at the ballot box. So make a plan to vote as soon as possible. Our democracy needs all hands on deck.”

“Trump’s false claims about the integrity of our elections aren’t about election security. They’re about distracting the American people from rising costs and a failing economy under a Republican-controlled White House and Congress. But Americans aren’t buying it. Our elections are the foundation of our democracy, and despite this administration’s attempts to undermine public trust, our elections remain secure. The best way to push back against these attacks and protect our democracy is to make your voice heard and exercise your right to vote,” said Senator Heinrich.

“Exercising your right to vote is the highest, most sacred responsibility as an American citizen. No matter how desperately Donald Trump tries to sow doubt and chaos in our electoral processes, our free and fair elections and our peaceful transitions of power are two of the hallmarks that have separated America from authoritarian regimes—and it will be no different this November,” said Senator Duckworth. “Trump has made clear he’s ready and willing to deploy troops to polling places to intimidate voters, and we know he isn’t above crying that an election is ‘rigged’ because he doesn’t like the results. These authoritarian tactics are the antithesis of our democracy, and Americans cannot become discouraged and let a wanna-be dictator’s fearmongering chip away at their trust. Because the power of the people will always matter more than the people in power, and the best and only way we will remain a government of, by and for the people is by making our voices heard.”

The report is available here.

title: Padilla, Costa Denied Entry to Golden State Annex Facility in Central Valley as Death Toll in ICE Custody Reaches More Than 60 Under Trump
text:
MCFARLAND, CA — Today, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Immigration Subcommittee, and Representative Jim Costa (D-Calif.-21) were denied entry to the Golden State Annex in Kern County, California, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility. Padilla and Costa attempted to exercise their congressional oversight role as the Trump Administration escalates immigration enforcement operations across the Central Valley and throughout California.

Golden State Annex is operated by the GEO Group, a for-profit private prison company. The lawmakers were turned away as Golden Annex officials claimed that ICE agents were not present on site to allow them into the facility.

“More than 60 people have now died in ICE custody since Donald Trump returned to office. That is a staggering and unacceptable loss of life, and the Trump Administration continues to refuse to answer basic questions about the conditions inside its detention facilities,” said Senator Padilla. “Today I visited the Golden Annex in McFarland to demand answers and accountability. My office continues to receive alarming reports about conditions inside these facilities and agency officials won’t even answer basic questions about whether they’re respecting due process rights and protecting the fundamental human rights of those in their custody. Their refusal to grant us access to the detention facility raises serious questions about what they’re trying to hide. Families deserve answers. The American people deserve transparency. And this Administration must be held accountable for its cruel and inhumane mass deportation agenda. I will keep showing up, demanding answers, and fighting to ensure the law is followed and people’s rights are protected.”

“Today’s visit with Senator Padilla to the Golden State Annex detention facility once again demonstrated ICE’s lack of accountability and transparency,” said Congressman Costa. “As members of Congress, we have a constitutional right to conduct oversight of these facilities and ask basic questions about the conditions, medical care, and treatment of detainees. Instead, we were denied access to basic information and given the runaround. As my district and communities across our state continue to be impacted by ICE activity, I remain committed to working alongside my colleagues to hold ICE accountable and demand transparency.”

Padilla has repeatedly conducted oversight visits to immigration detention facilities and holding centers across California to examine conditions firsthand and demand accountability from federal officials. His visits include facilities in California City, Otay Mesa, San Francisco International Airport, Downtown Los Angeles, Sacramento, and San Diego.

Last month, Padilla demanded answers from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) over increased immigration enforcement and resident detentions in Mendota. Padilla also urged DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to immediately recall ICE officers hired during the 2025 surge period. In September, Padilla called on DHS to halt immigration enforcement activity near schools and educational institutions in San Diego County. In August, Padilla called out the Trump Administration’s continued abuses of power and inhumane treatment of detained immigrants, after sounding the alarm on the significant increase in deaths among detainees in ICE custody since January 2025.

Photos and video of today’s oversight visit are available here.

title: Rosen Applauds Funding for University of Nevada, Reno Critical Mineral and Energy Innovation
text:
RENO, NV – U.S. Senator Jacky Rosen applauded the recent announcement that the University of Nevada, Reno (UNR) will receive $1 million in federal funding to grow the workforce required to produce, process, recover, and recycle critical minerals in the United States. The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation has chosen UNR as one of 16 universities across the country to receive this funding, which seeks to double the number of graduates with mining, minerals, and associated supply chain credentials across the United States within two years. Funding for this program was made possible through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which Senator Rosen helped write and pass into law.

“As the United States races with other global powers to acquire and leverage the critical minerals that power the modern economy, it is essential that we invest in and develop the skilled workforce needed to compete in today’s world,” said Senator Rosen. “I am thrilled that the University of Nevada, Reno is being recognized as one of the schools at the forefront of these efforts. Northern Nevada is one of the leading producers of critical minerals in the country, and a vital anchor for our domestic mineral supply chain. I’ll always work to make sure our state has the federal funding and support it needs to remain a key player in the race for critical minerals and American innovation.”

Senator Rosen has been a leader in supporting the critical mineral and rare earth industry, both domestically and abroad. Most recently, she helped introduce the Critical Mineral Executive Coordination Act and the bipartisan National Critical Minerals Council Act, which will create a more comprehensive domestic and global strategy in accessing critical minerals and addressing vulnerabilities in global critical mineral supply chains. Senator Rosen also introduced bipartisan legislation to bolster the American critical mineral mining workforce and support the growing industry through the creation of a mining Fulbright exchange program. In 2022, Senator Rosen helped pass the bipartisan CHIPS and Science Act and secured a provision to grow the next generation of mining engineers, promote the use of critical minerals, and develop a secure and reliable supply chain. This led to nearly $21 million in federal funding for the Lithium Loop Tech Hub, a project led by the University of Nevada, Reno.

title: Van Hollen Joins Peters, Kim, Colleagues in Demanding Census Bureau Rescind Proposed Rule That Violates Constitution
text:
U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) joined Senators Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Ranking Member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on the Census, led a bipartisan group of 24 colleagues urging the U.S. Census Bureau to rescind a proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from census counts and eliminate questions on race and ethnicity.

In their letter, the Senators warn that the exclusion of non-citizens violates the Constitution, which expressly says that the census must count the “whole number of persons in each state.” The Bureau has proposed two methods by which it would exclude non-citizens, both of which would cause undercounts and errors in the census counts.

“We write to urge that you rescind your proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from decennial census counts and omit questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census. The proposed rule violates the clear meaning of the Constitution, which requires that the Census Bureau count the ‘whole number of persons in each state.’ The proposed rule would also cause communities across the country to be counted inaccurately, jeopardizing their fair representation in Congress and access to billions of federal dollars for education, health care, and public safety services,” the senators wrote.

The letter also describes how the Bureau’s proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions would undermine the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws and would degrade the quality of all census data. The compliance of civil and voting rights laws rely on demographic data, and only the decennial census provides accurate and precise data. Additionally, eliminating the collection of race and ethnicity data from the decennial census undermines other federal survey data. Businesses and local governments that depend on such data have said that they would be harmed by this proposed rule.

“In its attempt to undermine the data used for the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws, the Bureau will degrade the accuracy of all other federal survey data, particularly for small and rural geographic areas. The Bureau writes in its own regulatory filing that the proposed rule ‘deteriorates the accuracy’ of ‘fertility/mortality rates, cancer rates, poverty rates, unemployment rates, [and] labor force participation’ because the Bureau relies on accurate decennial census information to adjust and design other survey estimates,” the senators continued. “The Bureau also admits in its filing that the proposal would hamper the usability of data for state and local governments who rely on precise and accurate population estimates for small geographic areas. Businesses and local governments that depend on reliable and complete federal data have warned that the Census Bureau’s proposal would increase costs as data is degraded.”

Joining Senators Peters and Kim in sending the letter were Senators Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.), Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Angus King (I-Maine), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.).

The full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Under Secretary Meyer and Deputy Under Secretary Cook,

We write to urge that you rescind your proposed rule that would exclude certain noncitizens from decennial census counts and omit questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census (Fed. Reg. Vol. 91, No. 57524, Thursday September 10, 2026). The proposed rule violates the clear meaning of the Constitution, which requires that the Census Bureau count the “whole number of persons in each state.” The proposed rule would also cause communities across the country to be counted inaccurately, jeopardizing their fair representation in Congress and access to billions of federal dollars for education, health care, and public safety services. The proposed rule would also undermine the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws by eliminating the only appropriate data used for compliance. We request that you rescind this proposed rule to ensure the decennial census complies with the Constitution and allows civil and voting rights laws to be enforced.

I. The Bureau’s Proposal to Exclude Certain Non-Citizens from Census Counts Violates the Constitution

The proposal to exclude certain non-citizens, including those who are legal immigrants, from apportionment counts violates the Constitution. The Fourteenth Amendment is clear: the Census Bureau must count the “whole number of persons in each state” in the United States, including non-citizens.

This interpretation of the Constitution has been accepted from the founding of our nation to the present, by our founders, courts, members of Congress, and leaders of the Census Bureau from both parties, including Secretary Howard Lutnick. In 1788, James Madison wrote in Federalist No. 54 that the apportionment was to be “founded on the aggregate number of inhabitants,” recognizing no distinctions among types of persons to be counted except for those explicitly excluded in the text of the Constitution itself. During consideration of the Fourteenth Amendment, Congress debated and expressly rejected proposals to change the “persons” counted for apportionment to “voters” or “citizens.” During the first half of the twentieth century, Congress considered and rejected proposals to pass statutes to exclude non-citizens from apportionment counts on the basis that it would take a constitutional amendment to change the requirement. In 1929, the Senate’s Legislative Counsel concluded that excluding certain noncitizens from apportionment counts would be unconstitutional. In 1980, a court rejected a lawsuit seeking that the Bureau exclude certain non-citizens from apportionment counts. Even current Secretary of Commerce Lutnick testified to Congress in February that “citizenship is not in the Constitution for the [Census] apportionment... that is not a necessary factor”. This unbroken history of our reading of the Constitution, including courts, Congress, and Census Bureau leaders, is clear: the Census Bureau must count every person.

II. The Bureau’s Proposed Methods to Exclude Certain Non-Citizens Would Cause Undercounts and Errors in Census Counts

The Bureau has proposed two methods for carrying out its unconstitutional exclusion of certain non-citizens: directly asking every person detailed questions about their immigration status and relying on administrative records. Both proposed methods would cause undercounts of both citizens and non-citizens and errors in the population counts.

First, the Bureau proposes asking each person their legal immigration status so that it can exclude certain non-citizens, but such a question would cause both citizens and non-citizens to not answer the census. This would likely lead to undercounts and errors in census counts. The Bureau has never asked detailed questions about legal immigration status on any nationwide survey before, let alone the decennial census, because of concerns about privacy and accuracy. The Bureau’s own research before the 2020 Census showed that including even a question about citizenship status on the decennial census, itself a less complicated question than immigration status, would cause fewer citizens and non-citizens to complete the census. In addition, the Government Accountability Office previously found that if statistical agencies directly asked about immigration status, they would create invalid, imprecise, and inaccurate estimates. In 2006, the Government Accountability Office recommended that federal agencies should not pursue adding even indirect immigration questions to surveys, and the Census Bureau concurred with that recommendation.

In addition, the Bureau alternatively proposes relying on administrative records acquired from federal agencies, state and local governments, and private data brokers to exclude certain non-citizens from apportionment counts. This approach would also lead to undercounts and inappropriately exclude citizens and non-citizens from census totals. The Bureau previously found that if it relied solely on administrative records the decennial census would misestimate the total population by over 1.3 million people, overcounting non-citizens and undercounting citizens. It also found that relying on administrative records undercounted people in rural areas and group quarters, such as nursing homes and college campuses. The Treasury Department commented on a draft of this very rule warning that using tax records to identify people’s usual address would cause people to be counted in the wrong location. This evidence shows that both of the Bureau’s proposed methods to carry out this unconstitutional effort would cause errors and undercounts, denying people fair representation in Congress and jeopardizing the fair and full allocation of resources.

III. The Bureau’s Proposal to Omit Demographic Questions Would Undermine Enforcement of Civil and Voting Rights Laws and Degrade the Quality of All Census Data

We also express our strong opposition to the Bureau’s proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census, because it would harm the ability to enforce civil and voting rights laws and cause the quality of all census data to deteriorate. Only the decennial census provides the reliable demographic data necessary for compliance with civil and voting rights laws. Congress has made clear that decennial census data should be used to enforce these laws, and the Trump Administration even recognized the legal need to collect this data for enforcing civil rights laws when it published its planned questions for the 2020 Census.

For example, Congress enacted the Fair Housing Act, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Public Health Service Act to ensure that individuals are not discriminated against on the basis of race or ethnicity in housing, employment, and health care, respectively. The Supreme Court has held that statistical evidence using census data can be used to demonstrate violations and ensure compliance with these laws. The Bureau admits in its own regulatory filing that no other federal survey that collects information about race and ethnicity, including the American Community Survey (ACS), can substitute for the decennial census, because other surveys like the ACS cannot create precise population estimates for areas smaller than 65,000 people. This means there is no real alternative for all Americans to bring claims under civil rights laws if the Bureau eliminates collecting information about race and ethnicity on the decennial census. Similarly, Congress enacted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act to prohibit voting practices or procedures that discriminate on the basis of race, including congressional redistricting. While the Supreme Court narrowed the standards to bring a claim under the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais, the Court maintained that the Voting Rights Act is violated “when the evidence supports a strong inference that the State intentionally drew its districts to afford minority voters less opportunity because of their race.” Such evidence requires the availability of decennial census data about race and ethnicity for enforcement, because the Voting Rights Act applies to even small political subdivisions where no other federal data is accurate.

The elimination of data about race and ethnicity would particularly undermine the federal government’s ability to meet its responsibilities and obligations to tribal governments. By eliminating the collection of information about American Indian and Alaska Native identity, the Bureau makes it effectively impossible for the government to administer the Indian Housing Block Grant program, the Indian Community Development Block Grant program, and the Indian Health Service – each of which depend on accurate estimates of American Indian and Alaska Native populations to plan and allocate funding. In its own regulatory filing, the Bureau admits that other federal surveys “may not be a suitable substitute for all federally recognized tribes,” because other surveys do not provide accurate and precise estimates of American Indian and Alaska Native populations. The Bureau previously told Congress that relying on alternative options to collect information about American Indian and Alaska Native populations, like asking about tribal enrollment or relying on administrative records, would cause inaccurate estimates and infringe on the private sovereign information of tribes.

In its attempt to undermine the data used for the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws, the Bureau will degrade the accuracy of all other federal survey data, particularly for small and rural geographic areas. The Bureau writes in its own regulatory filing that the proposed rule "deteriorates the accuracy” of “fertility/mortality rates, cancer rates, poverty rates, unemployment rates, [and] labor force participation” because the Bureau relies on accurate decennial census information to adjust and design other survey estimates. The Bureau also admits in its filing that the proposal would hamper the usability of data for state and local governments who rely on precise and accurate population estimates for small geographic areas. Businesses and local governments that depend on reliable and complete federal data have warned that the Census Bureau’s proposal would increase costs as data is degraded.

With these considerations in mind, we urge the Census Bureau to rescind its September 10 proposed regulation.

Sincerely,

title: Van Hollen, Peters Urge Trump Admin to Cancel Mass Deportation Flights to Afghanistan and Iran
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) joined Representative Scott Peters (D-Calif.-50) and over 60 bicameral Members of Congress on a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, demanding the immediate cancellation of any deportation flights carrying Afghans and Iranians, whether sent directly or through another country.

This letter comes after reports that over 150 Afghans could be deported to Pakistan in the coming days, which would constitute one of the largest single expulsions of Afghans ever. San Diego has served as a primary hub for incoming Afghan refugees, with nearly 5,000 resettling in the region. The Members also expressed concern over another flight with a mass deportation of Iranians — the first since the U.S. launched its military conflict against Iran— and that relatives of Afghans who helped American troops could be among those on board.

“Our nation made a promise to stand by Afghans who risked their lives and their families’ safety to stand by U.S. service members,” the Members wrote, adding that deporting them “is a violation of that promise and our moral obligations to the Afghan community who stood alongside our troops.”

The Members emphasized the well-documented danger awaiting deportees. The State Department lists Afghanistan as a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” country, and for those who aided U.S. forces, “their assistance to U.S. troops puts a target on these individuals and their families to this day.” They detail the torture, detention, and extrajudicial killing of dissidents and LGBTQ persons, as well as the severe repression of women — noting that women and LGBTQ refugees could be on the flight.

The Members also raised alarm over reports that Iranians, including women, Christian converts, and pro-democracy activists, may be deported to Iran, where they face imprisonment, torture, and a possible death sentence. “Sending people who sought protection from the Islamic Republic of Iran back to a war zone and a repressive regime is unconscionable,” they wrote. They cited how even President Trump has warned about the dangers faced by pro-democracy and anti-government protesters in Iran.

The Members stressed that routing a flight through a third country does not change U.S. obligations, and urged the Trump Administration to warn Pakistan that the U.S. will not accept its participation in sending deportees onward to the Taliban.

These individuals “came to the U.S. because they believed in its promise of democracy, religious freedom, and liberty,” the Members concluded, and “we must uphold those values and commitments, not abandon people to autocratic regimes.”

“Sixty-six members of Congress, from both chambers, needed less than 24 hours to say what every veteran of the Afghanistan war already knows: you don’t hand the people who stood with our troops to the Taliban. When even the Taliban are voicing ‘serious concern’ about your deportation plan, you’ve lost the moral argument and the national security one. This flight isn’t immigration enforcement. It’s a betrayal with a boarding pass, and the whole world is watching whether America keeps its word. We are grateful to Rep. Peters for leading. Secretary Rubio and Secretary Mullin, ground this plane,” said Shawn VanDiver, U.S. Navy veteran and President and Founder of #AfghanEvac.

"Having effectively dismantled our protection system, this administration is set to deport vulnerable people back to Afghanistan and Iran, in violation of our human rights commitments and our nation's values," said Sarah Mehta, deputy director of immigration policy at the ACLU. "So many of these men and women never had a meaningful opportunity to defend their claims and are now the casualties of this administration's assault on asylum. We thank Congressman Peters for his leadership and all the members standing against these unconscionable deportations back to persecution, torture, or even death."

The Members requested an immediate response.

The full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Secretary Rubio and Secretary Mullin,

We are writing about the alarming reports that over 150 Afghans could be deported to Afghanistan in the coming days. This flight has now been reported in multiple court filings and media outlets, and as the New York Times notes, it would constitute “one of the largest single expulsions of Afghans” ever. We understand that relatives of Afghans who helped our troops could be on this flight. We have also received credible reports that this flight will be followed by the first mass deportation of Iranians since the United States launched its military conflict against Iran. We are extremely concerned that sending vulnerable people who sought safety in the United States to Afghanistan or Iran will result in their persecution, torture, or even death. We urge you to cancel any deportation flights of Afghans and Iranians, either directly or through any other country. Our nation made a promise to stand by Afghans who risked their lives and their families’ safety to stand by U.S. service members. This mass deportation – potentially to their deaths – is a violation of that promise and our moral obligations to the Afghan community who stood alongside our troops.

As you know, Afghanistan remains an extremely dangerous country, and particularly deadly for the people who supported the U.S. government and troops. The U.S. State Department lists Afghanistan as a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” list and where many of those on the flight are likely to be persecuted, tortured, or even killed. Afghans who helped U.S. forces and who were left during the speedy evacuation have gone into hiding, been targeted for persecution and in some cases killed. Their assistance to U.S. troops puts a target on these individuals and their families to this day.

Dissidents, LGBTQ persons, and many others who do not “conform” to the Taliban’s extremely restrictive rules have been subject to torture, detention, and extrajudicial killings. For women, Afghanistan is the most repressive country in the world; not only are girls and women excluded from education and public life, but many have been detained and beaten by authorities for “morality crimes.” Women have been subjected to rape and other sexual violence by the Taliban and other authorities, including as punishment for exercising their rights to press speech or as “discipline” by a husband. LGBTQ people in Afghanistan, where their status is largely criminalized, are routinely targeted for abuse and sexual violence, and their families are also targeted and persecuted by the Taliban. We have heard that there could be women and LGBTQ persons on this flight; if they are deported to Afghanistan, they will face extreme danger.

We are similarly shocked to receive reports that this administration may also deport several Iranians – including women, Christian converts, and pro-democracy activists – to Iran, where they face imprisonment, torture, and in some cases, a possible death sentence. The United States has not ceased its military operations against Iran, and sending people who sought protection from the Islamic Republic of Iran back to a war zone and a repressive regime is unconscionable.

In the U.S. State Department’s last human rights report on Iran, in 2024, it recorded: “The government executed hundreds of prisoners, including many who confessed under torture and faced unfair trials. There were new cases of violent enforcement of women’s dress code restrictions. While some political prisoners, including persons detained in connection with protests related to the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, were released from prison, other participants in the protests were arrested, sentenced to prison and death, subjected to torture, or executed during the year. Restrictions on religious freedom were severe during the year. ” President Trump has himself warned about the dangers faced by pro-democracy and anti-government protestors, including women, in Iran, and sending these individuals to Iran would expose them to significant harm.

Sending dozens of people back to one of the most dangerous countries on earth, and where they are likely to be targeted for their or their family’s suspected support of the U.S. government or criticism of the Taliban, is a death sentence. Our country made a promise never to abandon the Afghans who sacrificed their own and their family’s safety to stand with American service members.

The United States is also bound not to return anyone to a country where they would face torture, and that obligation does not disappear because a flight makes a stop along the way. It is the policy of the United States not to effect the involuntary return of any person to a country where there are substantial grounds for believing they would be in danger of being subjected to torture.

The New York Times has reported that the plan is to fly Afghans from Louisiana to Pakistan. We also urge you to make clear to the Government of Pakistan that the United States will not accept its participation in sending these individuals onward to the Taliban. Under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act and Executive Order 13818, the United States may impose sanctions on foreign persons who are responsible for, complicit in, or materially assist serious human rights abuse. Officials who help deliver people to torture or death should expect us to press for exactly those sanctions, and for a full accounting of their role.

We urge your agencies to cancel any plans for deportation flights to Iran or Afghanistan so that this administration is not complicit in horrendous human rights abuses. These people came to the U.S. because they believed in its promise of democracy, religious freedom, and liberty. We must uphold those values and commitments, not abandon people to autocratic regimes.

We request a response to this letter by November 2nd and expect your assurances that these flights will not proceed.

Sincerely,

title: Warner, Kaine Announce $8.8 Million in Federal Funding to Improve Rail Crossing Safety Across Virginia
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Sens. Mark R. Warner and Tim Kaine (both D-VA) announced $8,810,502 in federal funding for four projects to improve railroad crossing safety, reduce traffic delays, and strengthen the movement of people and goods across Virginia. The funding was made possible by the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which the senators helped negotiate and pass.

“Safe and reliable rail transportation is essential to keeping Virginia families, businesses, and our economy moving,” said the senators. “These federal investments will improve safety at railroad crossings, cut down on traffic delays, and help goods travel more efficiently across the Commonwealth. We’re thrilled to see the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law continuing to deliver for Virginia communities.”

The funding will support the following projects:

$3,520,000 for the Portlock Road Grade Separation Project in Chesapeake to support final design work for the elimination of a railroad crossing along the Norfolk Southern rail corridor. The project will improve safety for drivers and pedestrians, reduce delays for emergency responders, and help freight move more efficiently to and from the Port of Virginia.

$2,000,000 for the U.S. Route 15 Railroad Overpass Improvements Project in Haymarket to support environmental review and preliminary engineering for a future grade separation at a highway-rail grade crossing at U.S. Route 15 and the Norfolk Southern B-line. The project will eliminate a crossing frequently blocked by trains, reducing traffic delays, improving emergency response times, and enhancing safety along a key commuter and freight corridor.

$1,719,342 for the Hampton Roads Transportation Planning Organization Grade Crossing Project in Chesapeake to support planning and safety evaluations of approximately 35 public highway-rail grade crossings along a major freight corridor serving the Port of Virginia. The project will identify opportunities to eliminate or separate crossings and improve safety technology in coordination with Norfolk Southern Railway and the Norfolk & Portsmouth Belt Line Railroad, as well as reduce traffic disruptions, strengthen access for emergency responders, and support freight movement through one of the nation’s busiest port complexes.

$1,571,160 for the Spotsylvania County Rail Safety Corridor Project to support final design work for safety improvements at three highway-rail grade crossings along the Richmond, Fredericksburg, and Potomac rail Corridor. Planned improvements include separating Landsdowne Road from the railroad, upgrading warning devices at Mine Road, and installing active warning devices at Benchmark Road to reduce the risk of collisions and improve safety for motorists.

This funding was awarded through the Department of Transportation’s Railroad Crossing Elimination (Crossing Safety) Grant Program, which supports projects to eliminate dangerous rail crossings, improve transportation safety, reduce traffic delays, and strengthen the movement of people and goods. Each project will also be supported by a 20 percent non-federal cost share from local or regional partners.

Sens. Warner and Kaine have secured hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding to modernize Virginia’s transportation infrastructure. Earlier this month, the senators announced $3.6 million to modernize the Shenandoah Valley Railroad. In August, the senators announced more than $17 million in federal funding for passenger rail improvement projects across Virginia, and in July, the senators announced more than $76 million for Virginia transportation infrastructure projects. Many of the investments were made possible by the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, a transformative investment in American infrastructure needs.

###

title: Warner, Kaine Statement on New Report Showing Effects of Infrastructure Law’s Expiration on Virginia
text:
WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Sens. Mark R. Warner and Tim Kaine (both D-VA) issued the following statement after a new report from the Senate Commerce Committee showed the effect that President Donald Trump’s refusal to work to reauthorize the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law—which Warner and Kaine helped negotiate and pass in 2021—will have on infrastructure projects throughout Virginia:

“Infrastructure should be an area in which both parties can find common ground, and as a matter of fact, we did: in 2021, we helped get the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law passed. But so far, the Trump-Vance Administration has refused to work in a bipartisan way to reauthorize that landmark legislation, meaning Virginia is facing millions of dollars in cuts to crucial infrastructure projects. Trump’s tariff policies and war of choice with Iran have sent prices for everything from building materials to gasoline through the roof—the last thing anyone needs now is for job-creating, economy-boosting infrastructure projects to dry up. Trump and the GOP can either come to the table and work with Democrats on reauthorizing this historic legislation, or infrastructure will join the long list of broken promises from the Trump-Vance Administration.”

According to the report from the Senate Commerce Committee, the expiration of the BIL will lead to more than 50 infrastructure projects in Virginia going unfunded, including 16 freight and rail projects and 40 roadway projects. The BIL has been delivering for Virginia, much like it has for the rest of the country, with nearly 100 transportation projects receiving funding from fiscal years 2022­–2026. The legislation must be reauthorized by December 11, 2026, or cuts to these programs may become permanent.

The full report can be found here, with Virginia-specific data available here.

title: Warnock, Ossoff Secure Over $12 Million in Federal Funding to Repair Roadways Damaged by Natural Disasters
text:
Senators Reverend Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff successfully secured over $12 million in federal funding from the Department of Transportation to repair and reconstruct roads damaged by natural disasters across Georgia

The funding is provided through the Federal Highway Administration Emergency Relief Program

The funding will support critical roadway repairs across Georgia, including in the Chattahoochee and Oconee National Forests, following damage caused by Hurricane Helene, Hurricane Rafael, and severe ice storms

Senator Reverend Warnock: “This federal funding will help repair roads damaged by these storms and make sure Georgians can safely get where they need to go”

Washington D.C. — U.S. Senators Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA) and Jon Ossoff (D-GA) secured over $12 million in federal funding to repair and reconstruct roads damaged by natural disasters across Georgia. The funding, provided through the U.S. Department of Transportation’s (DOT) Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) Emergency Relief Program, will support roadway repairs across Georgia, including in the Chattahoochee and Oconee National Forests, following damage caused by Hurricane Helene, Hurricane Rafael, and severe ice storms.

“Communities across our state have been through a lot in the wake of these devastating storms, and for many, the work of rebuilding is far from over,” said Senator Warnock. “This federal funding will help repair roads damaged by these storms and make sure Georgians can safely get where they need to go.”

“Bringing Republicans and Democrats together, we are delivering these resources to help improve Georgia’s roads and highways that were impacted after Hurricane Helene and other storms,” said Senator Ossoff.

The funding includes $8.9 million to repair roadways and drainage structures in the Chattahoochee and Oconee National Forests that were heavily damaged during severe ice storms earlier this year. The funding package also includes $2.3 million to address widespread damage to traffic signals, roadways, signs and sign structures that were impacted by Hurricane Helene. Nearly $841,000 will support communities in South and East Georgia where Hurricane Rafael caused several rivers to overflow their banks, flooding roadways, damaging culverts and causing washouts.

Senator Warnock has remained focused on securing critical disaster relief funding for Georgia communities recovering from devastating storms. Since Hurricane Helene made landfall in September 2024, he has secured over $2.2 billion in federal disaster relief for Georgia communities to support recovery efforts. Earlier this year, Senator Warnock successfully secured over $54 million in federal DOT funding to improve Georgia’s roadway infrastructure and help strengthen road safety for bicyclists, pedestrians, and drivers.

title: Welch, Min Demand Answers from Former Trump Attorney Alina Habba-Mildon on Influence over President’s Pardon of Corrupt Venezuelan Banker Julio Herrera Velutini
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, and U.S. Representative Dave Min (D-CA-47), Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and Chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ Anti-Corruption Task Force, are demanding answers from former Senior Adviser to the Attorney General Alina Mildon on her reported role in President Trump’s decision to grant Julio Herrera Velutini—who pleaded guilty to violating U.S. campaign finance laws—a full presidential pardon. The letters come as President Trump criticized his former attorney’s $50 million agreement with Mr. Herrera as “totally obnoxious and outrageous,” and “not acceptable.”

In their letters, the lawmakers express concern that the timing of Ms. Habba-Mildon’s hiring and Mr. Herrera’s daughter’s contribution to MAGA Inc. raise questions about whether improper considerations, including quid pro quo or “pay-to-play” dynamics, may have affected President Trump’s decision to pardon him. These letters are part of a broader bicameral investigation led by Senator Welch and Representative Min into potential corruption surrounding President Trump’s decisions to grant presidential pardons.

The lawmakers write: “Article II, Section 2, Clause 1 of the U.S. Constitution authorizes the President to ‘grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offenses against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment.’ The U.S. Supreme Court has characterized executive clemency as ‘an act of grace’ exercised for the ‘public welfare.’ President Trump’s use of this authority appears to deviate from this traditional purpose. Congress has a compelling interest in ensuring that the constitutional pardon power is exercised with fairness and transparency. Given these circumstances, we are seeking additional information to better understand the extent to which influence and access may have overridden the standard pardon review process.”

In August 2022, Mr. Herrera was criminally charged with providing $300,000 to a super political action committee (PAC) in violation of a campaign finance law barring contributions or donations by foreign nationals to U.S. federal, state, or local elections. Mr. Herrera financially supported the reelection campaign of Puerto Rico’s governor in exchange for her pledge to remove a top banking regulator who had scrutinized one of Mr. Herrera’s banks.

According to public reporting, Ms. Mildon entered into an employment agreement with Mr. Herrera’s family in late 2025, while she was serving as an adviser at the Justice Department. She also previously served as President Trump’s personal lawyer and as the Acting U.S. Attorney for New Jersey. In the hiring contract, Mr. Velutini’s family agreed to pay her $50 million over four years to be general counsel at Concord Partners, a company set up by Mr. Velutini’s daughter days before she signed the contract. Ms. Mildon finalized the deal with Concord Partners while she was still serving at the Justice Department.

Ms. Mildon then began working for Concord Partners on January 1, 2026, while serving as a senior adviser to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, overseeing U.S. attorneys. Two weeks later, Mr. Herrera received a pardon on January 15, 2026. Since President Trump’s election in November 2024, his 27-year-old daughter, a self-employed financial consultant, also donated $3.5 million to MAGA Inc., a Trump-supporting super PAC.

Read and download the lawmakers’ full letters to Alina Habba-Mildon and Julio Herrera Velutini.

In May, Senator Welch and Rep. Min sent letters to 17 individuals who received pardons or commutations under circumstances that warrant further congressional scrutiny, including several individuals connected to major fraud schemes, financial crimes, and high-profile political or financial relationships tied to President Trump and his associates. The earlier letters sought information regarding the clemency process, including whether financial contributions, lobbyists, intermediaries, or personal connections played a role in securing presidential clemency.

Among the individuals who received letters are convicted fraudsters, political fundraisers, corporate executives, and wealthy donors, such as Changpeng Zhao, whose cases have generated public reporting suggesting unusual access to Trump’s network of political allies and associates, direct lobbying efforts, large political donations, or other concerning connections surrounding their clemency requests.

The lawmakers continued their investigation in June, sending four additional letters to the Department of Justice’s Office of the Pardon Attorney, the White House Office of Records Management, the White House Pardon Czar, and the United States Secret Service. In October, the lawmakers initiated a probe into the influence of cabinet members, U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin, in Trump’s decision to pardon convicted felons.

###

title: Whitehouse, NAM Convene Roundtable with RI Manufacturing, Labor, and Business Leaders to Support Permitting Reform
text:
Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act aims to unleash renewable energy, lower emissions and electricity costs, and fight climate change

Pawtucket, RI – Today, U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (EPW), and Jay Timmons, President of the National Association of Manufacturers (NAM), convened a roundtable with leaders from Rhode Island’s manufacturing, labor, and business communities to discuss Whitehouse’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The roundtable followed a tour of the Cooley Group’s manufacturing facility in Pawtucket.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will deliver cheaper energy, more well-paying jobs, and responsible growth by accelerating the permitting and construction of critical energy and infrastructure projects while maintaining key environmental and historic preservation safeguards. The bipartisan legislation would bolster Rhode Island’s growing blue economy and clean energy industry, create loads of well-paying local union jobs, and build a more flexible energy grid that Rhode Island businesses and communities can rely on. BAAJA has received support from a broad national coalition of labor leaders, energy producers, and nonprofits.

“Rhode Islanders want lower energy bills and more well-paying union jobs. Passing this bipartisan bill will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy, make sure data centers start paying their fair share, and provide regulatory certainty to small businesses. A cleaner, safer, more abundant, and less expensive energy future awaits us on the other side of this permitting bill,” said Whitehouse, Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee. “The Trump administration must now end their mischief and show some real regulatory good faith to unlock the votes necessary to seal this deal.”

“Senator Whitehouse’s leadership in crafting and advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a breakthrough for manufacturing in America. He understands that manufacturers need certainty to build, grow and invest — and that once a permit is issued, a project should be able to move forward without years of unnecessary delays. Our broken permitting system costs manufacturers nearly $8 billion annually — resources we’d much rather spend on ribbon cuttings than red tape. Thanks to Senator Whitehouse’s leadership, we have a real opportunity to modernize this outdated system, unleash investment and create good-paying jobs while maintaining strong environmental protections and meaningful community engagement. Manufacturers are grateful for his unwavering commitment, and we’re proud to stand with him to get this bipartisan legislation across the finish line,” said Jay Timmons, President & CEO, National Association of Manufacturers.

The legislation was negotiated by Whitehouse along with U.S. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Chairman of the EPW Committee; Mike Lee (R-UT), Chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; and Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Ranking Member of the ENR Committee. It was unveiled late last month.

“The Cooley Team was pleased to welcome Senator Whitehouse to our Pawtucket operation and thanks NAM for bringing together this important discussion on permitting reform and the future of American manufacturing. Growth, job creation, and environmental stewardship can and should advance together. With leaders like the Senator championing bipartisan reform, we can encourage investment and hiring, expand access to affordable, reliable, cleaner energy, and maintain strong environmental protections,” said Dan Dwight, President & CEO, Cooley Group and NAM Executive Committee Member.

“We need Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act right away. There is no time to lose when it comes to passing a bill of this magnitude to create good union jobs and lower families’ energy bills,” said Michael F. Sabitoni, General Secretary-Treasurer of the Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA). “This legislation is an example of what leaders in Washington can accomplish when they set differences aside to work across the aisle and improve the lives of working men and women across the country.”

“The only way we are truly create a cleaner and greener economic future is to build new renewable energy infrastructure. We can no longer be held back by a permitting regime designed to thwart that development. The Rhode Island labor movement is leading on climate, and this proposal goes a long way towards helping Rhode Island meet its Act on Climate goals,” said Patrick Crowley, President, RI AFL-CIO.

“For U.S. manufacturers, access to reliable, affordable energy is essential to remaining competitive, creating jobs, and driving economic growth. This bipartisan permitting reform legislation represents one of the most significant efforts in decades to eliminate unnecessary regulatory barriers, modernize our electric grid, expand energy supply, and accelerate critical infrastructure investments. We commend Senator Sheldon Whitehouse for his leadership in advancing reforms that will strengthen grid reliability, help reduce energy costs, and ensure American manufacturers have the energy infrastructure necessary to innovate, grow, and compete globally,” said Melissa Travis, President & CEO, Rhode Island Manufacturers Association (RIMA).

“For Rhode Island businesses, time is money – and lengthy and unpredictable permitting processes can stall a project or send it to another state entirely,” said Liz Catucci, executive director for The Partnership for Rhode Island. “The Partnership supports the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 because faster, more reliable permitting will help Rhode Island compete for the infrastructure and energy investments that create good-paying jobs here. We’re grateful for Senator Whitehouse’s leadership and willingness to work across the aisle on an issue that directly affects our businesses.”

“An outdated permitting process is holding up economic development in Rhode Island. Modernizing that system will help streamline energy, manufacturing, and infrastructure projects, bolster local small businesses, and create new jobs,” said Laurie White, President of the Greater Providence Chamber of Commerce. “I applaud the leadership of Senator Whitehouse and his bipartisan negotiating partners, and Congress should immediately prioritize passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.”

The bipartisan legislation provides greater certainty for projects that have already been permitted and financed, including by preventing future administrations from arbitrarily blocking entire classes of energy projects, while establishing clear timelines for environmental reviews and legal challenges. It also includes targeted reforms to expand and modernize the electric grid, speed the development of geothermal and other energy projects, and ensure that rapidly growing data centers pay the full cost of their associated transmission needs rather than passing those costs on to families and small businesses.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would:

Build more transmission, faster by strengthening the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC) “backstop” siting authority — giving the federal government stronger authority to approve power lines when a state rejects or does not act upon an application – and allowing applications for large lines to be processed simultaneously with state reviews, helping needed projects move through permitting faster.

Get more energy onto the grid by:

Requiring regional and interregional transmission planning that accounts for where new transmission is needed.

Requiring advanced transmission technologies, such as advanced conductors and grid-enhancing technologies, which make better use of the grid we already have.

Requiring coordinated generation interconnection and transmission planning – which is not happening in most areas of the country – and using computing technologies to evaluate requests to connect new energy projects to the grid, reducing the cost and speeding up the process of bringing new generation onto our grid.

Mandating that transmission planning organizations (RTOs and ISOs) allow aggregations of distributed energy resources to operate as virtual power plants and participate in wholesale electricity markets, helping meet growing demand with more available supply.

Requiring BLM to complete geothermal drilling permits and authorizations in 60 days and exempting low disturbance exploration and development activities from additional environmental reviews.

Force data centers pay their fair share by requiring data centers, and not American families and small businesses, to pay for their cost of service and upgrades to the transmission network; right now, data centers are only required to pay for service or upgrades, not both.

Create jobs across the energy supply chain by boosting the build out ofmore transmission, clean energy, supply manufacturing, and other grid infrastructure.

Create greater certainty for projects permitted and financed across administrations by prohibiting any administration from delaying or blocking permitting of a class of energy projects – meaning no administration can block all solar, wind, or other class of energy project permits without facing legal action and fines.

Set clear deadlines for environmental reviews — including a two-year deadline for Environmental Impact Statement reviews and a one-year deadline for Environmental Assessment reviews, with consequences for agencies that miss those deadlines. That means environmental reviews still happen, but not indefinitely.

Establish a new National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) consultation process that runs alongside National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) reviews with a defined time limit, securing a statutory role for Tribes in determining how projects affect historic and cultural resources and protecting Tribes’ rights to formally consult during the processes — two things the Section 106 reforms attempted to eliminate.

Limit the types of impacts that projects are required to mitigate, creating clearer boundaries around which effects a project must mitigate or minimize.

Set clear limitations on when and how a project may be legally challenged.

Sets a 150-day deadline for legal challenges under the Clean Water Act (CWA), Endangered Species Act (ESA), NEPA, and NHPA.

Generally limits who can bring a legal challenge to people or groups that participated in the relevant comment period or Tribal consultation process.

Limits when a court can temporarily stop a project from moving forward, while preserving the existing ability to seek that relief under the Administrative Procedures Act.

Allow states to handle endangered species consultations when they have the capacity to do so. States with the demonstrated staffing, expertise, and resource capacity to take over certain wildlife-related consultations are permitted to do so.

Clarify the limits on state water-quality reviews by limiting state certifications to water pollution directly caused by a specific source for gas pipelines and transmission lines and prohibiting use of the process to address unrelated issues.

Prevent the federal government from changing the rules after the fact for certain wetlands and waterways by stopping EPA from preemptively or retroactively removing areas of land from the federal water-quality certification process.

Fund a first-of-its-kind Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund, providing a mandatory funding source dedicated to cleaning up abandoned hardrock mines.

The bill text is available here.

title: Wicker Pushes Legislation to Advance Mississippi Maritime Research
text:
Washington – U.S. Senator Roger Wicker, R-Miss., is pushing legislation to protect maritime research initiatives at Mississippi universities.

Senator Wicker recently introduced the Cooperative Institute Act of 2026, bipartisan legislation that would codify and modernize the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) research partnerships at colleges and universities across the country. These cooperative institutes aid NOAA in its mission to forecast floods and hurricanes, protect fish and wildlife, and preserve coastlines.

Currently, NOAA supports 17 cooperative institutes at more than 80 universities and research institutions across the country. Senator Wicker’s bill seeks to enhance these programs by establishing eligibility and selection criteria, strengthening congressional oversight, and providing a clear statutory framework.

This legislation is co-sponsored by U.S. Senators Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and John Hickenlooper, D-Colo.

“For coastal states like Mississippi, maritime research is crucial to our economy and security. The scientific data will support our fisheries and mitigate the devastating impacts of perilous hurricanes,” said Senator Wicker. “The Cooperative Institute Act of 2026 would bolster partnerships among NOAA and outstanding academic institutions, such as Mississippi State, the University of Southern Mississippi, and Jackson State University. Their collaboration has borne great fruit for the Magnolia State and beyond.”

“The Cooperative Institute Act will create greater certainty for NOAA and the wonderful universities, like Mississippi State and Southern Miss, in understanding, protecting, and harnessing our natural resources,” said Senator Hyde-Smith. “We want to ensure that the Northern Gulf Institute and the Cooperative Institute for Fostering Aquaculture Research and Markets, which benefit Coastal Mississippi, can continue to benefit our nation and grow to meet future challenges and opportunities. This bipartisan legislation is national in scope, which should help generate broad support in Congress.”

NOAA’s Partnerships with Mississippi Universities:

Mississippi State University, the University of Southern Mississippi, and Jackson State University have all partnered with NOAA.

In September, NOAA chose Mississippi State to host a new cooperative institute that will serve as an asset for researchers conducting studies in the Northern Gulf. This program aims to build upon the school’s 20 years of success in leading NOAA’s Northern Gulf Institute.

In June, Southern Miss joined the Cooperative Institute Fostering Aquaculture Research and Markets (CIFARM), a NOAA cooperative institute dedicated to aquaculture that promotes seafood production. The university also participates in NOAA’s Ocean Exploration Cooperative Institute (OECI).

At Jackson State University, NOAA’s OECI supports an internship program that gives students a hands-on opportunity to explore their interest in oceanic studies. The university will also participate in the newly established cooperative institute dedicated to research in the Northern Gulf.

If passed, this legislation will establish a permanent framework for these initiatives, providing long-term stability for those conducting this research.

“Mississippi State University is proud to lead this next chapter of NOAA research in the Gulf, building on 20 years of partnership and collaboration through the Northern Gulf Institute. This new cooperative institute will harness expertise from across the region to advance science and technology that strengthen our coastal communities, protect critical resources and support economic growth. We are especially grateful to Senator Roger Wicker and Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith for their leadership and continued commitment to NOAA’s cooperative institutes and to the world-class research capabilities that exist here in Mississippi,” said Dr. Scott Willard, Interim Vice President for Research and Economic Development.

“Over the past two decades, Southern Miss has participated in four NOAA Cooperative Institutes, giving us a firsthand view of the power of these partnerships. By bringing together NOAA scientists and university researchers, Cooperative Institutes help turn agency priorities into innovation, discovery, and real-world solutions. As NOAA’s needs evolve, this model provides the flexibility and expertise needed to address challenges from the deepest parts of the ocean to the farthest reaches of the atmosphere,” said Dr. Kelly Lucas, Vice President for Research at the University of Southern Mississippi.

“Through supporting maritime research, we are supporting the Mississippi economy,” said Dr. Denise Jones Gregory, President of Jackson State University. “Being part of such meaningful work is a great opportunity for our research faculty and students, and I appreciate Dr. Brent Thoma and the JSU Division of Research and Economic Development for leading our participation in this collaborative effort.”

Senator Wicker’s Record on Maritime Research:

Senator Wicker has been a champion for maritime research, development, and exploration along the coast of Mississippi throughout his time in the Senate. As part of the fiscal year 2027 appropriations cycle, Senator Wicker is fighting to secure federal resources to support storm and weather tracking at the National Data Buoy Center. He is also working to deliver funding for a research vessel for Southern Miss.

Earlier this Congress, Senator Wicker introduced the Integrated Ocean Observation System Reauthorization Act that would maintain funding for NOAA’s ocean observation research projects. This legislation passed the Commerce Committee and now heads to the Senate floor.

In 2018, the senator introduced and worked to pass the Commercial Engagement Through Ocean Technology (CENOTE) Act. This legislation expanded NOAA’s ability to use unmanned maritime systems to explore uncharted waters, collect data, and improve weather tracking.

title: Wicker Reports $22 Million for Mississippi Infrastructure Upgrades
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Roger Wicker, R-Miss., welcomed a series of federal grants that will bring more than $22 million in funding to Mississippi to advance infrastructure improvement projects across the state.

The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) awarded funding for three local governments to support the removal of several at-grade crossings, which adversely affect traffic flows and road safety. These grants stem from the Rail Crossing Elimination Program created under the bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), of which Senator Wicker was the lead Republican negotiator.

“Eliminating rail grade crossings will allow Mississippians to commute to and from work with fewer disruptions and dangers,” said Senator Wicker. “Each of these grants will empower local communities to improve traffic patterns without having to bear the full cost of these projects.”

Pike County Board of Supervisors: $4,000,000 to grade separate a rail crossing at Metro-Pike Industrial Park to carry U.S. Highway 51 over a Canadian National Railroad industrial spur in the county

City of Hattiesburg: $2,489,608 to support the development of future grade separations within the city

George County Board of Supervisors: $1,300,000 to study the possible grade separation or elimination of two railroad crossings

In addition, the DOT awarded funding for six road safety projects across the state under the Safe Streets and Roads for All grant program. This program was also established through the bipartisan infrastructure law of 2021.

“This funding provides local governments and universities with resources to carry out thoughtfully designed projects that will improve safety for drivers and pedestrians alike,” said Senator Wicker. “For Mississippi to continue to grow, we must have dependable infrastructure that can accommodate our residents and attract new business.”

Town of Byhalia (Marshall County): $200,000 to support planning activities for a corridor safety study on MS 309

City of Biloxi (Harrison County): $600,000 to construct continuous sidewalk and pedestrian safety improvements along the south side of Pass Road from McDonnell Avenue to west of Tara Lane

City of Columbus (Lowndes County): $4,664,741 to implement the Fifth Street Corridor Safety Enhancement Project along 5th Street from Main Street to 5th Avenue North and at six intersections in downtown Columbus
