title: Boston Globe: Katherine Clark will be the first woman majority leader of the House. Here’s what to know about her rise.
text:
Election Night saw plenty of history making across the country, and some milestones are still to be set.

With Democrats taking the US House, Massachusetts’ own Katherine Clark is poised to become the next House majority leader — the first woman ever to hold the role.

The progressive lawmaker has been on the rise over the last decade or so. As second-in-command, the Revere Democrat will hold an important leadership role under Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who’s expected to be elected as the first Black House Speaker when the new Congressional term starts in January.

Here are a few things to know about Clark, and the position of majority leader.

She was first elected in 2013

Clark was first elected to Congress in a special election to fill Ed Markey’s House seat after voters elected him to the Senate. (He just won a third Senate term Tuesday.) At the time, she was serving in Massachusetts’ state Senate.

Clark’s ascent in national politics has looked almost effortless. She was elected as vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus in 2018, moving up to the assistant speaker position in 2020. In 2022, she ran unopposed for the Democratic Whip, becoming only the second woman to hold the title after former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

But as the Globe reported in 2022, the congresswoman spent months quietly securing support before running for her party’s second-in-command slot.

“I never contemplated politics as a career for myself,” Clark told the Globe in 2022. “My interest in politics really came out of working very closely with the state Legislature and watching how important those decisions were to the families that they impacted.”

The ‘silent assassin’

Clark has built a reputation among her colleagues for being tough, caring, and unafraid to approach the other side of the aisle.

While on the midterm campaign trail in Ohio, US Representative Marcy Kaptur said Clark would return “a sense of order” to the House if Democrats took the majority. Fellow Ohio Democrat, US Representative Emilia Sykes, told Politico earlier this month that Clark knew how to “push” her colleagues “to where you need them to be or not need them to be, and you only get that from getting to know people well.”

As the party’s No. 2, Clark is charged with maintaining communication between Democratic leadership and its members, and rallying lawmakers behind key legislation even in face of intra-party divides.

Those duties will be critical in the next Democratic-led House, which will be built of progressives, moderates, and a few members who identify as Democratic socialists.

“This isn’t going to be my-way-or-the-highway from any one given group,” Clark told Politico when speaking about the possibility of a Democratic majority. “We’re not always going to agree. People disagree with calls I make as the whip all the time, but the point is to understand the caucus, pull us together on those common values and threads.”

Colleagues of Clark have told the Globe in previous years that the Democratic Whip has a nickname among some in the House — the “silent assassin.”

“My takeaway is don’t mess with Katherine Clark,” California Representative Pete Aguilar told the Globe in 2022.

Second-in-command to Jeffries

As majority leader, Clark will be tasked with scheduling legislation for floor consideration, setting weekly agendas, and pushing Democrats’ priorities forward.

The second-in-command of the House does not serve on standing committees or typically lead floor debates. But Clark will be essential to building winning coalitions to pass key legislation and will act as a spokesperson for House Democrats next term.

In an interview with WBUR published Wednesday, Clark said among her short-term goals for Democrats was to “restore the cuts that the Republican Party has done.”

“Their so-called One Big Beautiful Bill that has just ravaged families and has made life so hard,” Clark said. “So we’re talking about putting back Medicaid cuts, Medicare, veterans’ benefits and food programs across this country.”

When asked about potentially becoming the first woman to serve as House majority leader, Clark called it “an incredible privilege and honor.”

“And it is the voices of moms that I’ve met … the hope that they have that they can still hopefully build a better future,” Clark said. “Those are the voices that I’m going to bring to the leadership table with me, and that is the opportunity that the American voters have given us in this new Congress, the 120th Congress.”

—

title: Cambridge Day: ‘Blue wave’ makes Clark likely majority leader in House
text:
During Tuesday’s much-anticipated midterm elections, West Coast polls were just starting to close when media outlets like CNN and NBC began to project control of the U.S. House of Representatives would flip to Democrats. While final counts are still pending, eyes have already begun to turn to January’s leadership elections within the party, in which current House Minority Whip Katherine Clark is poised to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader.

Clark represents Massachusetts’ 5th Congressional District, which covers most of the western half of Cambridge and stretches from Winthrop to Framingham. She ran unopposed in this year’s general election, winning her eighth term.

Clark has held some form of elected office in Massachusetts for a quarter of a century. She launched her political career when she was elected to the Melrose School Committee in 2001, then served in the state House and Senate before claiming the U.S. House seat left vacant when then-Rep. Ed Markey ran for U.S. Senate in 2012. She climbed the ranks of House leadership, and served as assistant speaker of the House of Representatives from 2021-2023 alongside then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi (the assistant speaker role no longer exists due to a restructuring of party leadership following the 2022 midterms).

She’s not the only Democratic leader expected to make history, as Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D.-N.Y., will likely become the first Black speaker of the House.

For this year’s midterms, Clark has modeled a disciplined message focused on affordability that has been a winning recipe for Democrats in purple districts. Near-term priorities of hers include improving oversight of the Trump administration and bringing a swift end to the war with Iran.

As results showed Democrats retaining seats in districts Republicans redrew to improve their electoral prospects in states such as Florida, Clark told NPR “It’s all good news for the American people,” she said. “We are on the road to a very solid majority.”

—

title: WaPo: Democratic women surge past 100 House seats as Republican women lose ground
text:
Women will lead more states as governors and represent more congressional districts than at any time in American history come January.

The blue wave putting Democrats back in control of Congress is also creating a House Democratic caucus that looks much more like the nation, in terms of gender, than ever before. Democratic women’s gains also widen a significant gap between the number of Democratic women and Republican women in power.

For the first time, next year, more than 100 Democratic women will serve in the U.S. House, according to Associated Press race calls and a tally by the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University.

With dozens of races still uncalled Wednesday morning, Democratic women had already locked up at least 102 seats. And Democratic women were leading in more than a dozen other races.

“That kind of representation, seeing us move over that 100-woman mark — it matters,” House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Massachusetts) said, speaking at a coffeehouse in Kissimmee, Florida, days before the election. “I think that’s important for people to be able to look at Congress and see themselves reflected back.”

Democratic women had also won more than six times as many seats as Republican women, who had claimed 16. Four more Republican women were ahead in races not yet decided. If those leads hold, Republican women’s presence in the House would shrink from 30 seats to 20.

If the current leads hold, women would make up about 30 percent of the House, though the chamber would still fall short of fully reflecting a country that is about 51 percent female.

Fifteen women won governor’s races Tuesday, and a 16th, Democrat Cindy Holscher in Kansas, was narrowly ahead in a race that had not been called. Among the winners was Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, who will be the first Black woman governor in U.S. history.

It was a night of firsts. In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton will become the first woman elected governor of Ohio. In New Mexico, Democrat Deb Haaland will be the nation’s first Native American woman governor. Democrat Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor of Texas.

“A lot of Latinas in Texas grew up hearing ‘No te dejes’” — which translates to “don’t let yourself be pushed around” — “from their own mothers and abuelas,” Hinojosa said in her victory speech. “This year, we lived them, and we changed this state.”

Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R) was elected Tuesday as Tennessee’s first woman governor. And two female Republican governors, Kelly Ayotte in New Hampshire and Sarah Huckabee Sanders in Arkansas, won reelection.

In 1985, the two parties had about the same number of women in the House: 12 Democrats and 11 Republicans. That’s when Emily’s List, a group that trains, endorses and fundraises for Democratic women who support abortion rights, was founded. Democrats such as Rep. Lori Trahan (Massachusetts) credit such groups and other political infrastructure created to support women for the gains since then.

“You have to be really intentional about making progress like that,” said Trahan, who came to the House in 2019 as part of a class that Clark, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s vice chair for recruitment at the time, helped recruit.

Clark, a seven-term Democrat, is positioned to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader. It is not a glass ceiling as high as the one Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-California) broke nearly 20 years ago when she became the first woman speaker, but it is a sign of the pipeline of Democratic women ascending Washington’s ranks of power.

Tuesday’s historic numbers come 10 years after Hillary Clinton’s loss to Donald Trump. Clinton’s defeat in the 2016 presidential election, in some ways, built this wave.

In the two years before that election, about 900 women contacted Emily’s List about running for office; by the end of 2017, more than 25,000 had, according to the group. The surge showed up in 2018, when a record 36 women were newly elected to House seats. Three members of that class will lead states in January: Abigail Spanberger and Mikie Sherrill, who won the Virginia and New Jersey governorships last year, and Haaland.

No woman has yet won the presidency, and Kamala Harris’s 2024 loss to Trump revived quiet doubts among some Democrats about whether women can win, NBC News reported last year. Sherrill said then that she heard those doubts from party insiders.

Rep. Kat Cammack (Florida), chairwoman of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said she is not surprised that gains among Republican women in recent decades have been far more meager compared with Democratic women. Plenty of barriers still hold them back, she said.

Women with children often are questioned about running for office while parenting, she said, and female candidates get labeled “a certain way” when fundraising with the “exact same amount of aggressiveness” as men.

“The fact remains that within the GOP we have to do a better job of recruiting women,” Cammack said. “We are looking at people’s résumés rather than the person themselves and how they match up to the district, and that has been a consistent struggle.”

The Florida congresswoman said she has witnessed many instances in which a Republican woman who had maybe served as a mayor, a sheriff, a business leader or a “titan” in her community was overlooked by the GOP “because the guy standing next to her could self-fund the race, and he gets all the institutional support.”

House Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain (Michigan), the highest-ranking woman in the House GOP, sees the issue differently. Asked about the party’s struggle to build a pipeline for female candidates, she said in a statement that the GOP is the “only party that can identify what a woman is,” a reference to the debate over transgender rights.

“Moreover, we are the only party that believes in issues women care about: protecting girls’ sports, defending parental rights, and helping hardworking families keep more of their money,” she said.

Democrats are planning a variety of bills to advance issues of particular importance to many women, such as child care and maternal health, Clark said.

Clark, for one, has long championed making child care more affordable.

“Most parents make decisions around child care, but we know the majority of that burden falls on women,” she said.

Even with a new Senate majority, it may be difficult for Democrats to notch legislative wins under President Donald Trump, who can veto their bills.

Still, some Democratic women said they remain optimistic about being able to strike deals with Republicans on these issues.

“If you think about these issues, especially around caregiving, whether it is child care, caring for our disabled loved ones or caring for our elders … those issues don’t discriminate by party affiliation,” said Rep. Marilyn Strickland (D-Washington).

Cammack agreed. She has championed bipartisan legislation that serves women, including two measures that mandated clean, private lactation spaces in airports and federal buildings.

“If we have people that are wanting to work towards the goal of better care and accessibility without it actually hurting people in the long run, I think there’s room for us to come together,” she said.

—

title: WBUR: Rep. Clark, poised to become House Majority Leader, talks priorities as Democrats take Congress
text:
Massachusetts Congresswoman Katherine Clark, the second most powerful House Democrat, is poised to help lead a sizable Democratic majority next session. Clark ran uncontested in the general election and is returning to the House for her eighth term. She joined WBUR’s Morning Edition to discuss the road ahead for her party.

Below are highlights from their conversation, which have been lightly edited.

Interview Highlights

On her top short-term goal for next year, when Democrats take control of the House…

“Restore the cuts. Restore the cuts that the Republican Party has done. Their so-called One Big Beautiful Bill that has just ravaged families and has made life so hard. So we’re talking about putting back Medicaid cuts, Medicare, veterans’ benefits and food programs across this country.

“And as I traveled around the district, and Massachusetts, and to districts throughout the country, it was the pain of people who just simply cannot afford the basics, and they are the ones that we’re going to govern for. So we’re going to do quick things, small things, and also start to work on big transformative policies, but all focused on making sure that we are fighting for those families who feel like they are drowning in this cost of living crisis.”

On California Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia’s warning to the Trump family that they should ‘lawyer up’…

“There were three planks that we ran on and connected with the American people: lower costs; healthcare that every family can afford and can find where they live when they need it; and holding the crooks accountable. And that is going to mean looking at this administration, looking at what they have done to profit personally – Trump and his family, and other figures in the administration – all at the cost of the taxpayer.”

On whether investigating the Trump administration is a misread of voters’ directive…

“I can tell you that what we have seen across the country is that voters understand, and we saw this happen last night, that corruption is tied to the cost of living. And that when people are getting enriched, when we have a system where Donald Trump came in, took away a trillion dollars from people’s healthcare, all to benefit the very wealthy, who then turned around and poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the midterms in the hopes to save it. It’s a pay-for-play scheme.”

On whether Democrats will impeach Trump…

“It is a tool on the table, but we are focused on what gives the American people the fastest relief. And we’re not taking any tool off the table, but we are going to hold people accountable and bring down that cost of living, and that is tied to corruption and the war that Donald Trump has recklessly gotten us into.”

On the prospect of becoming the first woman to serve as House Majority Leader…

“It is an incredible privilege and honor, and I’m so grateful that my district has sent me back to Congress, back to represent them. And the thought of being the first woman majority leader I see as not only something I really never dreamed of, but what a responsibility.

“And it is the voices of moms that I’ve met, of women across this country and across the commonwealth who haunt me, and the sacrifices they are making to feed their children, to try and get a pediatrician appointment, the hope that they have that they can still hopefully build a better future.

“Those are the voices that I’m going to bring to the leadership table with me, and that is the opportunity that the American voters have given us in this new Congress, the 120th Congress. And it’s one that I intend to deliver for families in this country and set an agenda for legislation that is focused on them.”

—

title: WGBH: Katherine Clark poised to become first-ever woman House Majority Leader
text:
The “blue wave” of Democrats taking the majority in both chambers of Congress could make soon make Rep. Katherine Clark one of the most powerful people in Washington.

Clark, who ran uncontested in her reelection bid in District 5 and is currently the House Democratic Whip, is poised to likely become House Majority Leader. She would be the first woman to have that role.

Speaking after the Democrats’ sweeping victories, Clark talked about the stories of everyday Americans who have struggled with high costs.

“Their stories are what are going to propel us forward,” Clark said. “And we are proud of the Democrats who have won tonight. But we are so proud when we are gonna be able, on January 3, to get to work for them.”

Peter Ubertaccio, a political scientist at Stonehill College, said Clark’s chances of becoming majority leader are about as excellent as one could imagine.

“When your party is as successful as it was last night, there’s no real reason for party members to consider dispensing with their leadership,” he said.

Ubertaccio said Clark has developed a reputation around her thoughtfulness, attentiveness and organizational skills. And while it’s not automatic that Clark gets the role, he said there’s every reason to believe that Democrats will line up behind her and other party leaders after the performance in the midterm elections.

“It’s pretty rare to see popular leaders like Katherine Clark seriously challenged for [a] leadership position,” Ubertaccio said.

If she gets the role, Clark would be second to only the Speaker of the House, a role likely to be filled by current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries. Ubertaccio said the skills Clark has honed as Whip would help her, although she would be taking on a much more expansive role.

But he said the next two years will be a challenge for Democrats in both the House and Senate, with President Donald Trump already gearing up to use his veto power.

“Her challenge is twofold: Keep your caucus together and that is always a challenge … But then do so when the president is of a different party,” Ubertaccio said. “And so the compromises that you may have to make in order to get a president to not veto a bill, if that’s the goal, is going to test the allegiance of your party members.”

Erin O’Brien, political scientist at UMass Boston, said being number two in the majority party comes with much more control than being in the minority. And she pointed out that having a person in such a high-ranking position could bode well for Massachusetts.

“There’s a lot of national players in Massachusetts politics, and Katherine Clark has quietly ascended to an important role,” she said.

—

title: Rep. Mullin’s Statement on Democrats Winning House Majority
text:
The American people have spoken loud and clear: they want leaders who will fight to lower costs, protect access to affordable health care, root out corruption, and defend human rights.

Trump and Republicans’ destructive policies have caused immense pain and suffering across the country. While that damage will not be undone overnight, we can begin to rebuild through hard work, accountability, and a renewed commitment to putting the needs of the American people first.

I am grateful for the trust my constituents have once again placed in me and I look forward to welcoming a new freshman class. As we prepare to be in the House majority next year, I am committed to continuing to advance an agenda to put families over billionaires, end foreign wars, and hold the Trump Administration accountable for its rampant corruption.

title: REP LIEU STATEMENT ON BEING RE-ELECTED TO THE U.S. HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Ted W. Lieu (D-Los Angeles County) issued the following statement after being re-elected to serve California’s 36th congressional district in the U.S. House of Representatives for the 120th Congress.

“Today, I want to express my deepest gratitude to the residents of California’s 36th congressional district for once again placing their trust in me to represent them in Congress. Serving our beautiful community is truly the honor of my lifetime. I am incredibly grateful to my family, whose support means everything to me.

“But the work is just beginning. Democrats will enter the new Congress ready to fight for American families. The American people have spoken and have emphatically repudiated the MAGA agenda of trump and Republicans.

“With a united House and Senate, Democrats will focus on bringing down costs. We will work to reverse trump and Republicans’ reckless tariffs, end their illegal war in Iran, and undo their cruel cuts to health care and food assistance. We will also hold the trump administration accountable for its corruption, abuses of power, and blatant violations of the law. We will advance an affirmative agenda that safeguards election integrity, reinforces states’ ability to prepare for and respond to natural disasters, and puts reasonable guardrails on AI. We will treat our neighbors with respect and dignity, not division and contempt.

“I do not take this re-election, or the trust of my constituents, for granted. I promise to bring everything I have to the fight for an America that puts working families first.”

###

title: Ranking Member Lofgren Announces She Will Seek Chair of House Science Committee as Democrats Win Control of Congress
text:
(Washington, DC) — This morning, Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren (D-CA) made the following statement after Democrats secured the majority of the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm election:

“Yesterday, the American people chose stability over chaos,” said Ranking Member Lofgren. “They chose people and policies that will make not only their lives better, but the lives of future generations better. Americans chose science and reason. They’ve put their trust in Democrats and our ability to deliver on our promises.

She continued: “I will be seeking the Chair of the House Science Committee. First and foremost, as Chairwoman, I will work to put a stop to Trump’s politicization of science. We will hold this administration accountable for the damage they have done to the American scientific enterprise. The oversight and investigations work we’ve been doing for the past two years in the minority will continue. We have a lot of work to do, and we’ll be ready to hit the ground running come the start of the 120th Congress, with Democrats in control of the House and Senate.

“We will also set out to fix what Trump has broken. We’ll restore and advance support for our premiere science institutions and the dedicated people who work there. We will build protections for federal science and innovation programs so Trump-era corruption cannot happen again.

“The future is unfolding before us with groundbreaking technologies like AI, quantum, and fusion energy. We need to build responsible regulations for AI while also fostering innovation. We must invest holistically in quantum to meet emerging challenges for our competitiveness in this field. This administration’s climate denialism has set us back. We need to advance climate solutions now. Fusion, with its limitless, emission-free power, will help us achieve our clean energy future. Breakthrough after breakthrough in fusion energy science has been encouraging—and we need to match this momentum with federal support.

“The U.S. research ecosystem used to be the envy of the world. People brought their ideas and energy here—and our Nation reaped the rewards of that talent in discoveries and the resulting economic growth. That is now all at risk. I will stop at nothing to earn back the trust of our allies across the globe, end the brain drain, restore scientific integrity across our agencies, and reaffirm our leadership in science. The American people deserve no less.”

title: Rep. Nancy Mace Congratulates Nancy LaCore on SC-01 Victory
text:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (Nov. 4, 2026) – Congresswoman Nancy Mace today issued the following statement congratulating Congresswoman-elect Nancy LaCore on her victory in South Carolina's First Congressional District:

“Congratulations to Congresswoman-elect Nancy LaCore on her win last night, and to all of South Carolina’s newly elected officials.

“Serving the people of South Carolina is a tremendous responsibility. I wish each of them success as they begin this next chapter of public service.

“Our office is committed to ensuring a smooth transition because serving our constituents comes FIRST. Anyone who needs help can reach us anytime at mace.house.gov/constituentservices.

“It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve South Carolina. I will continue to work hard for the Lowcountry until my very last day.”

###

title: Congressman Morgan McGarvey on 1 Year Commemoration of UPS Plane Crash in Louisville
text:
Louisville, KY (November 4, 2026) – Congressman Morgan McGarvey released the following statement one year after the tragic UPS plane crash that took the lives of fifteen people and injured dozens of Louisvillians near Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport:

“Today, a year after the devastating plane crash in Louisville, we continue to mourn those we lost, hold their loved ones close in our hearts, and express our gratitude for the hard and incredible work of our first responders. On this especially painful day, our strength lies in our ability to support each other, grieve together, and rebuild as a community.”

###

Congressman Morgan McGarvey represents Kentucky’s Third Congressional District, including Louisville and Jefferson County. He serves on the House Veterans Affairs, Small Business, and Budget Committees.

title: Griffith Announces $2 Million ARC Grant for Regional Workforce Development
text:
The Appalachian Regional Commission (ARC) has awarded the New River/Mount Rogers Workforce Development Area Consortium, whose board is based in Radford, Virginia, a $2,000,000 grant for workforce development. The funding will support the training of 450 individuals and help 75 businesses access a developed workforce and/or related services.

In response to this grant notice, U.S. Congressman Morgan Griffith (R-VA) issued the following statement:

“A strengthened workforce in Southwest Virginia produces better opportunity.

“This ARC grant for $2 million helps the New River/Mount Rogers Workforce Development Area Consortium develop a talent pool that benefits growth in our regional workforce and local economy.”

BACKGROUND

Project “POWERing Pathways: Advancing Southwest Virginia’s Workforce” will expand access to training programs for roughly 450 people. These opportunities will serve businesses and employees throughout Bland, Carroll, Floyd, Giles, Grayson, Montgomery, Pulaski, Smyth, Washington and Wythe Counties. The talent pool in the Cities of Bristol, Galax and Radford will also receive support.

ARC will collaborate with community partners and advance relationships in high-demand employment sectors related to health care, manufacturing and skilled trades.

###

title: Rep. Panetta’s Statement on His 2026 Reelection
text:
Monterey, CA – United States Representative Jimmy Panetta (CA-19) released the following statement on the results of his 2026 reelection:

“I am deeply honored and humbled that the people of California’s 19th Congressional District again elected me to represent them in the United States Congress. My work in Congress has always been guided by the principle that good governing is good politics. Tonight’s overwhelming results reaffirm that belief, bolster my work, and strengthen my commitment to delivering for the people that I proudly serve.

“Over the past two years, the division and dysfunction in Washington could lead many across the nation to be disillusioned and disengage from the responsibilities of living in our democracy. However, tonight’s results demonstrate that Americans don’t cower during dark times. Instead, we face our challenges, stand together, and embrace our obligations through the democratic process of voting. By giving us robust Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, the American voters also gave us a mandate to govern in the 120th Congress.

“With our agency, we must now set the agenda and provide answers for Americans when it comes to the issues of affordability and accountability. Living up to our Constitutional responsibilities and our system of checks and balances, we will legislate to bring down the cost of living, and, at the same time, we will investigate any and all misdeeds by this Administration. I look forward to upholding my Constitutional oath through my service in the 120th Congress, my willingness to work with anybody who helps me govern, and my will to fight anybody who threatens our democratic values.”

###

title: Pelosi Statement on California’s 11th Congressional District Election
text:
San Francisco — Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi issued this statement on the results of the election for California’s 11th Congressional District:

“Connie Chan brought courage, conviction and a deep love for San Francisco to this campaign. As a working mom, a public servant, and an immigrant, she gave voice to families whose struggles she knows firsthand. I was proud to support her, and I am so proud of the campaign she ran.

“To Connie and the volunteers, workers and community leaders who stood with her: your work matters beyond this election. The people you brought together and the voices you lifted up will continue to strengthen our city. San Francisco needs your organizing, your advocacy and your determination to build a better future.

“I congratulate Scott Wiener on his election to the Congress. Representing San Francisco is an extraordinary honor and a profound responsibility. My office stands ready to assist in the transition, and I wish him success in service for the people of our city.

“For nearly four decades, San Franciscans have entrusted me with the privilege of being their voice in the House. My gratitude is boundless, and my confidence in our City’s future remains strong. Our work for a fairer, more just America continues.”

title: Pelosi Statement on Historic Election of More Than 100 Democratic Women to the House
text:
San Francisco — Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi issued this statement on the election of more than 100 Democratic women to the House of Representatives:

“Today, House Democrats made history on many fronts. One milestone fills me with particular joy and pride: the election of more than 100 Democratic women to the House of Representatives.

“This victory reflects the extraordinary quality of our women candidates and a deliberate commitment to their success. Leader Hakeem Jeffries and DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene joined with the Democratic Women’s Caucus, Elect Democratic Women, our partners in Labor and women’s organizations to recruit, support and elect outstanding women. Together, they turned opportunity into victory.

“Electing Democratic women has been my passion since I first came to Congress in 1987, when there were only twelve of us. We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power — and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward. California has been especially generous, with our Ultimate Women’s Power lunches and events in the North and South helping women win across the country.

“The impact of women in Congress is measured in the progress we have delivered: better healthcare, greater economic opportunity, stronger protections for our rights and a brighter future for our children. With more than 100 Democratic women bringing their experience, courage and determination to the House, even greater progress is within reach.

“On a personal note, serving alongside women in positions of power has been one of the greatest honors of my public service — and one of its greatest joys. We have worked hard, won consequential fights and had a great deal of fun along the way. Above all, we have proved what is possible when women have the opportunity to lead. These extraordinary women will now write the next chapter. When women succeed, America succeeds!”

title: Congressman Carter Celebrates Historic Elections Powered by Voters of Color
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Troy A. Carter, Sr. (D-LA), released the following statement regarding the midterm results from November, 3, 2026:

“We’ve just witnessed a historic election night. A blue wave reached across this country powered by Black voters and other voters of color, including in places some people thought were too red to change. The American people spoke, and they entrusted Democrats with majorities in both the House and the Senate by wide margins.

“Here in Louisiana, I’m deeply grateful that the people of the Second District have placed their trust in me again. As I enter my fourth term in Congress, I do so with new responsibilities and challenges. I will continue to lead with humility and honor and fully understanding that, for whom much is given, much is required.

“Now, it’s time to get to work. We have a duty to defend the right to vote and hold this administration accountable. We must also answer the questions families are asking at their kitchen tables: Can I afford my prescriptions? Can my children afford a place to live? Will my paycheck get me through the month? Those questions will still be there when the celebrations are over. I stand ready with my Democratic and Republican colleagues next Congress to answer them.”

###

title: Rep. Watson Coleman Statement on Election Results
text:
Congresswoman Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12) made the following statement regarding Tuesday night's election results:

Last night, voters here in Central Jersey and around the country sent a clear message:

We reject hate and division. We stand with our neighbors. We reject a violent, reckless foreign policy. We demand an economy where if you work hard, you can do well. Where the economy works for working people, not just the billionaires.

It has been one of the great honors of my life to serve you these past 12 years. When I was elected, I was the first Black woman to represent New Jersey in Congress.

Last night, the 12th District carries on that legacy, breaking another barrier and sending the first Muslim to Congress in state history. And so, it is my distinct honor to pass the torch to Dr. Adam Hamawy, the next Congressman from New Jersey’s 12th District.

title: America Has the Energy. Permitting Reform Can Help Make It Affordable.
text:
America Has the Energy. Permitting Reform Can Help Make It Affordable.

HOW THE BAAJA WILL LOWER ENERGY COSTS AND PROTECT RATEPAYERS

America has the energy resources to meet growing demand. But permitting bottlenecks delay the pipelines, power plants, and transmission lines needed to deliver them—constraining supply and raising costs. The bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act addresses both challenges: make it easier to build affordable energy infrastructure and protect existing customers from costs driven by major new electricity users.

THE PROBLEM WITH THE STATUS QUO

New England illustrates the consequences of not building. Although the United States is the world’s largest natural gas producer, pipeline constraints limit access to nearby Pennsylvania gas. During a January 2026 cold snap, oil overtook natural gas as the region’s leading source of electricity. When affordable fuel cannot reach consumers, more expensive alternatives fill the gap.

The costs extend nationwide. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce estimates that permitting delays are holding up as much as $1.5 trillion in critical infrastructure investment. Meanwhile, research commissioned by the Corporate Energy Buyers Association finds that restricting new wind and solar development could add $121.2 billion to U.S. energy expenses from 2027 through 2033. Whether the obstacle is a pipeline or a power line, limiting supply means fewer options and higher costs.

HOW THE BIPARTISAN BILL HELPS

The bill addresses both the cost of building infrastructure and who pays for it. As the Bipartisan Policy Center explains, it would streamline pipelines and transmission development, accelerate connections for new generation and storage, and expand capacity on the existing grid. Faster construction and more available supply can reduce costs. The bill would also require covered data centers to pay infrastructure costs attributable to their expansion rather than shifting those costs onto existing customers.

Research points to substantial savings:

The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates that achieving the bill’s envisioned two-year environmental-review deadline could reduce annual household electricity bills by 178–251.

The Rhodium Group projects 50–78 in annual household electricity bill savings by 2040 from the bipartisan bill’s transmission, pipeline, and data-center provisions.

Resources for the Future estimates more than $350 billion in cumulative electricity-system savings through 2050 from modeled provisions of the bill.

C2ES and Greenline Insights project roughly $19 billion in residential savings through 2040 from comparable transmission and interconnection reforms.

While the studies examine different provisions and scenarios, they point in the same direction: building infrastructure faster and using the grid more efficiently can lower electricity costs.

WHO SUPPORTS IT — AND WHY

The affordability case spans industries and energy sources. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce argues that modernizing permitting can unlock investment and lower everyday costs. Enbridge CEO Greg Ebel put it simply: “If we can’t build it, we can’t afford it.” Corporate Energy Buyers Association CEO Rich Powell called for “the low-cost, reliable power” Americans need. Advanced Energy United CEO Heather O’Neill says reform can “tamp down energy costs,” while Solar Energy Industries Association CEO Tim Pawlenty anticipates “downward pressure on energy prices.”

Utilities agree. “Permitting reform is not a partisan issue. It is an affordability issue,” said American Gas Association CEO Karen Harbert. The American Public Power Association and National Rural Electric Cooperative Association have endorsed the bill, with APPA CEO Scott Corwin emphasizing the need to “keep electricity affordable” while maintaining reliability.

Support also crosses ideological lines. Club for Growth President David McIntosh sees a path to “lowering energy costs for families and businesses.” Inclusive Abundance Action President Derek Kaufman calls for “more power, built faster, at a price people can afford.” The Climate Leadership Council stresses building fast enough to meet demand, while Natural Allies’ Susan Waller sees a “generational opportunity to make energy more affordable.” The American Consumer Institute’s Kristen Walker warns that the status quo is “actively undermining affordability and reliability.”

Organized labor is making the same argument. LIUNA General President Brent Booker says the bill will “lower energy costs for all Americans.” Operating Engineers General President John Downey highlights putting skilled workers to work while “making energy more affordable and reliable for American families.” United Association General President Mark McManus likewise emphasizes delivering “reliable and affordable energy to American communities.”

title: Baldwin Joins Bipartisan Group Demanding Trump Admin Rescind Proposed Census Rule That Violates Constitution
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) and a bipartisan group of her colleagues are urging the U.S. Census Bureau to rescind a proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from census counts and eliminate questions on race and ethnicity.

In their letter, the Senators warn that excluding non-citizens violates the Constitution, which expressly says that the census must count the “whole number of persons in each state.” The Bureau has proposed two methods for excluding non-citizens, both of which would cause undercounts and errors in the census counts. Undercounting people in the census threatens funding for public education, infrastructure, and other essential services for states.

“We write to urge that you rescind your proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from decennial census counts and omit questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census. The proposed rule violates the clear meaning of the Constitution, which requires that the Census Bureau count the ‘whole number of persons in each state.’ The proposed rule would also cause communities across the country to be counted inaccurately, jeopardizing their fair representation in Congress and access to billions of federal dollars for education, health care, and public safety services,” Baldwin and the Senators wrote.

The letter also describes how the Bureau’s proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions would undermine the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws and would degrade the quality of all census data. The compliance of civil and voting rights laws rely on demographic data, and only the decennial census provides accurate and precise data. Additionally, eliminating the collection of race and ethnicity data from the decennial census undermines other federal survey data. Businesses and local governments that depend on such data have said that they would be harmed by this proposed rule.

“In its attempt to undermine the data used for the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws, the Bureau will degrade the accuracy of all other federal survey data, particularly for small and rural geographic areas. The Bureau writes in its own regulatory filing that the proposed rule ‘deteriorates the accuracy’ of ‘fertility/mortality rates, cancer rates, poverty rates, unemployment rates, [and] labor force participation’ because the Bureau relies on accurate decennial census information to adjust and design other survey estimates,” the Senators continued. “The Bureau also admits in its filing that the proposal would hamper the usability of data for state and local governments who rely on precise and accurate population estimates for small geographic areas. Businesses and local governments that depend on reliable and complete federal data have warned that the Census Bureau’s proposal would increase costs as data is degraded.”

Senator Baldwin has long fought to ensure every Wisconsinite is counted and that communities across the state receive their fair share of federal resources. In 2019, during the first Trump Administration, Baldwin criticized the administration for pursuing a question on citizenship and threatening to delay the census. And in 2020, she opposed the Administration's proposal to shorten the census counting period, warning that the change could undermine the accuracy of the census and leave communities undercounted.

The letter was led by Senators Gary Peters (D-MI) and Andy Kim (D-NJ) and cosigned by 23 other Senate colleagues.

Full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Under Secretary Meyer and Deputy Under Secretary Cook,

We write to urge that you rescind your proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from decennial census counts and omit questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census (Fed. Reg. Vol. 91, No. 57524, Thursday September 10, 2026). The proposed rule violates the clear meaning of the Constitution, which requires that the Census Bureau count the “whole number of persons in each state.” The proposed rule would also cause communities across the country to be counted inaccurately, jeopardizing their fair representation in Congress and access to billions of federal dollars for education, health care, and public safety services. The proposed rule would also undermine the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws by eliminating the only appropriate data used for compliance. We request that you rescind this proposed rule to ensure the decennial census complies with the Constitution and allows civil and voting rights laws to be enforced.

I. The Bureau’s Proposal to Exclude Certain Non-Citizens from Census Counts Violates the Constitution

The proposal to exclude certain non-citizens, including those who are legal immigrants, from apportionment counts violates the Constitution. The Fourteenth Amendment is clear: the Census Bureau must count the “whole number of persons in each state” in the United States, including non-citizens.

This interpretation of the Constitution has been accepted from the founding of our nation to the present, by our founders, courts, members of Congress, and leaders of the Census Bureau from both parties, including Secretary Howard Lutnick. In 1788, James Madison wrote in Federalist No. 54 that the apportionment was to be “founded on the aggregate number of inhabitants,” recognizing no distinctions among types of persons to be counted except for those explicitly excluded in the text of the Constitution itself. During consideration of the Fourteenth Amendment, Congress debated and expressly rejected proposals to change the “persons” counted for apportionment to “voters” or “citizens.” During the first half of the twentieth century, Congress considered and rejected proposals to pass statutes to exclude non-citizens from apportionment counts on the basis that it would take a constitutional amendment to change the requirement. In 1929, the Senate’s Legislative Counsel concluded that excluding certain non-citizens from apportionment counts would be unconstitutional. In 1980, a court rejected a lawsuit seeking that the Bureau exclude certain non-citizens from apportionment counts. Even current Secretary of Commerce Lutnick testified to Congress in February that “citizenship is not in the Constitution for the [Census] apportionment... that is not a necessary factor”. This unbroken history of our reading of the Constitution, including courts, Congress, and Census Bureau leaders, is clear: the Census Bureau must count every person.

II. The Bureau’s Proposed Methods to Exclude Certain Non-Citizens Would Cause Undercounts and Errors in Census Counts

The Bureau has proposed two methods for carrying out its unconstitutional exclusion of certain non-citizens: directly asking every person detailed questions about their immigration status and relying on administrative records. Both proposed methods would cause undercounts of both citizens and non-citizens and errors in the population counts.

First, the Bureau proposes asking each person their legal immigration status so that it can exclude certain non-citizens, but such a question would cause both citizens and non-citizens to not answer the census. This would likely lead to undercounts and errors in census counts. The Bureau has never asked detailed questions about legal immigration status on any nationwide survey before, let alone the decennial census, because of concerns about privacy and accuracy. The Bureau’s own research before the 2020 Census showed that including even a question about citizenship status on the decennial census, itself a less complicated question than immigration status, would cause fewer citizens and non-citizens to complete the census. In addition, the Government Accountability Office previously found that if statistical agencies directly asked about immigration status, they would create invalid, imprecise, and inaccurate estimates. In 2006, the Government Accountability Office recommended that federal agencies should not pursue adding even indirect immigration questions to surveys, and the Census Bureau concurred with that recommendation.

In addition, the Bureau alternatively proposes relying on administrative records acquired from federal agencies, state and local governments, and private data brokers to exclude certain non-citizens from apportionment counts. This approach would also lead to undercounts and inappropriately exclude citizens and non-citizens from census totals. The Bureau previously found that if it relied solely on administrative records the decennial census would misestimate the total population by over 1.3 million people, overcounting non-citizens and undercounting citizens. It also found that relying on administrative records undercounted people in rural areas and group quarters, such as nursing homes and college campuses. The Treasury Department commented on a draft of this very rule warning that using tax records to identify people’s usual address would cause people to be counted in the wrong location. This evidence shows that both of the Bureau’s proposed methods to carry out this unconstitutional effort would cause errors and undercounts, denying people fair representation in Congress and jeopardizing the fair and full allocation of resources.

III. The Bureau’s Proposal to Omit Demographic Questions Would Undermine Enforcement of Civil and Voting Rights Laws and Degrade the Quality of All Census Data

We also express our strong opposition to the Bureau’s proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census, because it would harm the ability to enforce civil and voting rights laws and cause the quality of all census data to deteriorate. Only the decennial census provides the reliable demographic data necessary for compliance with civil and voting rights laws. Congress has made clear that decennial census data should be used to enforce these laws, and the Trump Administration even recognized the legal need to collect this data for enforcing civil rights laws when it published its planned questions for the 2020 Census.¹7

For example, Congress enacted the Fair Housing Act, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Public Health Service Act to ensure that individuals are not discriminated against on the basis of race or ethnicity in housing, employment, and health care, respectively. The Supreme Court has held that statistical evidence using census data can be used to demonstrate violations and ensure compliance with these laws. The Bureau admits in its own regulatory filing that no other federal survey that collects information about race and ethnicity, including the American Community Survey (ACS), can substitute for the decennial census, because other surveys like the ACS cannot create precise population estimates for areas smaller than 65,000 people. This means there is no real alternative for all Americans to bring claims under civil rights laws if the Bureau eliminates collecting information about race and ethnicity on the decennial census. Similarly, Congress enacted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act to prohibit voting practices or procedures that discriminate on the basis of race, including congressional redistricting. While the Supreme Court narrowed the standards to bring a claim under the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais, the Court maintained that the Voting Rights Act is violated “when the evidence supports a strong inference that the State intentionally drew its districts to afford minority voters less opportunity because of their race.” Such evidence requires the availability of decennial census data about race and ethnicity for enforcement, because the Voting Rights Act applies to even small political subdivisions where no other federal data is accurate.

The elimination of data about race and ethnicity would particularly undermine the federal government’s ability to meet its responsibilities and obligations to tribal governments. By eliminating the collection of information about American Indian and Alaska Native identity, the Bureau makes it effectively impossible for the government to administer the Indian Housing Block Grant program, the Indian Community Development Block Grant program, and the Indian Health Service – each of which depend on accurate estimates of American Indian and Alaska Native populations to plan and allocate funding. In its own regulatory filing, the Bureau admits that other federal surveys “may not be a suitable substitute for all federally recognized tribes,” because other surveys do not provide accurate and precise estimates of American Indian and Alaska Native populations. The Bureau previously told Congress that relying on alternative options to collect information about American Indian and Alaska Native populations, like asking about tribal enrollment or relying on administrative records, would cause inaccurate estimates and infringe on the private sovereign information of tribes.

In its attempt to undermine the data used for the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws, the Bureau will degrade the accuracy of all other federal survey data, particularly for small and rural geographic areas. The Bureau writes in its own regulatory filing that the proposed rule "deteriorates the accuracy” of “fertility/mortality rates, cancer rates, poverty rates, unemployment rates, [and] labor force participation” because the Bureau relies on accurate decennial census information to adjust and design other survey estimates. The Bureau also admits in its filing that the proposal would hamper the usability of data for state and local governments who rely on precise and accurate population estimates for small geographic areas. Businesses and local governments that depend on reliable and complete federal data have warned that the Census Bureau’s proposal would increase costs as data is degraded.

With these considerations in mind, we urge the Census Bureau to rescind its September 10 proposed regulation.

Sincerely,

###

title: Bennet, Durbin, Grassley Demand Trump Administration Swiftly Obligate Congressionally Appropriated Baltic Security Initiative Funding
text:
As Vladimir Putin intensifies aggression around the Baltic region, the Senators request the disbursement of funds by end of the year

Denver— Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, joined Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Senator Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), and other bipartisan colleagues on a letter to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging them to swiftly obligate Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Congressionally appropriated funds for the Baltic Security Initiative (BSI), which a Department of Defense program to bolster the defense capabilities of key U.S. allies Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.

“We write to follow up on Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Congressionally appropriated funds for the Baltic Security Initiative (BSI). Since 2021, the BSI has enhanced the defense capabilities and interoperability of our Baltic allies. We urge you to ensure the swift obligation of this funding and execution of programs considering intensified Russian aggression in the region against key frontline allies,” wrote the senators.

“In light of recent [Russian] airspace incursions, gray-zone tactics, and heightened nuclear warnings against the Baltics, accelerating the delivery of assistance under the BSI must be a priority. We urge disbursement by the end of the calendar year and ask that you provide an update on such plans no later than November 19, 2026,” concluded the senators.

Bennet helped codify the BSI and enhance regional planning as part of the FY26 National Defense Authorization Act, which also included several provisions supporting Ukraine. Bennet leads legislation in the Senate FY27 intelligence and defense bills, both of which have passed their respective committees, to bolster intelligence-sharing and drone cooperation with Ukraine.

Earlier this year, Bennet also joined Durbin and Grassley to introduce the Baltic Security Assessment Act, legislation requiring the Secretaries of State and Defense to report to Congress on emerging threats posed to the Baltics. This past spring, Bennet joined a bipartisan letter demanding that Secretary Hegseth immediately release stalled Ukraine funding and the BSI.

In addition to Bennet, Durbin, and Grassley, U.S. Senators Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), John Cornyn (R-Texas), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), and Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) signed the letter.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Secretary Hegseth and Secretary Rubio:

We write to follow up on Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Congressionally appropriated funds for the Baltic Security Initiative (BSI). Since 2021, the BSI has enhanced the defense capabilities and interoperability of our Baltic allies. We urge you to ensure the swift obligation of this funding and execution of programs considering intensified Russian aggression in the region against key frontline allies.

We welcome the BSI spend plan provided by the Department of Defense (DoD) on May 29, 2026, which targets investments in integrated defense, maritime security, irregular warfare, and other critical capabilities as required by statute. On September 15, a second update from DoD indicated that BSI was prioritized for notification and in its final stages of coordination, including with the Department of State. While this is important progress, escalating Russian threats, specifically against the Baltic States, demand more urgent U.S. security assistance. In light of recent airspace incursions, gray-zone tactics, and heightened nuclear warnings against the Baltics, accelerating the delivery of assistance under the BSI must be a priority. We urge disbursement by the end of the calendar year and ask that you provide an update on such plans no later than November 19, 2026.

Thank you for your attention to this important matter.

###

title: Bennet, Welch, Meeks, Colleagues Demand Answers from Musk on Ukraine Starlink Disruptions
text:
Ukraine relies on Starlink and its military-grade version to defend against Russian attacks on civilians

Denver — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, joined U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), House Foreign Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), and other bicameral colleagues on a letter demanding that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk explain what he and his company know about disruptions to Ukraine’s access to satellite communications provided by Starlink and Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink. Ukraine relies on both systems for its self-defense against Russian President Vladimir Putin’s unrelenting aggression.

In their letter, the lawmakers underscore that while Musk publicly asserted that limits to Starshield access are “decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” reporting indicates that Musk personally suggested that President Trump throttle Ukraine’s Starshield access. Musk himself said that he restricted Ukraine’s Starlink access.

“Since the failure of his ground invasion, Russian leader Vladimir Putin turned to a brutal air campaign targeting Ukrainian civilians to wear down public morale. Just last month, more than 300 Ukrainian civilians were killed and 2,000 injured by Russian drone and missile strikes. Ukraine has built an innovative network of drone systems to defend against the thousands of strikes launched each month by Russia. However, these life-saving systems often depend on Starlink’s military version, Starshield, for accurate communication and transmission of targeting data,” wrote the lawmakers.

“Last week on October 13, 2026, Ukrainian officials said that their forces suddenly lost access to Starshield communications inside Ukraine for drones moving over 100 miles per hour. That interruption halted Ukraine’s ability to guide its self-defense drones against incoming Russian missiles and drones and stopped Ukrainian attacks against Russian positions. That very night, Russia launched a record-setting coordinated drone and missile barrage at Ukrainian civilian energy infrastructure, using at least 39 ballistic and hypersonic missiles and 128 Shahed-type drones. The strikes killed at least three civilians, including a child, and injured at least 21,” continued the lawmakers.

“As a publicly traded company, SpaceX has a legal obligation to disclose to shareholders and the public material events that could affect your business model. The revelation that you personally wielded control over a foreign country’s military communications would require disclosure of elevated risks for corporate governance, geopolitical exposure, and potential adverse actions by foreign governments,” concluded the lawmakers.

The lawmakers requested answers to the following questions by October 31, 2026:

Have you or any SpaceX official at any point discussed limiting Starlink access for Ukrainian forces inside Russia or Ukraine with Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Trump, or any officials or representatives acting on their behalf? Please provide any such communications or records of communications.

Did you, SpaceX, or entities operating on SpaceX’s behalf reduce, shut off, or throttle Starlink access to Ukrainian forces this month—either inside Russia or Ukraine? If so, why and on whose orders?

Have you or any official at SpaceX communicated to Ukrainian officials any conditions or actions required for a full or partial resumption of Starlink access for Ukrainian defense forces?

Did President Trump or the White House, in fact, make a request to restore Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield systems? Have those systems been fully restored? If so, when? And if not, why not?

Which specific individuals, agencies, or entities control the operational decisions from this day forward on restoring full and non-capped access to Starlink and Starshield communications systems for Ukrainian forces?

Bennet continues to lead Congressional efforts to support the Ukrainian people’s fight against Putin’s aggression.

Upon news of the Starshield and Starlink disruptions, Bennet demanded that SpaceX restore full service. He also expressed his support for Congressional efforts to support the development of alternatives to SpaceX so that Elon Musk does not execute a veto over U.S. national security.

Bennet leads legislation in the FY27 Senate intelligence and defense bills, both of which have passed their respective committees, to bolster intelligence-sharing and drone cooperation with Ukraine. Bennet recently joined bipartisan colleagues to introduce and pass the Sanctioning Russia Act. He also sponsors legislation to impose sanctions on entities trading in Russian oil, to expose and punish Russia’s systematic persecution of religious communities in Ukraine, and to repurpose frozen Russian sovereign assets held in the United States to support Ukraine, building on legislation he co-sponsored that former President Joe Biden signed into law in April 2024. Earlier this year, Bennet led seven colleagues in a letter to Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent urging the Trump administration to crack down on a Russian state-backed cryptocurrency sanctions evasion network funding Putin’s war.

In addition to Bennet, Welch, and Meeks, Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the House Rules Committee Jim McGovern (D-Mass.), and Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) signed the letter.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Mr. Musk:

Your company’s Starlink communications system has been instrumental in allowing Ukraine to defend itself against Russian missile and drone attacks targeting civilians. Access to Starlink has recently been throttled or cut off entirely, without a clear explanation as to why.

Since the failure of his ground invasion, Russian leader Vladimir Putin turned to a brutal air campaign targeting Ukrainian civilians to wear down public morale. Just last month, more than 300 Ukrainian civilians were killed and 2,000 injured by Russian drone and missile strikes. Ukraine has built an innovative network of drone systems to defend against the thousands of strikes launched each month by Russia. However, these life-saving systems often depend on Starlink’s military version, Starshield, for accurate communication and transmission of targeting data.

Last week on October 13, 2026, Ukrainian officials said that their forces suddenly lost access to Starshield communications inside Ukraine for drones moving over 100 miles per hour. That interruption halted Ukraine’s ability to guide its self-defense drones against incoming Russian missiles and drones and stopped Ukrainian attacks against Russian positions. That very night, Russia launched a record-setting coordinated drone and missile barrage at Ukrainian civilian energy infrastructure, using at least 39 ballistic and hypersonic missiles and 128 Shahed-type drones. The strikes killed at least three civilians, including a child, and injured at least 21.

You have publicly asserted that limits to Starlink access are “decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.” Yet public reporting indicates that you personally brought the suggestion to President Trump to slow down Ukrainian communications through SpaceX’s Starlink systems, and U.S. government officials have reportedly indicated that you personally ordered the speed cap on Ukrainian military use of Starshield. Reports published yesterday indicate that President Trump called you to personally ask for restoration of Starshield capabilities and the President has asserted it was restored, and yet public reports indicate the system remains severely restricted for Ukraine’s defense forces.

As a publicly traded company, SpaceX has a legal obligation to disclose to shareholders and the public material events that could affect your business model. The revelation that you personally wielded control over a foreign country’s military communications would require disclosure of elevated risks for corporate governance, geopolitical exposure, and potential adverse actions by foreign governments. We therefore ask for your responses to the following by October 31, 2026:

Have you or any SpaceX official at any point discussed limiting Starlink access for Ukrainian forces inside Russia or Ukraine with Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Trump, or any officials or representatives acting on their behalf? Please provide any such communications or records of communications.

Did you, SpaceX, or entities operating on SpaceX’s behalf reduce, shut off, or throttle Starlink access to Ukrainian forces this month—either inside Russia or Ukraine? If so, why and on whose orders?

Have you or any official at SpaceX communicated to Ukrainian officials any conditions or actions required for a full or partial resumption of Starlink access for Ukrainian defense forces?

Did President Trump or the White House, in fact, make a request to restore Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield systems? Have those systems been fully restored? If so, when? And if not, why not?

Which specific individuals, agencies, or entities control the operational decisions from this day forward on restoring full and non-capped access to Starlink and Starshield communications systems for Ukrainian forces?

###
