title: Illinois And Midwestern Farmers Are Overcharged On Crop Insurance, Say Durbin, Duckworth, Budzinski, Sorensen, Call For USDA To Recalculate And Provide Refunds
text:
As farmers face sky-high costs, the lawmakers say USDA Risk Management Agency must rebalance premium costs and refund Illinois and Midwestern farmers

SPRINGFIELD – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), a member of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, and U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), along with U.S. Representatives Eric Sorensen (D-IL-17) and Nikki Budzinski (D-IL-13), both members of the House Agriculture Committee, today sent a letter to the Administrator of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Risk Management Agency, calling for a review of the Federal Crop Insurance Program to rebalance payments for farmers that are routinely overcharged for federal crop insurance premiums. While the Federal Crop Insurance Act requires crop insurance premiums to roughly equal the indemnity payouts over the long term, Illinois corn and soybean farmers have been systemically overcharged for crop insurance premiums as they rank among the lowest in the nation for crop insurance payouts.

“Farmers face record costs for farm inputs, including diesel, fertilizer, seed, and equipment. As policymakers explore options for relief, we ask USDA to begin a targeted review as soon as possible of the counties and crops that have consistently been overcharged in the Federal Crop Insurance Program, and to accordingly reduce those crop insurance premiums,” the lawmakers wrote. “We also request that once an adjustment has been made, that USDA consider refunds to those farmers for the current crop year, and make the full correction at once to avoid prolonging this overcharging.”

As the lawmakers note, Illinois and Midwestern corn and soybean farmers have been overcharged by the Federal Crop Insurance Program as their long-term loss ratios are far below the target 1.0 loss ratio for the program. This has been documented by the University of Illinois in analyses from 2023, 2024, and two additional reports this year. New analysis from North Dakota State University (NDSU) requested by Durbin in August has shown that 10 Midwestern states, including Illinois, have long-term loss ratios far below 0.80, which means that for every dollar that Midwestern farmers have paid in premiums, less than 80 cents have gone back to them in indemnities over time. An adjustment in the Federal Crop Insurance Program to account for Midwestern farmers’ low loss ratios would provide an 11 percent decrease in premium costs for Midwestern farmers, including a 22 percent decrease for corn and a 19 percent reduction for soybeans.

The lawmakers urged USDA to immediately review the premiums rates to stop Illinois and Midwestern farmers from paying unnecessarily high costs for such a critical program.

“USDA has the authority to undertake this review and adjustment…While the USDA Risk Management Agency (RMA) reviews premium rates on a rotating schedule across crops, this process has not been enough to prevent this significant overcharging of Illinois and Midwestern corn and soybean farmers,” the lawmakers wrote.

They continued: “As most farm groups have repeatedly said, crop insurance is the most important risk management tool. Farmers appreciated USDA’s decision to delay the due date for premiums this year to give farmers temporary relief. Yet, the real issue within crop insurance affordability and cash flow, is that farmers of certain crops and farmers in certain regions are being systemically overcharged.”

The lawmakers concluded their letter by underscoring that the Trump Administration’s short-sighted trade policies and war of choice in Iran have pushed farming costs sky-high, putting undue economic stress on farmers. Durbin, Duckworth, Sorensen, and Budzinski make clear that this adjustment to the Federal Crop Insurance Program would deliver critical, and deserved, relief to Midwestern farmers.

“Farmers are facing the prospect of future years of economic harm. There is a major drop in agricultural export demand due to tariffs and international conflicts. On-farm diesel costs are up by 80% over the past year, more than the on-the-road diesel prices at the pump. USDA’s own September Farm Sector Income Forecast shows that the aggregate cost of production is up $21.2 billion to nearly $493 billion,” the lawmakers wrote.

“We urge you to help farmers confronting this affordability crisis by addressing this long-standing issue of better aligning crop insurance premiums with risk, which would have the effect of cutting premium costs for thousands of farmers,” the lawmakers concluded their letter.

A copy of the letter can be found here and below:

November 6, 2026

Dear Administrator Swanson:

Farmers face record costs for farm inputs, including diesel, fertilizer, seed, and equipment. As policymakers explore options for relief, we ask USDA to begin a targeted review as soon as possible of the counties and crops that have consistently been overcharged in the Federal Crop Insurance Program, and to accordingly reduce those crop insurance premiums. We also request that once an adjustment has been made, that USDA consider refunds to those farmers for the current crop year, and make the full correction at once to avoid prolonging this overcharging.

USDA is required by law to target a 1.0 loss ratio for federal crop insurance, which means total insurance premiums should roughly equal indemnity payouts over the long-term. Unfortunately, this has not been the case for Illinois and Midwestern corn and soybean farmers, who are systematically overcharged for crop insurance premiums and have been for years. This has been substantially documented by several economic reports by the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Another recent analysis from North Dakota State University (NDSU) again shows that 10 Midwestern states have long-term loss ratios far below 0.80, which means that for every dollar that Midwestern farmers paid in premiums, less than 80 cents has gone back to them in indemnities over time. An NDSU simulation to bring these extremely low loss ratios closer to 0.80—still below the target of 1.0—and starting with the lowest counties first, would cut what farmers are being overcharged by $762 million per year, including more than $10 million in each of the 12 Midwestern states. A USDA adjustment of this nature would provide an 11% decrease in premium costs for Midwestern farmers, including a 22% decrease for corn and a 19% reduction for soybeans.

USDA has the authority to undertake this review and adjustment. Section 508(i) of the Federal Crop Insurance Act directs the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation to periodically review its rating methodologies, analyze rating and loss history by area, and adjust premium rates it determines are excessive for an agricultural commodity in an area. While the USDA Risk Management Agency (RMA) reviews premium rates on a rotating schedule across crops, this process has not been enough to prevent this significant overcharging of Illinois and Midwestern corn and soybean farmers.

As most farm groups have repeatedly said, crop insurance is the most important risk management tool. Farmers appreciated USDA’s decision to delay the due date for premiums this year to give farmers temporary relief. Yet, the real issue within crop insurance affordability and cash flow, is that farmers of certain crops and farmers in certain regions are being systematically overcharged.

Farmers are facing the prospect of future years of economic harm. There is a major drop in agricultural export demand due to tariffs and international conflicts. On-farm diesel costs are up by 80% over the past year, more than the on-the-road diesel prices at the pump. USDA’s own September Farm Sector Income Forecast shows that the aggregate cost of production is up $21.2 billion to nearly $493 billion. Analysis by the American Farm Bureau Federation found, despite increased prices for some commodities, that farmers are expected to operate below breakeven and could potentially be underwater into the 2027 crop year as the disruptions continue.

We urge you to help farmers confronting this affordability crisis by addressing this long-standing issue of better aligning crop insurance premiums with risk, which would have the effect of cutting premium costs for thousands of farmers. Thank you for your consideration of this request.

-30-

title: Fetterman Tours City of Washington’s Flood Prone Areas
text:
WASHINGTON, PA – Today, U.S. Senator John Fetterman (D-PA) visited the City of Washington to tour flood prone areas due to the Chartiers Creek and met with JoJo Burgess, Mayor of Washington, Demond Nixon, Mayor of East Washington, and other city officials. The group discussed further action and how the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ resource opportunities can help the City.

“I’m proud to stand by the City of Washington and the Borough of East Washington so that we can find solutions to address the flooding from Chartiers Creek. We need to use every lever of the federal government to protect people and property as flooding continues to impact the area,” said Senator Fetterman. “I applaud this joint effort and look forward to working together to turn the conclusions of this study into a reality on the ground.”

The City of Washington has dealt with flooding from the Chartiers Creek for decades and each year becoming more drastic. The US Army Corps of Engineers flood study will focus on the entirety of the Chartiers Creek watershed which runs through Washington and Allegheny Counties to the Ohio River. The study is 100% federally funded and is expected to be completed in 2028, with additional project funding to be approved by Congress. Senator Fetterman has identified resources for the City of Washington, including funding from the Army Corps and FEMA.

title: Fetterman Tours Erie Air Traffic Control Tower
text:
ERIE, PA – Today, U.S. Senator John Fetterman (D-PA) met with union representatives from the National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) and leaders at the Erie International Airport’s Air Traffic Control Tower to discuss tower operations, staffing and training, controller pay, working conditions, and upcoming technology and infrastructure improvements at Erie International Airport.

“Air traffic controllers have high pressure jobs with absolutely zero room for error. We need to recognize the importance of their work by investing in our airspace and giving them the resources and support they need,” said Senator Fetterman. “I’m deeply grateful for the opportunity to hear from our air traffic controllers and union members at Erie Tower and learn more about all they do to keep Northwestern Pennsylvania’s skies safe.”

NATCA is the primary labor union representing 20,000 aviation safety professionals, including air traffic controllers, nationwide. The organization advocates for aviation safety, adequate staffing, workforce protections, and national modernization of air traffic control infrastructure.

As a member of the Senate Commerce Committee’s Subcommittee on Aviation, Space, and Innovation, Senator Fetterman is committed to aviation safety. During the 119th Congress, he joined his colleagues in unanimously passing the ROTOR Act to strengthen aviation safety technology standards. In September, he also joined his colleagues in passing U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth’s (D-IL) Aviation Medication Transparency Act and U.S. Senator John Hoeven’s (R-ND) John A. Hauser Mental Health in Aviation Act to improve Federal Aviation Administration medication guidelines and mental health access for air traffic controllers, respectively.

title: Gallego joins TMZ, Grills Elon Musk and Calls on Him to Testify
text:
WASHINGTON — Yesterday, Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) joined TMZ’s Jacob Wasserman to chat about the senator’s call to subpoena Elon Musk after he kneecapped Ukraine in their war against Russia when he limited their critical access to the military version of Starlink, Starshield. In the wake of that decision, civilians were killed.

Watch: TMZ: Sen. Ruben Gallego: We’re Playing Musical Chairs After Election Chaos… Then We’ll Go After Elon

On why Americans should be worried about Elon Musk’s throttling of Starshield: “What happened with Starshield being shut down in Ukraine should scare us all.

“A private company interfering in international relations, national security,and foreign security — everything else like that — that potentially affects our relationships, our alliances, our goals, and ensuring our interests as a nation should scare us. And, so, we should be subpoenaing Elon Musk to see what happened.

“Who made the decision to shut down Starshield? That cost the Ukrainians, by the way, hundreds of civilians’ deaths.

“I want to know what the decision-making process was. Was it Elon Musk making the decision? Did he talk to somebody about this? Did he ask permission from the U.S. government? Was it somebody in Europe that he talked to? Or did he just make a decision on his own?

“We have a right — because we are big vendors of Starlink and Starshield — to know what was the process, and is this a national security threat?”

On how soon the new Congress should subpoena Elon Musk: “January. Because we don’t know how extensive this is.

“What happens if he does this again? What happens if he does this again to Ukraine, in the middle of winter, when they’re going to get attacked by Russia?

“What happens if he gets pissed off by whatever we do? Can he shut down our contracts with Starshield or Starlink? The American public needs to know. And my job as a senator is to make sure that he’s not a threat.”

title: Gillibrand, Schumer Announce Nearly $2 Million In USDA Funding For New York State
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a member of the Senate Appropriations Agriculture and Rural Development Subcommittee, and U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer announced $1,915,024 in U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) grants for New York State. This federal funding will support New York’s ongoing efforts to connect farmers with customers and make food more affordable. The funding is distributed through the Farmers Market Promotion Program (FMPP) and Local Food Promotion Program (LFPP) grant programs. Of these funds, more than $1.1 million is dedicated to local food promotion programs, and more than $700,000 will fund farmers market food promotion programs.

“As New York continues to expand access to healthy food while SNAP benefits are being targeted by the Trump administration, I am proud to secure these federal dollars for both urban and rural communities,” said Senator Gillibrand. “These grants will be used to expand the reach of local food programs and farms, boosting regional economies and helping to ensure New Yorkers can eat healthfully. I will keep pushing for funding that helps New Yorkers afford sustainable, regionally sourced ingredients.”

“I’m proud to deliver nearly $2 million in federal funding to support food programs and farmers across New York,” said Senator Schumer. “As cruel Trump administration SNAP cuts begin to take effect, this funding will help make healthy, locally-grown food more accessible and affordable. I will always fight to support our farmers, strengthen rural communities, and keep food on the table for New York families.”

The offices of Senator Gillibrand and Schumer will continue surveillance over the issuing of these grants to ensure they are administered efficiently to their recipients.

title: Q&A: Unfinished Business
text:
With U.S. Senator Chuck Grassley

Q: What’s on Congress’ plate before the end of the year?

A: With the midterm elections behind us, the 119th Congress returns to Washington with a plate of unfinished business to address. That includes passing the annual defense authorization bill, keeping the government open beyond the short-term funding bill that expires on Dec. 11 and reauthorizing key rural healthcare programs, including the Medicare-dependent and low-volume hospital programs, Rural Community Hospital Demonstration Program and a Medicare payment floor for rural doctors and clinics. For 65 years in a row, Congress has worked across the aisle to pass the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The annual legislation sets defense-related policy and authorizes appropriations for the Pentagon, such as procurement for weapon systems, ships, and aircraft; payroll and personnel; military construction; and, nuclear weapons programs at the Department of Energy. The NDAA is often called must-pass legislation because it authorizes funding that supports military families, from housing to healthcare, and sets guidance on the nation’s defense programs that protect national security. It’s one of the most consequential bills every year on Congress’ to do list. For example, the fiscal year 2025 NDAA included 794 pages of policy measures and discretionary authorizations exceeding $883 billion. The bill is often a vehicle for other homeland security legislation to get passed. This year, I’ve filed bipartisan amendments to the NDAA that would protect kids online, fight organized crime and stem illicit drug use.

I’ll also be pushing to enact the five-year Farm Bill that’s been stalled for the last three years and operating under annual extensions. Unfortunately, Senate Democrats have refused to join Republican-led efforts to cut fraud from the food stamp program. Meanwhile, farmers need certainty and are counting on Congress to update conservation, rural development and farm credit policies that are operating under the 2018 farm law. I’m also committed to getting permanent, year-round nationwide E15 across the finish line that was included in the Farm Bill that passed the Senate Agriculture Committee. Getting E15 signed into law will help lower gas prices, boost corn demand and pump $14 billion into the farm economy. I’m hopeful lawmakers will reach a consensus once and for all to get the Farm Bill to the president’s desk before the end of the year.

Q: Why is permitting reform a bipartisan priority?

A: There is too much red tape in Washington. Public policies set decades ago to protect the environment are in dire need of an update to reflect changes in technology and address the regulatory and legal quagmire that’s standing in the way of bringing costs down for the American people. The federal permitting process that determines when and if critical infrastructure projects move from the drawing board to shovels in the ground is ineffective and costly. The heavy-handed bureaucratic review process is forcing American families to pay more for energy and consumer goods. Lawmakers on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and the Energy and Natural Resources Committee have rolled up their sleeves in good faith to hammer out a bipartisan bill called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. It would reform the nation’s environmental review and federal permitting framework that’s driving up costs for Americans and impeding economic growth. By responsibly untangling the regulatory thicket that takes years and even decades for infrastructure projects to get started — from pipelines to transmission lines needed to boost the nation’s energy grid — Congress can fix the broken permitting process, better protect natural resources, pave the way for more affordable and reliable clean energy and foster economic development across the country. Importantly, the bill would help provide certainty to infrastructure projects that have received permitting approvals and secured financing by preventing future administrations from unwinding or blocking entire classes of energy projects. What’s more, the Senate bill would ensure data centers pay for their energy costs and protect families from footing the bill. For years, Congress has taken bites at the permitting reform apple. It’s time to get the job done and responsibly meet surging demand for affordable electricity so the U.S. economy isn’t left behind.

title: Heinrich Demands Answers on Trump Administration’s Push to Build Data Centers on Public Lands
text:
Heinrich: “I am extremely concerned with the Trump administration's actions to develop data centers on public lands.”

WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, raised the alarm on the Trump administration’s push to develop AI data centers on public lands, demanding answers from Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Director Steve Pearce on the agency’s actions to greenlight data center buildout.

“I am extremely concerned with the Trump administration’s actions to develop data centers on public lands,” Heinrich began.

Heinrich’s letter follows his online post earlier today stating simply, “No data centers on public lands. Period.”

Heinrich's letter to Pearce comes after multiple actions from the Trump administration to develop data centers on public lands, including the June 2026 BLM approval of the 88-acre Townsite Data Center in Boulder City, Nevada. While the project was paused by the Department of the Interior’s Board of Land Appeals in September 2026, its approval was initially spurred by a 2025 Trump Executive Order that expedited the permitting of data center development on public lands.

BLM is now reportedly considering at least 15 proposals to build data centers or related infrastructure on public lands, covering more than 17,000 acres of public lands and stretching across six Western states. According to the Salt Lake Tribune, BLM asked state directors to identify public lands ready for data center development — something the Department of the Interior’s leadership told officials is a high priority.

“When BLM makes decisions about public land, it should always consider the best interest of the public and the communities that will be directly impacted by its decision,” Heinrich wrote.

“BLM should listen to the voices of the American people and carefully consider the many uses of public land before hastily greenlighting data center buildout on public lands,” Heinrich continued.

In the letter, Heinrich specifically requests a complete list of all authorities BLM is using to support data center development on public lands, all data center-related development proposals BLM is considering on public lands, and the public lands BLM has identified that are eligible for data center development.

Read the full letter here and below.

Director Pearce:

I am extremely concerned with the Trump administration’s actions to develop data centers on public lands.

In June 2026, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) approved the first data center on public lands—the sprawling 88-acre Townsite Data Center located in Boulder City, Nevada. At the time, BLM amended an existing right-of-way grant for a solar and battery-storage project to allow for the development of the data center. On September 1, following an appeal by Boulder City, Nevada, and environmental groups, the Department of the Interior’s Board of Land Appeals paused development of the data center, citing BLM’s decision to approve the project without conducting a new National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review. The Board found that Boulder City and the environmental groups “made a persuasive showing that BLM violated NEPA and acted arbitrarily or capriciously when it determined that the data center project is ‘substantially the same’ as the solar plant project for purposes of its NEPA analysis.”

BLM’s decision to approve the Townsite Data Center followed an Executive Order signed by President Trump in July 2025 that expedited the permitting of data centers on public lands. In September, the President signed another Executive Order that grants Secretary Burgum additional independent authorities over energy production on public lands. BLM is now reportedly considering at least 15 proposals to build data centers or related infrastructure on public lands. The development proposals cover more than 17,000 acres of public lands and stretch across six western states. According to a report, BLM recently asked state directors to identify public lands ready for data center development and the Department of the Interior’s leadership told officials that the topic is high priority.

When BLM makes decisions about public land, it should always consider the best interest of the public and the communities that will be directly impacted by its decision. The Multiple Use – Sustained Yield principle of public land management requires the BLM to consider the other uses of public land when considering whether to site a data center in any specific location. BLM should listen to the voices of the American people and carefully consider the many uses of public land before hastily greenlighting data center buildout on public lands.

In light of questions and concerns about BLM’s review of data center development proposals on public lands and related actions, I request you provide the following information by November 20, 2026:

A complete list of all authorities BLM is using to support data center development on public lands. Please include the specific precedent and legal rationale.

A complete list of all data center related development proposals BLM is considering on public lands. For each proposal, please include the specific entity that is backing the project; the precise location of the project; the total acreage of federally owned land under review for development; the precise use of the federally owned land under review for development (e.g., for transmission lines, roads, or physical data center structures); whether the review will entail a NEPA review, or in the case of an existing right-of-way grant, a new NEPA review; and whether the proposal will have a public comment period.

A complete list of all public lands BLM has identified that are eligible for data center development.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this request. Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact my staff at (202) 224-4971.

Sincerely,

title: NEW DATA: Heinrich’s Bipartisan American Affordability & Jobs Act Will Hold Data Centers Accountable, Lower Electricity Bills by $50-78 Annually, Save $54 Billion in Health-Related Costs, and Lead to Cleaner Air and Healthier Communities
text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M.– New independent analyses released this week from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), Rhodium Group, and Grid Strategies LLC find that Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich’s (D-N.M.) Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would lower household electricity bills by $50 to $78 annually by 2040, reduce power sector emissions by approximately 20 percent, and avoid $54 billion in cumulative public health damages.

The analyses also find that the legislation would accelerate the connection of clean energy projects to the grid and require data centers to pay billions more toward the transmission infrastructure needed to serve their electricity demand.

“Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years,” said Heinrich. “These independent analyses show exactly what we stand to gain by fixing our broken permitting system: lower electricity bills, cleaner air, healthier communities, and more reliable energy infrastructure. BAAJA will help get more affordable energy connected to the grid while making sure massive energy consumers like data centers pay up. We should be building the infrastructure America needs, not making families foot the bill for permitting delays.”

BAAJA will deliver lower costs and cleaner air for Americans:

Lower electricity bills: Reduce household electricity bills by $50 to $78 annually by 2040, representing a 3–5 percent decrease in electricity prices, according to Rhodium Group.

Reduce pollution: Cut cumulative power sector CO2 emissions by approximately 20 percent between 2028 and 2035 compared with current law, according to SEIA.

Save billions in health costs: Reduce cumulative public health damages by an estimated $54 billion, according to SEIA.

Accelerate clean energy: Enable an additional 167 Gigawatt Alternating Current (GWac) of net solar capacity additions between 2028 and 2035 compared with current law, according to SEIA.

Connect more clean energy to the grid: Drive an additional 17–249 Gigawatts (GW) of clean energy resources to connect to the grid through 2040, according to Rhodium Group.

Increase clean energy generation: Increase solar and wind generation to 37.4 percent of total power generation, compared with 19.6 percent under the current permitting regime, according to SEIA.

Avoid massive amounts of emissions: Avoid as much as 1.5 gigatons of cumulative emissions through 2040, according to Rhodium Group — equivalent to almost 35 million gasoline-powered cars off the road or taking 39 coal plants offline for a decade.

BAAJA will also make data centers pay their fair share:

Recover $55 billion in transmission costs: Grid Strategies estimates that changes to federal transmission pricing policy under BAAJA could result in data centers contributing approximately $55 billion toward transmission costs over the next decade.

Collect $35 billion more from data centers: That represents approximately $35 billion more than data centers would otherwise pay under current policy.

title: Sen. Markey, Rep. Adams Reintroduce Legislation to Protect Critical Records from Environmental Damage
text:
Bill Text (PDF)

Washington (November 6, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee and Environment and Public Works Committee, and Congresswoman Alma Adams, Ph.D. (NC-12) today announced the introduction of the Public Archives Resiliency Act to authorize grants to support long-term climate resiliency, preservation, and continuity of records and documents for archival intuitions, including libraries and museums.

As the climate crisis continues to worsen, the need to protect historic government records from damage is vital. This includes records generated through birth, death, marriage, taxes, military service, education, immigration, property ownership and much more. Too many of the institutions responsible for managing the preservation of these documents are at risk of environmental damage and lack the necessary resources to protect the indispensable records of their communities. If these records are destroyed, individuals’ ability to access critical government benefits and services are delayed and historic cultural artifacts are lost.

“Our nation’s history is not only told through monuments, museums, and founding documents—it’s written in birth certificates, marriage licenses, military records, and countless other documents that tell the stories of everyday Americans,” said Senator Markey. “As we celebrate America’s 250th birthday, we must ensure that Americans’ irreplaceable personal records are protected from environmental catastrophe. The Public Archives Resiliency Act will help safeguard these vital records from climate-fueled disasters, protecting Americans’ identities, rights, and benefits for years to come.”

“I am proud to reintroduce the Public Archives Resiliency Act with Senator Markey,” said Congresswoman Adams. “Protecting public registries, Tribal records, museums, and libraries is an essential part of preserving our nation’s cultural identity. This bill will ensure that our record-keeping institutions have the resources to withstand future disastrous events, so that no family will lose the documents safeguarding their legal and financial rights.”

“America’s archives have a unique role in underpinning legal and civic life, and preserving cultural memory. Archives are part of the foundational infrastructure of our democracy. The growing frequency and severity of climate change-related disasters have serious consequences for America’s archives and the archivists who steward these vital records. This legislation is critically important to address this increasingly urgent issue, and to safeguard our shared American history,” said Eira Tansey, internationally recognized expert on the impacts of climate change on archives, and author of A Green New Deal for Archives.

“For over forty years, America’s repositories have been trapped in what an early 1980s National Historical Publications & Records Commission (NHPRC) report termed ‘a cycle of poverty’—bearing the weight of structural underfunding and precarious staffing while stewarding the bedrock of our nation’s civic memory. Chronic underfunding directly compounds this crisis: it leaves facilities vulnerable to severe weather, stalls preventative mitigation, and denies staff the capacity to build emergency safeguards before disaster strikes. The Public Archives Resiliency Act is the vital federal intervention we have needed for decades. By investing directly in archival workers and resilient infrastructure through the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) and NHPRC, this legislation breaks that exhausting cycle and ensures our democracy’s documentary heritage will endure,” said Brenda Gunn, President of the Society of American Archivists.

“The resiliency of our public archives is a cornerstone of democratic accountability and constitutional governance. Budget pressures, uncertain grant funding, and other challenges across the United States underscore the need for increased public support for independent, secure archives. Individuals often rely on the creation and preservation of records - censuses, taxes, military service, education, legal proceedings, property ownership, among others - to protect their rights and property, to secure benefits, and to recover from disaster. We must invest in the institutions and people that accomplish this essential work to be sure these records are collected, preserved, and made accessible without disruption,” said Joy Banks, Executive Director of the Council of State Archivists.

title: Sen. Moran Hosts Under Secretary of War Michael Duffey in Wichita
text:
WICHITA, Kan. – U.S. Senator Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) – a senior member of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense – today hosted Michael P. Duffey, the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment, in Kansas to tour the defense manufacturing capabilities at the National Institute for Aviation Research (NIAR) at Wichita State University (WSU). Moran. “NIAR’s work is helping address sustainment challenges, improve military readiness and support the men and women of our armed forces. title: Murphy Statement on Discharge from Hospital
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — U.S. Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) released the following statement upon discharge from The Johns Hopkins Hospital. Murphy will miss the next several weeks of votes in the Senate as he continues his recovery.

“Thank you for the outpouring of support my family and I have received over the last few days. I want to be direct with you, so here is my diagnosis. Last Saturday afternoon, I felt something was not right with my body and called 9-1-1 out of an abundance of caution, and I’m glad I did. I was diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of my brain.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today.

“This has been a scary experience for me and my family, and I appreciate the continued respect for our privacy. As I'm working towards a full recovery, I am staying engaged with my team and colleagues remotely, and my staff continues to carry out our legislative priorities, serve constituents, and ensure the work of my office continues uninterrupted. I want to extend my deepest thanks to the excellent doctors and staff at Johns Hopkins who have treated me and cared for my family.”

Statement from Dr. Jose Suarez, Chief of Neurosciences Critical Care at The Johns Hopkins Hospital:

“Senator Murphy experienced a small hemorrhagic stroke. He has shown tremendous progress, and at the current rate of improvement, we expect that he will make a full recovery following rehabilitation.”

title: ON THE JOB FOR MICHIGAN: Hemlock Semiconductor CEO Highlights Peters’ Efforts to Expand U.S. Semiconductor Production, Support Michigan Industries and Workers
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – In a new “On the Job” video from U.S. Senator Gary Peters’ (MI) office, Hemlock Semiconductor (HSC) Chairman and CEO AB Ghosh highlights Peters’ efforts to expand U.S. production of semiconductor chips, which are critical to Michigan’s auto industry and products ranging from cars, cell phones, home appliances, solar panels, agriculture equipment, and defense technologies. HSC, headquartered in Hemlock, Michigan, is the nation’s leading producer of hyper-pure polysilicon for the semiconductor industry and one of only five companies in the world capable of producing the highest quality polysilicon for semiconductor chips. Peters helped pass the CHIPS and Science Act into law, including a provision Peters authored that ensures federal incentives to boost semiconductor manufacturing include U.S. suppliers that produce the materials for semiconductor manufacturing, such as HSC. This provision ensured HSC would be eligible for the $325 million in federal funding it was awarded in 2024 to build a new, state-of-the-art manufacturing facility on its existing campus in Hemlock, creating thousands of good-paying jobs in Michigan. The video is part of the On the Job for Michigan series, which highlights Peters’ leadership and advocacy on behalf of Michigan constituents and communities.

“[Hemlock Semiconductor] serves two critical supply chains, namely semiconductors and solar energy, which is critical for U.S. national security and its energy independence,” said HSC Chairman and CEO AB Ghosh. “The CHIPS and Science Act was the first big legislation put down to onshore the tech supply chain. This grant of $325 million is critical for the future generation of this business. It’s going to allow us to make the polysilicon for the next generation AI chips, and that’s critical for the U.S. nation.”

“The work that we're doing here, it's awesome because there's only a handful of companies that can even produce the material at this purity level,” said Strategic Project Leader Elizabeth Stelzer. “And so, we get to play a part in making sure that the supply chain is steady and stable.”

Watch the “On The Job” video here.

“Semiconductor chips are critical to both U.S. national security and the future of our auto industry here in Michigan,” said Peters. “I believe you can't be a great country unless you actually make things, and they’re making great things right here at Hemlock Semiconductor. We must continue to support their cutting-edge work to strengthen this essential supply chain and create good-paying, local jobs.”

Peters has made strengthening American manufacturing and securing domestic supply chains a top priority. The CHIPS and Science Act also includes a provision Peters authored to support the domestic production of mature semiconductor technologies and ensure that projects supporting critical manufacturing industries are given priority status, which would include the automotive sector. This was in addition to $50 billion already in the law to incentivize U.S. production of all types of semiconductors, for a total of $52 billion. The CHIPS and Science Act additionally authorized increased funding for the Manufacturing Extension Partnership (MEP) program, which has been a priority for Peters.

Last year, the Senate passed Peters’ bipartisan legislation to strengthen federal efforts to expand domestic manufacturing of semiconductor chips. Peters’ Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act would direct the U.S. Department of Commerce’s SelectUSA program, in collaboration with other federal agencies and state economic development organizations, to develop strategies that would attract investment in U.S. semiconductor manufacturers and supply chains. The Senate also passed Peters’ bipartisan legislation to establish a National Manufacturing Advisory Council at the U.S. Department of Commerce to help strengthen federal manufacturing policy and U.S. leadership in global manufacturing.

Peters also helped enact the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which includes a provision authored by Peters to strengthen Buy American requirements and close loopholes to ensure the federal government is spending taxpayer dollars on American-made products that support American companies and workers. Peters additionally supported and helped pass the Inflation Reduction Act to strengthen domestic manufacturing of clean energy technologies and create millions of American jobs.

title: Ahead of Veterans Day, Rosen, Blackburn Announce Introduction of Bipartisan Bills to Support Veteran Education Programs
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Ahead of Veterans Day, U.S. Senators Jacky Rosen (D-NV) and Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) announced the introduction of two bipartisan bills to support and improve veterans’ education and career programs. The first bill, the Veterans Education Empowerment Act, would reauthorize and improve a grant program that helps establish and fund student veterans centers at colleges and universities. These centers serve as a critical resource for nearly one million veterans attending college each year, ensuring they have the support they need as they transition to the classroom and workforce.

The Senators also introduced the Veteran Technology Employment Success Act, a bill to improve the VET TEC High Technology program, which funds short-term, high-tech training for veterans and servicemembers to start careers in the tech industry. Specifically, this bill would require the VA to collect data on the success of the program and update implementation to ensure the training veterans receive is in line with industry demands.

“We owe our servicemembers an immense debt of gratitude for the sacrifices they have made, and the least we can do is to make sure they have the support and resources they need as they transition back to civilian life,” said Senator Rosen. “I’m proud to introduce these bipartisan bills to make pursuing an education or a technical career a little bit easier, allowing them to learn critical skills needed to succeed in today’s world.”

“Our veterans have earned every opportunity to succeed after their service, and the Veterans Education Empowerment Act will reauthorize and strengthen the student veteran centers that support nearly one million of them as they navigate higher education and pursue career opportunities,” said Senator Blackburn. “At the same time, the Veteran Technology Employment Success Act will improve the VET TEC program by requiring the VA to track results and align high-tech training with real industry demands.”

Senator Rosen has been a champion for Nevada’s veterans and their families. She recently helped introduce legislation to improve coordination between the VA and state veterans’ agencies to better connect veterans with their benefits. In September, Senator Rosen also introduced a bipartisan bill to improve veterans’ access to medical care in rural areas. Additionally, Senator Rosen is leading the charge in Congress to require the Department of Defense to join the Department of Energy in identifying all servicemembers and veterans who worked at locations where radiation and toxic exposure occurred, such as the Nevada Test and Training Range, and provide them with the same presumption of exposure, allowing such veterans to better access the VA health care and benefits they have earned. Last year, Senator Rosen introduced bipartisan legislation to incentivize employers to hire student veterans for part-time work and paid internships.

title: NEWS: After EPA Proposes Plan to Remove Federal Protections for Wetlands and Streams, Sens. Schiff, Markey Push EPA to Abandon Extreme Threat to Clean Drinking Water
text:
Senators write: “…The definitions proposed by the SNPRM [Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking] would remove federal protections for 80 percent of streams in the United States and 95 percent of individual wetlands, which makes a mockery of the congressional intent behind the Clean Water Act.”

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works’ Fisheries, Water, and Wildlife Subcommittee, and Ed Markey (D-Mass.) are calling on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to abandon their new proposal that threatens to harm public health and leave communities vulnerable to flooding and loss of access to clean drinking water.

The EPA’s new proposal to revise the definition of the Waters of the United States (WOTUS) rule replaces the proposed November 2025 standard with an even more extreme one, defining “relatively permanent” to mean “perennial” waters, stripping federal protections for hundreds of bodies of waters. Previously, in January 2026, the Senators urged the agencies to reverse this proposal.

“As we explained then, excluding these waters from federal protection threatens drinking water, increases downstream pollution and flood risk, and shifts substantial costs onto states, communities, and ratepayers. We are disappointed that your agencies have not only chosen to disregard all of these concerns, but have put out a second, more extreme proposal that does even more harm. We urge you to abandon this effort altogether and remember your statutory responsibilities to protect drinking water, public health, and the environment,” the Senators wrote in a letter to the EPA.

EPA’s latest proposal goes further to eliminate safeguards on bodies of waters that were already reduced by the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Sackett v. EPA. Additionally, the Senators raise concern with the subsequent harms this proposal will have on state and tribes’ capacity to manage waters, as well as on American households, who will bear the financial costs.

“…Pollution does not respect the arbitrary boundaries laid out in these proposals. When upstream waters lose federal protection, downstream communities do not cease experiencing their effects of that loss…the costs of additional pollution, degraded drinking water sources and the associated health risks, diminished flood protection, and lost aquatic habitat are shifted to states, Tribes, municipalities, water utilities, and ultimately the American taxpayer,” the Senators wrote.

“The Clean Water Act was enacted to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters.” Proposing to systematically exclude waters known to be critical to that integrity ignores science and defeats the purpose of the Act…We urge you to abandon this disastrous SNPRM as well as the 2025 proposal and leave the 2023 conforming rule in place,” the Senators concluded.

The EPW Committee’s Ranking Member, U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), also signed the letter.

The full text of the letter can be found here and below.

Dear Administrator Zeldin and Mr. Forsgren:

We write to express our serious concern regarding the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ September 9, 2026 Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM) that proposes to further narrow which waters would receive federal protections under the Clean Water Act. On January 28, 2026, we urged the agencies to abandon the proposed 2025 waters of the United States (WOTUS) rule. As we explained then, excluding these waters from federal protection threatens drinking water, increases downstream pollution and flood risk, and shifts substantial costs onto states, communities, and ratepayers. We are disappointed that your agencies have not only chosen to disregard all of these concerns, but have put out a second, more extreme proposal that does even more harm. We urge you to abandon this effort altogether and remember your statutory responsibilities to protect drinking water, public health, and the environment.

The core proposal of the SNPRM is to define “relatively permanent” waters to include only perennial waters, which the proposal suggests defining as “having standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year during ordinary conditions.” The SNPRM includes limited exceptions for drought, dry spells, and low tides, and allows only a single interruption of no more than 30 consecutive days annually. The SNPRM also considers a definition of “continuous surface connection” that would require even perennial surface water within a wetland to be continuously connected to a jurisdictional water in order to merit protection as WOTUS.

Limiting “relatively permanent” waters to perennial and interconnected waters would be scientifically indefensible and would put downstream water quality at risk. EPA’s own scientific record demonstrates why. EPA’s review of more than 1,200 peer-reviewed studies concluded that streams are connected to downstream waters regardless of their size or frequency of flow and strongly influence downstream physical, chemical, and biological conditions. That review, and numerous other independent scientific studies, found that perennial, intermittent, and ephemeral tributaries transport water, sediment, nutrients, contaminants, organic material, and organisms through river networks and collectively affect larger downstream waters. Further, the definitions proposed by the SNPRM would remove federal protections for 80 percent of streams in the United States and 95 percent of individual wetlands, which makes a mockery of the congressional intent behind the Clean Water Act.

Your agencies acknowledge these concerns in the SNPRM and recognize the functions served by ephemeral streams. The agencies also acknowledge that the majority of wetlands would not satisfy the supplemental definition of “continuous surface connection,” because most wetlands do not contain perennial surface water. Even more, your agencies concede that the 30-day threshold is not “scientifically-grounded” and is proposed only because it is “easy to administer.” Given these acknowledgements, it appears the entirety of the SNPRM is contradictory— proposing changes that go against the very scientific findings cited in the notice. “Easy to administer” does not justify the neglect of waterways that contribute on average 55% of the water found in larger rivers – the protection of which is the mission of your agencies and the Clean Water Act.

The SNPRM also includes an arbitrary five-year cutoff for waters impacted by drought conditions, a policy that would cause particular harm to more arid regions like the West. After five years of dry conditions, such drought conditions would be treated as the new baseline. As American Rivers explains in its public comment, this would “convert a growing share of currently ‘relatively permanent’ waters to non-jurisdictional status over time, particularly in the West, as droughts lengthen and recur more frequently.”

The agencies justify these contradictions and known harms in part by claiming that the proposal allegedly provides regulatory clarity, giving landowners clearer notice of Clean Water Act obligations. But administrative simplicity cannot provide cover for a scientifically and legally indefensible interpretation of the Clean Water Act, as its primary purpose is to protect waters from pollution. Moreover, this SNPRM would not provide clarity, as it would inevitably lead to litigation and overwhelm state and tribal capacity to manage waters. The agencies acknowledge in the supplemental proposal that “Tribes may disproportionately rely on the Federal Government for water program implementation and enforcement of water quality violations” and “many Tribes are still building capacity and may lack resources to create a Tribal water program.” This SNPRM will remove federal protections for many waters Tribes may care about, thus pulling the rug out from under them.

As we emphasized in January, pollution does not respect the arbitrary boundaries laid out in these proposals. When upstream waters lose federal protection, downstream communities do not cease experiencing their effects of that loss. And states are not going to be able to fill the gaps left by the SNPRM. One state’s hypothetical capacity to regulate their own waters, absent federal law, does not mean as much when an under-resourced, upstream state exports the cost of their water quality remediation downstream. Instead, the costs of additional pollution, degraded drinking water sources and the associated health risks, diminished flood protection, and lost aquatic habitat are shifted to states, Tribes, municipalities, water utilities, and ultimately the American taxpayer. Our previous letter warned that narrowing WOTUS in this manner would transfer responsibility and costs downstream rather than eliminate them. The recent supplemental proposal fails to heed that warning and would multiply these costs to the American people.

The Clean Water Act was enacted to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters.” Proposing to systematically exclude waters known to be critical to that integrity ignores science and defeats the purpose of the Act. Although we do not agree with its reasoning, the Supreme Court spoke in Sackett v. EPA, and EPA and the Corps conformed to that decision in 2023. There is no need for a further rulemaking, especially when that rulemaking envisions slashing federal water protections even further than the Supreme Court already has. The SNPRM your agencies have published includes a litany of contradictions and acknowledged significant harm to human health and the environment. We urge you to abandon this disastrous SNPRM as well as the 2025 proposal and leave the 2023 conforming rule in place.

###

title: Sen. Tim Scott gathers Charleston leaders for housing roundtable
text:
NORTH CHARLESTON, S.C. — Inside the council chambers at North Charleston City Hall, U.S. Senator Tim Scott (R-S.C.) brought together mayors, state legislators, county leaders, builders and business leaders from across the Lowcountry on Friday to put his 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act to work in South Carolina.

“Your efforts will allow the ROAD to Housing Act to hit the ground running throughout South Carolina,” said Sen. Scott. “One of the biggest motivating factors for my work on housing is remembering how I grew up in a single-parent household, mired in poverty, sharing a bedroom and a bed with my mom and my brother in a rental unit with dirt for the front yard and no backyard. The better we make people’s lives today, the brighter our future is together here at home in the great state of South Carolina.”

Fred Moore, housing advisor to Sen. Scott, walked participants through how the law clears the way for new construction and gives local leaders more flexibility to build. Bradford Traywick, regional director for Sen. Scott, led the conversation, which turned quickly to the Lowcountry’s biggest pressure points: workforce housing near new jobs, permitting timelines and zoning that keeps starter homes off the market.

“I want to thank Senator Scott and his staff for doing this. The information that was shared is so important, especially for folks from local government who are on the ground and actually doing the work. We have a major housing need: affordable housing, workforce housing, even market-rate housing and student housing in Orangeburg,” said Sidney Evering II, city administrator for the City of Orangeburg.

“Thanks to the Senator and the Banking Committee, what we have now is something that can really make a difference, to make that process more efficient, actually more business-like. My peers all across the country are talking about this act and trying to understand it. To be able to go to a forum here, in our community, and have someone from the staff come and explain it to us, that’s incredibly valuable,” said Kevin Sheilley, president and CEO of the Charleston Metro Chamber of Commerce.

“Housing is the crux of the entire conversation for economic development, for growth, for job opportunities. It’s a conversation we have all day long in our office when it comes to our employees being able to afford to live where they work. The growth here is not stopping, so we need to lean in,” said Marie Delcioppo, executive director of marketing and business development at Stubbs Muldrow Herin Architects.

“From what I understand, the ROAD to Housing Act is one of the most significant pieces of legislation in decades, and I’m excited to see what it can do for families across South Carolina. Dorchester County is growing fast, and I think this legislation will help us make sure we have the workforce for all of the great companies in the tri-county region,” said Gordon Rooney of Dorchester County Economic Development.

The North Charleston roundtable closed a three-city series that included stops in Duncan on October 28 and Columbia on October 29.

Watch the full event recap video here.

Background

In July 2025, Sen. Scott led the Senate Banking Committee in unanimously advancing the ROAD to Housing Act.

In March 2026, the full Senate passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act by a vote of 89-10.

On July 11, 2026, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law.

The law cuts red tape, unlocks housing supply and lowers costs for families, with no new federal spending.

title: ICYMI: Shaheen Receives Lifetime Achievement Award from New Hampshire Community Loan Fund for Championing Affordable Housing
text:
(Manchester, NH) – Yesterday, U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) was honored by the New Hampshire Community Loan Fund with its Community Champion Lifetime Achievement Award. The award was presented in recognition of Shaheen’s work on behalf of New Hampshire’s Resident Owned Communities (ROCs) and her efforts to expand affordable housing in the state. Shaheen also delivered remarks at the Annual Meeting, which is the New Hampshire Community Loan Fund’s marquee event. The nonprofit provides loans, coaching and guidance to New Hampshire communities and has invested more than $518 million in communities across the Granite State since its founding in 1983. Photos from the event can be found HERE.

“For over 40 years, the New Hampshire Community Loan Fund has provided transformative financial support, guidance and counseling to individuals, families and organizations across the Granite State. Nothing describes the organization’s philosophy better than ‘Neighbors Helping Neighbors,’ and its work has been indispensable to unlocking economic opportunity throughout New Hampshire,” said Senator Shaheen. “It is humbling to receive this Lifetime Achievement Award from such a critical institution in the state. I’ve been so proud to work alongside the Community Loan Fund, investors and local leaders to make great strides in advancing affordable housing, supporting manufactured housing communities and bolstering economic growth across New Hampshire.”

Throughout her time in the Senate, Shaheen has led efforts to lower housing costs, expand affordable housing and support New Hampshire’s manufactured housing communities. Earlier this year, Shaheen helped pass the landmark 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which, along with cutting red tape and streamlining the federal housing process, will directly lower construction costs for new, affordable manufactured housing. title: U.S. Senators Tina Smith, Amy Klobuchar Secure $28.6 Million to Improve Railroad Safety, Efficiency and Reliability in Minnesota
text:
The federal grants will upgrade tracks, equipment and rail cars in Greater MN and the Twin Cities metro

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senators Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) and Tina Smith (D-MN) secured $28.6 million in three separate U.S. Department of Transportation grants to improve railroad infrastructure, safety and reliability in Minnesota. The funds will ensure Minnesota’s railroad network can continue to safely move people, commodities and other goods that power small towns, rural communities and big cities.

“Minnesota farmers and businesses depend on a safe and reliable rail system to get their products to market and keep our economy moving. These federal grants will replace aging tracks, boost efficiency, and improve rail safety,” said Sen. Klobuchar. “Maintaining strong rail infrastructure is critical for the long-term economic well-being of our state and for keeping Minnesota competitive.”

“Railroads are the lifeblood for Minnesota farmers, producers and small businesses,” said Sen. Smith. “That’s why it’s critical to keep this economic engine on track by upgrading railroad lines and equipment, giving Minnesotans greater and safer access to national and international markets. Sen. Klobuchar and I are ‘all aboard’ on keeping Minnesota’s railway network reliable and efficient.”

“Twin Cities & Western is proud to partner with our Minnesota grain customers, the Federal Railroad Administration and our champions in Congress,” said Twin Cities & Western Railroad President Vic Meyers. “This project will ensure Minnesota farmers remain connected to the Mississippi River with safe, efficient and reliable rail service.”

The three grants are respectively awarded to the Twin Cities & Western Railroad Company, Minnesota Commercial Railway, and Northern Lines Railway. The grant funds come from the Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements Program within the DOT, funded partially by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act both Senators worked to pass in 2021.

Twin Cities & Western Railroad Company will receive up to $22 million to buy 200 new rail grain cars and upgrade select tracks and rail infrastructure around Renville, Stewart and Hector in Greater MN. The new upgrades are needed to carry the new, larger and heavier grain cars that give farmers and producers the opportunities to sell more commodities at once. The Twin Cities & Western Railroad will contribute a 20 percent cost share to the project.

Minnesota Commercial Railway will receive $5.36 million to replace worn tracks in Minneapolis, St. Paul and Roseville. The project will reduce the risk of derailment and improve the safety and reliability of passenger and freight service in the Twin Cities metro. The Minnesota Commercial Railway will contribute a 20 percent cost share.

Northern Lines Railway will receive $1.3 million to redo approximately 25 miles of track in and around St. Cloud, Cold Spring and Rockville. The new tracks will improve safety for the railcars carrying freight and hazardous materials. The Northern Lines Railway will contribute a 35 percent cost share.

Elfreth was joined by veterans, active-duty servicemembers, and military spouses for the discussion, which included an update on her work to expand physical and mental health care for veterans, other legislative updates from the Armed Services Committee, and input from the advisory council.

“There are more than 50,000 veterans who call Maryland’s Third District home – all who have selflessly served and sacrificed for our country. Ahead of Veterans Day, I reconvened our Veterans Advisory Council to deliver an update on my work in Washington and discuss how we can continue providing the highest quality of care to our servicemembers, veterans, and military families,” said Congresswoman Elfreth. “As the daughter and granddaughter of Army, Navy, and Air Force veterans, I know the sacrifice that these men and women have made, and it’s why I’m determined to continue uplifting their voices here in the halls of Congress.”

Elfreth was joined by the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families, VFW Post 7472, American Legion Post 156, Blue Star Families - Maryland Chapter, Veterans of Foreign Wars of the U.S., Howard County Veterans Foundation, Howard County Department of Community Resources and Services, Howard County Veterans and Military Families, Department of Maryland Veterans of Foreign Wars, and veterans from the U.S. Marine Corp, Army, and Navy.

“VFW Post 7472 is pleased to welcome Congresswoman Elfreth and distinguished guests to the Third Annual Veterans Advisory Council Roundtable,” said Jeff Kelley, Commander, VFW Post 7472. “This annual forum provides an important opportunity to address significant issues affecting veterans and their families. We value the perspectives and contributions of everyone participating and reaffirm our commitment to supporting those who have served our nation.”

“Blue Star Families Maryland Chapter appreciates Congresswoman Elfreth's continued leadership and commitment to ensuring that the voices of veterans, service members, and military families are represented in the conversations that shape public policy. The well-being of our military community extends beyond the service member and must include the families who serve alongside them through every transition, deployment, and challenge. Opportunities like the Veterans Advisory Council Roundtable are essential to bringing community organizations, veteran advocates, and policymakers together to identify needs, advance meaningful solutions, and strengthen the resources available to those who have served and those who continue to serve,” said Yolanda Rayford, Executive Director, Blue Star Families (Maryland Chapter).

At the roundtable, Elfreth delivered an update from her work as a member of the House Armed Services Committee, including an update on this year’s National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). Since the previous discussion, Elfreth has worked to improve veterans’ access to care and mental health services in Maryland and across the country.

Earlier this week, Elfreth led her colleagues in urging the Department of Defense and Department of Veterans Affairs to select Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland, to expand access to care for veterans. This would be part of the implementation of Elfreth’s “Improvement of Availability of Care for Veterans from Facilities and Providers of the Department of Defense”provision of last year’s National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). Elfreth has also fought to expand access to alternative therapies through bills like her bipartisan THRIVE Act.

Following the suicides at Fort Meade earlier this year, Elfreth has fought to remedy on-base mental health services. She has urged the appropriations committees to deliver $11 million to invest in occupational resiliency, mental health, and team training at the Fort. Elfreth is working to change the reporting requirements and include civilian employees in DoD’s suicide data, especially at installations like Fort Meade where civilian and uniformed officers work side by side on the same projects. She is also working to address delays with the transfer of mental health licenses from out of state.
