title: Baldwin, Johnson Introduce Bipartisan Resolution Congratulating Milwaukee Brewers on Historic World Series Championship
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) and Ron Johnson (R-WI) introduced a bipartisan resolution congratulating the Milwaukee Brewers on winning the 2026 Major League Baseball World Series, the first championship in franchise history. The win marked the end of a historic season, including a franchise-record 103 regular-season victories and their fourth consecutive National League Central Division title.

“In a season for the history books, the Milwaukee Brewers brought so much pride to Milwaukee and the entire state of Wisconsin. Generations of Wisconsin families cheered on the Brew Crew, kids stayed up well past their bedtimes, and game after game, this team showed what it means to win the Wisconsin way – with resilience, teamwork, and grit. This was a season to remember, and it is a privilege to recognize and honor the team that made history and the fans who cheered them on every step of the way,” said Senator Baldwin.

“Congratulations to the Milwaukee Brewers’ players, coaches, and staff on their historic World Series victory. I am thrilled for this team and its loyal fans, who have waited more than 40 years for this moment,” said Senator Johnson. “Wisconsinites are proud to call the Brewers our own and to celebrate this historic achievement together. Go Brewers!”

The Brewers’ World Series victory marked the first championship in franchise history and Milwaukee’s first Major League Baseball championship since the Milwaukee Braves won the World Series in 1957. After finishing the regular season with a franchise-record 103 wins, the Brewers defeated the San Diego Padres in the National League Division Series and swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series to secure their first pennant since 1982. The Brewers finished the postseason with an 11-2 record, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in five games to bring the Commissioner’s Trophy home to Milwaukee.

The resolution also celebrates the unwavering support of Brewers fans across Wisconsin, including the estimated 750,000 fans who attended the team's World Series championship parade, and recognizes the countless stadium workers and support staff who helped make the historic season possible.

A copy of the resolution can be found here.

title: Sens. Banks, Warren Statement on National Security Concerns Surrounding NVIDIA
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) joined Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) in releasing the following statement following NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy:

“In March, bipartisan members of Congress urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider NVIDIA’s export licenses to China and conduct a full national security review. Since then, NVIDIA has reportedly received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military, all while attempting to influence the debate over chip controls in Washington, D.C.

“NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China’s intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related.

This bill ensures that the chips powering the next generation of AI fuel American innovation and American national security, not the military and surveillance apparatus of the Chinese Communist Party.

The AI OVERWATCH Act codifies President Trump’s restrictions on exports of the most advanced AI Chips to foreign adversaries and was included in the Senate’s Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), ensuring that the chips powering the next generation of artificial intelligence strengthen American innovation and national security.

title: Bennet Draws Hard Line Against Iran War Funding, Pushes Senate to Refuse Appropriations Packages that Provide Spending for Trump’s War
text:
Washington, D.C. — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, sent a letter on Saturday to his Senate colleagues urging them to draw a hard line on Iran war funding and refuse to advance any funding package that includes further appropriations for President Trump’s disastrous war. Bennet will vote against any continuing resolution that includes Iran funding, and is working to rally his colleagues to join him.

“We return to the Senate with clear direction from the American people. Together, we must bring President Trump’s disastrous war with Iran to an end. His short-sighted misadventure has driven up the cost of gas, groceries, and fertilizer, while achieving none of the goals he set out. As you know, we have an important deadline before us. Government funding is set to run out on December 11. I believe we would abdicate our responsibility if we voted to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice in Iran. We must refuse to invoke cloture on any package that includes another cent for his war,” wrote Bennet.

Bennet has persistently fought to rein in Trump’s reckless war of choice with Iran. In March 2026, Bennethighlighted Trump’s failures to heed the Intelligence Community’s warnings that the war would lead to a more entrenched, hardline Iranian regime with greater incentive to pursue nuclear weapons. Bennet has demandeda full accounting of the costs of Trump’s war, introduced legislation to stop the Trump Administration from obscuring the true cost of this war, and called on President Trump to provide plans on how he intends to lower energy prices. In December 2025, Bennet voted – for the first time in his career – against the National Defense Authorization Act because of his grave concerns about President Trump’s reckless foreign policy and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s lawless Department of Defense.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

We return to the Senate with clear direction from the American people. Together, we must bring President Trump’s disastrous war with Iran to an end. His short-sighted misadventure has driven up the cost of gas, groceries, and fertilizer, while achieving none of the goals he set out. As you know, we have an important deadline before us. Government funding is set to run out on December 11. I believe we would abdicate our responsibility if we voted to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice in Iran. We must refuse to invoke cloture on any package that includes another cent for his war.

Americans all across the country are paying the price for President Trump’s war, a war that he is losing. At the grocery store and at the gas pump, families are facing higher prices and fewer options. Farmers and ranchers – who were already struggling under the weight of high tariffs and an ill-conceived trade war – have been hit with increased fertilizer and farm diesel costs. Our children will bear the costs of this catastrophe for decades.

The stakes are too high for us to fall into our usual shutdown politics. Instead, we should act in a bipartisan manner to forcefully reject the Administration’s request for additional funding for the Iran war, a war Congress never authorized and the American people do not want. If we fail to exercise our constitutional duty, we know from Afghanistan and Iraq that these Middle Eastern wars can take decades to end – all the while the American people will bear the cost. Together, we can bring this conflict to a close. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.

title: Capito Applauds Announcement of $202 Million for West Virginia Through the Rural Health Transformation Program
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), a leader on the Senate Appropriations Committee, applauded the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ announcement awarding an additional $202 million to West Virginia through the Rural Health Transformation Program. The program, made possible by the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill, delivers on Republicans’ promise to increase affordability and the standard of living for Americans across the country. Senator Capito voted for the legislation that made this award possible.

Senator Capito, through her position in Senate Republican leadership and as Chairman of the Senate Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies (Labor-HHS) Appropriations Subcommittee, played a central role in the creation of the Rural Health Transformation Program.

“I am pleased to see an additional $202 million in funding for West Virginia awarded through the Rural Health Transformation Program. I was proud to help shape this program from the start and to support the Working Families Tax Cuts Act that made this funding possible. I am grateful for President Trump’s continued leadership and commitment to ensuring our rural communities have access to the resources they deserve,” Senator Capito said.

BACKGROUND:

The $50 billion, five-year Rural Health Transformation Program was authorized by the Working Families Tax Cuts Act and empowers states to strengthen rural communities across America by improving healthcare access, quality, and outcomes by transforming the healthcare delivery ecosystem.

The program provides $10 billion annually among all states that apply. Half is distributed equally, while the other half is determined based on several factors, including progress and successful policy implementation. title: North Dakota Receives $206 Million in Second Year of Rural Health Transformation Program
text:
Delegation Advancing Efforts to Transform Health Care Delivery in Rural North Dakota

BISMARCK, N.D. – U.S. Senators Kevin Cramer (R-ND) and John Hoeven (R-ND) and U.S. Representative Julie Fedorchak (R-ND) today announced North Dakota will receive $206 million for the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP). The announcement supports ongoing efforts to build a continuum of care across the entire state and follows a roundtable the delegation held with U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. in North Dakota last week, with the goal of ensuring an effective partnership between HHS, the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS) and the state’s healthcare providers. Today’s award keeps the state on track to receive up to $1 billion over the five years of the RHTP.

“Rural hospitals are essential to our communities, and the Rural Health Transformation Program is an investment in their future,” said Cramer. “This second-year award provides an opportunity to build on the progress already being made. After a positive discussion with Secretary Kennedy last week, I look forward to working with our state leaders and CMS to deliver lasting improvements to transform healthcare delivery across our state.”

“This $206 million award builds on the progress North Dakota has made so far under the Rural Health Transformation Program and will unlock more opportunities to build a continuum of care across our state,” said Hoeven. “This award is timely, as we just had a productive conversation last week with HHS Secretary Kennedy, officials from the NDHHS and health care providers from across our state, part of our efforts to ensure this program works for our hospitals, clinics and other providers. We will continue working to support our state in implementing these funds, building effective partnerships and advancing solutions to truly transform rural health care services in North Dakota.”

“This additional $206 million in funding, on top of the $200 million we already received, represents an extraordinary opportunity to transform how we deliver health care in North Dakota, especially in our rural areas,” said Fedorchak. “I urge state leaders to think big and use these one time resources to fundamentally rethink and retool how we deliver healthcare in a way that maximizes access and quality at a cost that is sustainable.”

The delegation worked to establish the RHTP through the passage of the Working Families Tax Cut Act and supported Governor Armstrong and his team in putting forward a strong application. The state was awarded nearly $200 million for the program’s first year, which is twice the program’s baseline and comes as a result of the state:

Investing in statewide fiber optic infrastructure.

Building a network of new, state-of-the-art critical access hospitals (CAHs).

Leveraging both telehealth and CAHs to recruit and retain healthcare professionals and provide access to a comprehensive continuum of care.

NDHHS recently obligated the full year-one award, with the bulk of the funding going to the North Dakota Center for Rural Health, which will manage awards to sub-grantees. The state also advanced programs to make clinical equipment upgrades, improve healthcare workforce retention and support mobile mammography services.

text:
Durbin: “Americans, from one end of this nation to the other, exercised their right to vote last Tuesday, and in doing so, they changed the course of America and its politics for years to come.”

WASHINGTON – In a speech on the Senate floor, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, highlighted last Tuesday’s historic election wins—which included flipping both chambers of Congress.

“Americans have fought and died to protect the Constitution—they have marched and bled to change this document so that the promise of a more perfect union would be available to all men and women, not just a few. Was it perfect? By no means… Does the Constitution still work? I think anyone watching the results of last Tuesday’s election would say that it does… Americans, from one end of this nation to the other, exercised their right to vote last Tuesday, and in doing so, they changed the course of America and its politics for years to come. What happened on that day renewed my faith in this country,” said Durbin.

“The midterm elections were a repudiation of the toxic brand of politics we have faced for the past 10 years… Americans made it clear that our nation prefers love over hate and community over cruelty. We saw that message on full display in my home state of Illinois,” Durbin continued.

During his speech, Durbin offered his congratulations to Illinois’s Senator-elect, Juliana Stratton, noting that she has served Illinois as a member of the General Assembly and Lieutenant Governor and that he looks forward to seeing her success in her new role. In addition to Stratton, Illinois Democrats won every statewide race that was on the ballot, and they won in deep red counties like McHenry County, which had not voted for a Democrat for governor since 1852.

Durbin then highlighted how voters rejected the chaos, corruption, and cruelty of the Trump Administration’s policies.

“Those results are unsurprising for anyone who has had a chance to speak to Illinois families over the past two years, who have all too often faced the brunt of the cruelty, chaos, and corruption of this Administration. They saw the cruelty firsthand on our streets during ‘Operation Midway Blitz,’ when immigration agents raided and terrorized our communities in Illinois—jailing and beating immigrants and U.S. citizens alike… They saw chaos in our hospitals when patient after patient witnessed their health insurance premiums dramatically increase, if they even still had insurance at all, after this Administration’s health care cuts. And they saw the corruption in the White House when families struggled to afford groceries and gas while the President and his cronies enriched themselves beyond their wildest dreams… Illinoisans made it clear on Tuesday that they do not have confidence in this Administration’s leadership—and tens of millions of Americans across the country joined them in that effort,” said Durbin.

Durbin then highlighted the historic and diverse wins from the 2026 midterm election. Next Congress, 159 women will serve across the two chambers. In addition, voters elected the first Muslim American, the first Native American woman, and the first openly gay man to serve in the United States Senate. Senator Duckworth and Senator-elect Stratton will be the first women of color to serve a state simultaneously.

“In governors’ races, voters elected more women, and more women of color, to the highest state office than we have ever seen before. While there is still more to be done to ensure that the composition of our elected officials reflect the people who put us here, Tuesday brought us one step closer to a world where every American can see themselves in their representatives,” said Durbin.

Durbin then slammed President Trump for promoting Stephen Miller to serve as the White House Chief of Staff after the election.

Durbin continued, “As fortunate as Tuesday was, it was only the first step. Americans made it clear they demand change, and it is up to those in Washington to give it to them. You would think after this clear and resounding defeat, the President would listen to the voters. But what was one of his first decisions in the aftermath of this historic election? To choose Stephen Miller, architect of this Administration’s cruel mass deportation campaign, as his new chief of staff.”

Following American voters’ massive rejection of the Trump Administration’s immigration policies, Durbin concluded his speech by urging Congress and the President to pass his Dream Act, bipartisan legislation which would allow noncitizens without lawful status who were brought to the United States as children and meet certain education, military service, or work requirements to earn lawful permanent residence. These young people, known as Dreamers, have lived in America since they were children, built their lives here, and are American in every way except for their immigration status. However, under current law, there is often no chance for them to ever become citizens and fulfill their potential.

title: Ernst Names Small Business of the Week, Olson Iron Works
text:
RED OAK, Iowa – U.S. Senator Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), Chair of the Senate Small Business Committee, today announced her Small Business of the Week, Olson Iron Works of Greene County. Throughout the 119th Congress, Chair Ernst plans to recognize a small business in each of Iowa's 99 counties.

“For the past 14 years, Olson Iron Works has forged its way to success by serving its fellow Iowans and the greater community” said Chair Ernst. “Olson Iron Works has welded such strong relationships with its customers that 80% of them are repeat buyers”

At a young age, Shane Olson discovered a love for hands-on work after learning how to weld from his father and shop teacher. He used those skills to make gifts for his family and friends. At 17, Shane enlisted in the Marine Corps, where he worked on different equipment and continued building his skills. Upon his return to Iowa, Shane joined the Iowa Air National Guard as a firefighter and further strengthened his fabrication and welding abilities. Shane’s wife, Alisa, suggested that he turn his talent and passion into a business. Shane bought and remodeled an old barn establishing Olson Iron Works as a part-time venture in 2012.

What began as a small operation has now grown into a 14,000 square foot shop and a full-time profession. Additionally, Shane remains active in the veteran community where he is a lifetime member of the American Legion and VFW. Olson Iron Works also regularly makes and donates metal flags in honor of deceased veterans and fallen first responders in the area.

Stay tuned as Chair Ernst continues to recognize outstanding Iowa small businesses with her Small Business of the Week award.

title: Gillibrand Addresses Stephen Miller Chief Of Staff News, Says Democrats Must Focus On Lowering Costs, Ending Iran War On MS NOW’s Politicsnation With Al Sharpton
text:
Gillibrand: “People Were Fed Up With Trump’s Corruption And Chaos And High Costs. They Voted For Change. And So This Congress And In The U.S. Senate, We’re Going To Focus On Exactly What The American People Asked Us To Do.”

***Hear Senator Gillibrand’s Full Interview Here***

U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand appeared on MS NOW’s PoliticsNation with Al Sharpton to discuss Democrats’ plan to bring down the cost of living and deliver much-needed relief for working Americans under their newfound Senate majority.

She highlighted her party’s laser focus on lowering costs for American families, including by ending the Iran war, restoring access to healthcare, and holding the president accountable for his corruption and his prioritization of vanity projects over the wellbeing of American families.

Senator Gillibrand also addressed the president’s promotion of Stephen Miller to chief of staff and threats to veto commonsense legislation next Congress:

“[President Trump] did put in place the architecture of this culture of corruption and chaos and high costs in putting Stephen Miller as chief of staff, so he does not seem positioned to be listening to the American people to get stuff done. But that’s not going to daunt. It’s not going to stop us. We’re going to work on getting all those costs down by passing commonsense legislation. And if President Trump dares to veto restoring Medicaid, covering dental and vision and hearing, getting costs for medicines down – if he dares to veto things that get the cost of groceries and housing and fuel costs down, he will – his party will lose even bigger in ‘28.”

Watch Senator Gillibrand’s interview with Reverend Al Sharpton here. Full transcript of Senator Gillibrand’s interview below:

REV. AL SHARPTON: Senator, you said Democrats now have to end the war in Iran, lower cost, and hold President Trump accountable. What does that actually look like when you take control in January?

GILLIBRAND: Well, Reverend, as you said, this election was about change. People were fed up with Trump’s corruption and chaos and high costs. They voted for change, and so this Congress and in the U.S. Senate, we’re going to focus on exactly what the American people asked us to do. We’re going to try to get our healthcare costs down, make sure prescription drugs are more affordable, make sure people have access. Trump cut millions off of Medicaid. Make sure our seniors can get dental, vision, and hearing. So get costs down and make it more accessible, more affordable. Focus on food costs. Focus on housing costs. Focus on fuel costs. The war in Iran has driven up all of those costs, and it’s unauthorized. It’s illegal. The American people don’t want it. It is deeply unpopular. So we need to end the war to get those costs down, and address the chaotic tariffs, which are also keeping food costs and housing costs and medicine costs high. So we have to right the ship, get costs down, and hold this president accountable for his corruption and the chaos that he created across this country.

SHARPTON: Senator, President Trump is already calling himself Mr. Veto. And after losing Congress, he responded by putting Stephen Miller in charge of the White House. Not exactly a signal that he’s looking for compromise. How do you govern with a president who appears ready to fight you at every turn?

GILLIBRAND: Well, it’s true. President Trump does have his little veto cap, and he has threatened to use it. And he did put in place the architecture of this culture of corruption and chaos and high costs in putting Stephen Miller as chief of staff. So he does not seem positioned to be listening to the American people to get stuff done. But that’s not going to daunt, it’s not going to stop us. We’re going to work on getting all those costs down by passing commonsense legislation. And if President Trump dares to veto restoring Medicaid, covering dental and vision and hearing, getting costs for medicines down – if he dares to veto things that get the cost of groceries and housing and fuel costs down, he will – his party will lose even bigger in ‘28.

SHARPTON: Now, Senator, you and Senator Chuck Schumer deserve a lot of credit for what happened Tuesday. He helped recruit candidates like Roy Cooper and Sherrod Brown, and you, as a DSCC chair, helped build a map that expanded into states Democrats weren’t supposed to win. But there’s still a real debate about who should lead this new majority. At least five incoming Democratic senators have said they won’t support Schumer or want new leadership, and others still haven’t committed. What’s your view on this?

GILLIBRAND: Well, first of all, it really was a blue tsunami. I mean, the weight of what was accomplished is so significant. Our candidates were so brilliant; they understood exactly what was at stake in this election by listening to voters. And we have won seven Senate seats, and we are likely to win two more. And of those seven, five are in states that Donald Trump won by double digits. So I think people are grateful for the hard work that our candidates did, being on message, campaigning constantly, being in their communities, talking about costs and talking about solutions. And I think they’re grateful for Senator Schumer’s hard work in not only helping to marshal these incredible candidates, but raising them the resources they need to win. We were outspent astronomically by the Republicans because they had so many super PACs and so many billionaires. But our individual candidates went toe to toe with every one of their opponents and were able to communicate effectively. And that credit really has to go to Senator Schumer as well as all these incredible candidates that really got this done.

SHARPTON: Senator, as DSCC chair, you have to feel pretty good about this map. Democrats won states that Donald Trump, as you said, carried by double digits. But success also created different problems late in the race. Places that had been considered long shots became competitive. Angie Nixon lost Florida by less than three points. Jamie Davis lost Louisiana by less than two, and Scott Colom is still in a razor-thin race in Mississippi. This isn’t about second-guessing every spending decision, but is there a lesson here about expanding the map earlier and taking some of these red state candidates seriously sooner. What might the party do differently next time?

GILLIBRAND: Well, just so you know, we did take these candidates very seriously. I’ve been working with Scott Colom for over a year and a half. He’s come to a bunch of our big events nationally. Our supporters across the country got to know him. We invested $8 million early to register new voters in Mississippi. So Scott has been on our radar for a very, very long time, and so we were always trying to double down to expand the map. We had four expansion states, and we won three out of four. It was Mississippi, it was Kansas, it was South Carolina and Florida. And of the four states, Angie’s state just happened to be the most expensive. It is a behemoth of a state. It is deeply red. But it is a testament to her candidacy, her unbelievable, inspiring candidacy that she organized her state. She had a very late primary, and she still got her vote out. She ran an incredible race. We’ve always taken her seriously. I’ve personally done fundraisers for her, and she really hit the ground running. But what it does tell us is that all of these states are going to be in play next cycle. We have another shot at Florida next cycle. We have another shot at North Carolina next cycle. And we have Wisconsin. So we have so many opportunities for the next cycle to continue to build on this map to continue to raise the kind of money that allows us to keep expanding. Again, to win five states that Trump won with double digits, you will add to that two more if we win, and when we win, let’s just say, when we win Mississippi and Alaska because we are up in both of those states.

SHARPTON: All right, Kirsten Gillibrand. Always good to be with, have you with us, and to be talking to you. New York senator and chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Thank you.

###

title: Grassley Welcomes $216 Million in Federal Funds for Iowa Rural Healthcare, Delivered by Republicans’ Working Families Tax Cuts Law
text:
WASHINGTON – Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), a senior member and former chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, welcomed news that Iowa will receive $216 million in additional federal funding from Republicans’ Working Families Tax Cuts Act to strengthen rural healthcare across the state. The funding will be disbursed through the law’s Rural Health Transformation Program and will help provide for workforce recruitment and retention, medical equipment and cancer care across Iowa.

Last month, Grassley led the entire Iowa congressional delegation in a letter to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) supporting Iowa’s latest funding request for the program. With this announcement, Republicans’ Working Families Tax Cuts law has now invested $425 million into rural healthcare in Iowa.

“Under Republican leadership, Congress delivered the largest investment in rural healthcare in American history, which every Democrat in Congress opposed. I’m glad to see the Working Families Tax Cuts Act continue improving Iowans’ lives by investing $216 million more to support healthcare workforce recruitment and retention, cancer care access, maternal health and modernized medical equipment. In the years ahead, Iowans can look forward to sustained funding from Republicans’ historic law that will strengthen care close to home,” Grassley said.

Background:

The Grassley-backed Working Families Tax Cuts law included the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program to ensure hospitals, nursing homes, community health clinics and other rural providers can continue serving their communities and improving care. Over a five-year period, Iowa will receive, at a minimum, $100 million annually from this fund. Last year, Iowa was awarded $209 million for the first year of the program.

Grassley has repeatedly highlighted the positive impacts of the program’s investments in Iowa. At his 99 county meetings this year, Grassley witnessed the benefits of this funding firsthand, including during Q&As at hospitals in Cass, Cerro Gordo, Fayette, Grundy, Kossuth, Lucas, Mahaska, Poweshiek, Sioux and Webster counties.

In May, Grassley wrote an op-ed published in the Cedar Rapids Gazette detailing how the program is improving access to care in Iowa.

title: ICYMI—Hagerty Joins Sunday Morning Futures on Fox News Channel to Discuss Stephen Miller, Lame Duck Session, Iran
text:
Washington—On Sunday, United States Senator Bill Hagerty (R-TN), a member of the Senate Foreign Relations, Appropriations, and Banking Committees, joined Sunday Morning Futures on Fox News Channel to discuss White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller’s recent promotion, Congress’s upcoming lame duck session, and the latest news in Iran.

*Click the photo above or here to watch*

Partial Transcript

Hagerty on White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller: Stephen is extraordinarily talented. He is one of the greatest warriors [President Donald Trump] has ever had… We’ve worked together for more than two years. If you think about Memphis—it came out of the pandemic—we lost control of the city from a crime standpoint. Stephen helped bring to bear 1,600–1,700 federal agents every day on the ground. I’m talking about the [Internal Revenue Service (IRS)], [Housing and Urban Development (HUD)], the [Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF)], and of course the [Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)]. All of those resources took a lot of coordination. Stephen was able to deliver that. He’s going to make a great chief of staff. My hat is off to [former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles]. She delivered, working alongside President Trump, one of the greatest political comebacks in history. And she’s done a magnificent job. I wish her well.

Hagerty on Congress’s lame duck session: The American public certainly wants both [permitting reform and the Ratepayer Protection Act]. And we had bipartisan support coming into Election Day, but [Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY)] pulled it all down. He’d rather have chaos. All the Democrats were able to do these past two years is deliver two historically long government shutdowns. We’re going to vote on Monday night. We’ll see if they’re serious about permitting reform. My guess is they’ll try to pivot toward the Green New Deal. They’ll do more destructive economic policies—not only waging war against President Trump, but waging war against the American economy. You’ve done a great job this session talking about the economy. We just need to be messaging that and we have got to acknowledge the fact that there are some critical points—whether it’s at the gas pump or it’s at the grocery store—where when we deal with Iran in the Middle East, when we deal with Ukraine, that’ll have an impact on fertilizer, that’ll have an impact on gas and diesel. And I think we can begin to bring the American reality into connection with what people sense and feel. Clearly people did not feel it on Election Day, and I think it’s our job to talk about it the way I’ve talked about it here in Tennessee… Tennessee is doing everything right in terms of making this state an attractive place to invest. President Trump has done everything right with the Big Beautiful Bill, his trade policies that have attracted more capital coming into America than we have seen in our lifetimes. Let’s make the most of it.

Hagerty on GOP support for President Donald Trump’s actions in Iran: The President, in typical fashion, is putting all options on the table. The operation that [Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent] has run, Operation Economic Outcast, has put the Iranian economy in the tank. They have no currency; they have no growth. If you think about what we’ve done from a military standpoint, no Air Force, no Navy, President Trump has moved more military assets into the region, so he has every option available to him and I think he’s perfectly capable of bringing this to an end very quickly. It’s his decision to make, but I think that can certainly happen. Again, that puts us in a much better posture to put more pressure on Russia, and to deal with Ukraine as well, because… Iranian energy back on the marketplace removes a great deal of leverage that Russia has. I can see everything coming together again. With foreign policy successes, we will breed more domestic policy success as well.

title: Heinrich’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act Passes Key Senate Vote
text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released the following statement after the Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), bipartisan legislation to lower energy bills, hold data centers accountable, reduce emissions, and create good-paying jobs.

“If we have any hope of making energy cheaper and making data centers pay for their own energy costs, then we need to pass our Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act into law,” said Heinrich. “This bill delivers exactly what Americans told us they wanted on election day: Lower costs and more jobs for American workers — all while reducing our emissions and defending against the administration’s attacks on Tribal consultation.”

Heinrich continued, “Negotiating this bill hasn’t been easy and took a lot of compromise. Now, we need to roll up our sleeves, engage in the amendment process, and work across party lines to get this done. When we put working families ahead of politics, we can build a future that is affordable and put the American dream within reach.”

Independent analyses find that BAAJA will:

Require data centers to pay for increased grid and energy costs they create, estimated at $55 billion in the next 10 years;

Save $19 billion in residential electricity bills over the next 14 years;

Nearly double the amount of solar and wind that can connect to the grid;

Create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs; and

Avoid 1.5 gigatons of CO2 emissions, the equivalent of taking 39 coal plants offline for a decade.

Earlier today, Heinrich hosted a press conference with U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, to urge their Senate colleagues to pass BAAJA and help lower electricity bills for American families. title: VIDEO: Heinrich and Whitehouse Urge Senate Passage of Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act
text:
Heinrich: “We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs. We can do that today. Let’s pass permitting reform.”

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, held a press conference urging their Senate colleagues to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), bipartisan legislation to lower energy costs, hold data centers accountable for the costs they impose on American families, and create good-paying jobs.

With the Senate slated to vote on the legislation this evening, Heinrich and Whitehouse highlighted how BAAJA would help address rising electricity costs, accelerate the development of new energy infrastructure, and hold data centers accountable by forcing them to fully pay for their operational costs.

“Just one week ago Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do,” said Heinrich. “BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, directly hold data centers accountable, create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, and cut emissions up to 20% from the power sector over the next decade.”

“The American people spoke loud and clear that they wanted results on affordability. BAAJA will mean billions in lower energy costs, and tens of billions of dollars more in ratepayer savings because of the provisions cracking down on data centers. And it can actually begin to happen now. People want to see Congress do big, good things. This is a big, good thing,” said Whitehouse.

Independent analyses find that BAAJA would lower Americans’ electricity bills by 3–5 percent, save families billions of dollars, nearly double the amount of solar and wind that can connect to the grid, and create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs. The legislation would also require data centers to cover the increased grid and energy costs they create, estimated at $55 billion over the next decade.

U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Ranking Member U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) host press conference to urge Senate passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, November 9, 2026.

Watch the full video of Heinrich’s remarks here.

A transcript of Heinrich’s remarks as delivered is below:

Every once in a while, I don’t wear my Senate pin, even if it means I’m going to get stopped on the way in.

I wear this pin.

It’s my dad’s 60-year IBEW pin, and he spent those 60 years keeping people’s lights on and working to keep their electricity bills affordable.

A little over a month ago, Senator Whitehouse and myself announced, along with our Republican colleagues, our bipartisan permitting bill.

And today, just one week after Americans sent a pretty resounding message about their priorities, we are taking our first vote on that legislation.

And that message that the people sent was pretty clear: they want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable, and that’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do.

BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, so that families can have money in their pockets for more than just keeping the lights on and their homes warm.

This bill directly holds data centers accountable, forcing big corporations to pay their full share instead of pushing costs on the consumers.

That one provision is worth $35 billion dollars to American households.

That’s pretty remarkable.

BAAJA will create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, good-paying jobs that workers can be certain will be around to support their families through a project’s completion.

And BAAJA will cut emissions up to 20% from the power sector over the next decade, meaning cleaner air, healthier communities, and fewer healthcare costs.

This bill’s not perfect.

We’ve never pretended it was.

It is, after all, bipartisan, and that means that neither side got everything they want.

We had to find common ground.

We had to make compromises, and we had to work through some very real disagreements.

But bipartisanship doesn’t mean we stop listening, and it doesn’t mean we stop working to make the legislation better.

I have worked hard to incorporate the feedback that we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into our Manager’s Amendment, and I want to walk you through a few of those changes because they’re pretty important.

First, on Tribal consultation, I’ve heard directly from Tribal leaders about the importance of having a meaningful voice in decisions that affect their communities and affect their ancestral lands.

We work to strengthen that dramatically in this Manager’s Amendment.

Tribes will now have an equal seat with states in transmission planning, and federal agencies will be required, and let me say that again: required “shall” consult, not “may” consult, “shall” consult early with Tribes on projects that will affect important cultural sites, including on what properties are affected, the impacts of the project, and ways to avoid, minimize, or mitigate potential harms, and basically that means that mandatory Tribal consultation is now built into every single step of the Section 106 process by law.

We’ve also extended the window for objections to agency reports.

We’ve strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, and we’ve given states a way to ask FERC to investigate local utility projects that gouge consumers.

That, in my view, is particularly important as private equity and other outside investors seek to take a larger role in electric utilities.

States need the tools to protect their ratepayers.

Third, we’ve made sure that workers’ rights are protected.

The Manager’s Amendment preserves collective bargaining agreements for union employees of the power of bargaining administrations, so that those workers can continue to bargain collectively and stand up for workers’ rights.

And finally, we’ve added a new Department of Energy Data Center Community Assistance Program because when a community is considering whether or not to grant a permit to a major data center, it needs to understand what that project will mean for its electricity supply, costs, water resources, infrastructure, and local economy, in order for them to make a good decision.

This program will give state, local, and Tribal governments the technical assistance they need to make their own informed decisions.

These are meaningful improvements.

They reflect the feedback that we’ve heard and they make an important piece of legislation, in my view, even stronger.

And importantly, they don’t change what this bill was always about: lowering energy costs, building the infrastructure our country so desperately needs, creating good-paying jobs, protecting our communities, and making sure that data centers pay their fair share.

That’s what we set out to accomplish when we started this project, and that’s what we’re still working to deliver.

So I would urge all my colleagues: Let’s get this done.

Let’s make it possible for America to build big things in this country again.

The people sent us a very clear message on Tuesday that they expect us to lower the costs in their daily lives.

We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs.

We can do that today.

So let’s pass permitting reform.

title: Hickenlooper Votes to Advance Long Overdue Permitting Reform Bill
text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will lower costs, advance clean energy projects

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper released the following statement after he voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The Senate will vote on final passage early next week.

“Democrats across the country ran on lowering costs, holding Big Tech accountable, and stopping the Trump administration’s attacks on clean energy. Now we have an opportunity to deliver on all three.

“This bipartisan permitting deal would help lower electricity bills, make data centers pay their fair share, and accelerate the clean energy projects we need to reduce carbon emissions and combat climate change.

“This bill isn’t perfect. No bill is. We should continue working with Tribal Nations and environmental groups to strengthen it as it moves through the legislative process. But we have a golden opportunity to make good on our promise to voters to make energy more affordable. We cannot afford to let it slip away.”

Hickenlooper has long supported reforms to modernize what is all too often a decades-long timeline to build new transmission lines and energy production projects. He has hosted a series of bipartisan permitting dinners throughout the last three years, bringing key Senate negotiators together to build consensus and help move permitting conversations forward.

title: Hirono Statement on Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act
text:
WASHINGTON D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Mazie K. Hirono (D-HI), a member of the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources (ENR), released the following statement on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026:

title: ND Delegation: North Dakota Receives $206 Million in Second Year of Rural Health Transformation Program
text:
BISMARCK, N.D. – Senators John Hoeven and Kevin Cramer and Representative Julie Fedorchak today announced that North Dakota will receive $206 million for the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP). The announcement supports ongoing efforts to build a continuum of care across the entire state and follows a roundtable the delegation held with U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. in North Dakota last week, with the goal of ensuring an effective partnership between HHS, the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS) and the state’s health care providers. Today’s award keeps the state on track to receive up to $1 billion over the five years of the RHTP.

“This $206 million award builds on the progress North Dakota has made so far under the Rural Health Transformation Program and will unlock more opportunities to build a continuum of care across our state,” said Hoeven. “This award is timely, as we just had a productive conversation last week with HHS Secretary Kennedy, officials from the NDHHS and health care providers from across our state, part of our efforts to ensure this program works for our hospitals, clinics and other providers. We will continue working to support our state in implementing these funds, building effective partnerships and advancing solutions to truly transform rural health care services in North Dakota.”

“Rural hospitals are essential to our communities, and the Rural Health Transformation Program is an investment in their future,” said Cramer. “This second-year award provides an opportunity to build on the progress already being made. After a positive discussion with Secretary Kennedy last week, I look forward to working with our state leaders and CMS to deliver lasting improvements to transform healthcare delivery across our state.”

“This additional $206 million in funding, on top of the $200 million we already received, represents an extraordinary opportunity to transform how we deliver health care in North Dakota, especially in our rural areas,” Fedorchak said. “I urge state leaders to think big and use these one time resources to fundamentally rethink and retool how we deliver healthcare in a way that maximizes access and quality at a cost that is sustainable.”

The delegation worked to establish the RHTP through the passage of the Working Families Tax Cut Act and supported Governor Armstrong and his team in putting forward a strong application. The state was awarded nearly $200 million for the program’s first year, which is twice the program’s baseline and comes as a result of the state:

Investing in statewide fiber optic infrastructure.

Building a network of new, state-of-the-art critical access hospitals (CAHs).

Leveraging both telehealth and CAHs to recruit and retain health care professionals and provide access to a comprehensive continuum of care.

NDHHS recently obligated the full year-one award, with the bulk of the funding going to the North Dakota Center for Rural Health, which will manage awards to sub-grantees. The state also advanced programs to make clinical equipment upgrades, improve health care workforce retention and support mobile mammography services.

title: Kaine Statement on Permitting Reform Legislation
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Tim Kaine (D-VA) released the following statement regarding the Senate’s upcoming vote on permitting reform legislation:

“I applaud the bipartisan work to find a permitting reform bill and see much good in it. But, I have serious concerns about the section of the bill that makes significant changes to the National Historic Preservation Act. title: Warner, Kaine, McClellan Press Social Security Administration on Abrupt Defunding of VCU Disability Benefits Support Program
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senators Mark R. Warner and Tim Kaine (both D-VA) and U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan (D-VA-04) raised concerns about the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) abrupt decision to halt funding for the Work Incentives Planning and Assistance (WIPA) program’s National Training and Data Center (NTDC) at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU), threatening critical services that help Americans with disabilities navigate Social Security benefits while seeking employment.

The NTDC provides training, certification, and technical assistance to more than 900 benefits counselors serving individuals with disabilities across the country. On October 2, 2026, SSA abruptly declined to fund VCU’s contract for another year and ordered the university to immediately halt work, disrupting essential training and support services for 74 WIPA projects nationwide.

In a letter to SSA Commissioner Frank Bisignano, the lawmakers demanded an explanation for the decision and pressed the agency to clarify how it intends to restore these critical services and fulfill its statutory obligations.

The lawmakers wrote, “We write to inquire about the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) decision to defund the Work Incentives Planning and Assistance program’s (WIPA) National Training and Data Center (NTDC). We are aware that on Friday, October 2, 2026, the SSA exercised its option not to extend its contract with Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) to administer the NTDC and ordered VCU to immediately halt all work providing Community Work Incentives Coordinators (CWICs) nationwide with training, certification, technical assistance, and other resource support.”

The WIPA program helps individuals who receive Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) due to severe, long-term medical conditions understand how employment may affect their benefits. Benefits counselors provide free, individualized guidance to help Americans with disabilities pursue employment opportunities without inadvertently jeopardizing the benefits they rely on.

The lawmakers continued, “CWICs at WIPA projects help bridge the information gap for beneficiaries by looking at their individual circumstances and advising them on how to maintain their benefits while working. To ensure the efficacy of the WIPA programs, the law also required SSA to establish a corps of work incentives specialists and provide training and technical assistance for those specialists. CWICs provide information and resources to help beneficiaries make informed decisions on returning to work.”

Despite Congress appropriating $23 million for the WIPA program in Fiscal Year 2026, SSA’s decision has left benefits counselors nationwide without access to necessary training resources, certification services, performance data, and institutional knowledge. These resources are critical to training new counselors and ensuring that both new and existing counselors provide accurate, reliable guidance to Americans with disabilities. The sudden loss of these services raises serious concerns about SSA’s ability to meet its statutory obligations and ensure that beneficiaries continue receiving the support they need.

The lawmakers pressed SSA to explain the rationale and timing of its decision, identify what training and certification resources remain available to benefits counselors, address disruptions to required performance reporting, and clarify whether the agency intends to restore these services through VCU, bring them in-house, or award a new contract.

Read the full letter here and below.

Dear Commissioner Bisignano,

We write to inquire about the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) decision to defund the Work Incentives Planning and Assistance program’s (WIPA) National Training and Data Center (NTDC). We are aware that on Friday, October 2, 2026, the SSA exercised its option not to extend its contract with Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) to administer the NTDC and ordered VCU to immediately halt all work providing Community Work Incentives Coordinators (CWICs) nationwide with training, certification, technical assistance, and other resource support.

Disabled beneficiaries who qualify for SSDI or SSI benefits are among the most vulnerable populations who suffer from severe, long-term medical conditions. To maintain compliance, beneficiaries must navigate a series of strict and complex requirements set out by the Social Security Act, including on earned income. For beneficiaries who need to earn extra income to support themselves or their families, incorrectly interpreting the rules can lead to a termination of benefits.

The Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 directed the Commissioner of Social Security to establish a program to provide information about work and benefits to people who receive Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) because of a disability. Using that authority, SSA established 74 WIPA projects in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories. WIPA projects and community organizations employ over 900 benefits counselors who provide free in-depth counseling to disabled beneficiaries on the effect of work on their SSDI or SSI benefits.

CWICs at WIPA projects help bridge the information gap for beneficiaries by looking at their individual circumstances and advising them on how to maintain their benefits while working. To ensure the efficacy of the WIPA programs, the law also required SSA to establish a corps of work incentives specialists and provide training and technical assistance for those specialists. CWICs provide information and resources to help beneficiaries make informed decisions on returning to work.

In Fiscal Year 2026 Congress appropriated $23 million to operate the WIPA program, 0.1 percent of SSA’s annual administrative budget. However, despite clear Congressional intent in support of the WIPA program, SSA has decided to unilaterally disband a vital component of the program. Without the NTDC, WIPA projects nationwide have lost access to valuable training resources and performance data to train new CWICs and ensure both new and existing Coordinators provide accurate and relevant information to beneficiaries. WIPA projects are also losing access to an invaluable source of institutional knowledge.

After this abrupt decision, it is unclear how SSA intends to comply with the statutory requirements of the Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 and Congressional intent set out in the Fiscal Year 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act.

We request answers to the following questions by November 16, 2026:

Why was the decision made to defund NTDC? Please provide a full account of the facts that informed the decision to defund NTDC.

When was the final decision made to defund NTDC? When were NTDC staff and VCU staff informed of the decision?

What training resources, if any, do WIPA projects have access to following the closure of the NTDC?

WIPA projects are required to submit its quarterly performance data at the end of this month. The performance data WIPA projects submit to maintain grantee status was collected and tracked through the WIPA STAR system. Given the sudden cancellation of the WIPA STAR system, will the reporting deadline be extended?

To obtain/maintain certification, CWICs were required to receive training through VCU. How will CWICs now receive certification training? Will SSA waive certification requirements if CWICs are unable to access the training?

Will SSA bring the training and technical assistance previously performed by VCU in-house? If not, does SSA plan on issuing a recompete of the contract?

###

title: NY Times Opinion: Senator Kim’s MediKids Is One of the “8 Bold Ideas to Fix America”
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – This weekend, an opinion in the New York Times Opinion Section highlighted Senator Andy Kim’s (D-N.J.) MediKids Act as one of the “8 Bold Ideas to Fix America.” The opinion comes on the heels of last Tuesday’s elections, where the American people overwhelmingly called for Congress to pass and implement bold ideas that lower costs and provide the care every American deserves.

“Four million American children are uninsured. An estimated three million more are expected to lose insurance over the next decade because of Republicans’ Medicaid cuts taking effect in 2027. And although health care costs consistently rank among the top concerns for American voters, Congress has offered them no meaningful relief since the Affordable Care Act,” wrote physician and contributing opinion writer, Rachael Bedard for the New York Times.

“Democrats could finally be in a position to forge a real, substantive consensus on health care. Undoing the damage from Mr. Trump’s Medicaid cuts is a good start, but it isn’t enough. What’s needed is universal health care coverage for children,” said Bedard. “… Mr. Kim designed his legislation to be passed during reconciliation, when Democrats won’t need to beat the filibuster to get it to the president’s desk. If Republicans fight it, that opposition will only sharpen the distinction between the parties in advance of 2028: One party wants to lower costs for families, and the other doesn’t. Americans trust Democrats more than Republicans when it comes to their health care. Democrats can build on that trust if they actually do something with it.”

The New York Times’ feature emphasized MediKids’ strengths, including how:

MediKids would automatically enroll every child born into Medicaid until age 26, while allowing families to choose to opt out and use private insurance;

MediKids is designed his to be passed during reconciliation; and how,

MediKids would eliminate state-to-state variability in insurance coverage and raise standards for care and decrease administrative burden and expenses.

Learn more about MediKids and Senator Kim’s work to build a universal care movement.

title: King, Colleagues Defend “Clear Meaning of the Constitution” From Proposed Census Change
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Angus King (I-ME) and 25 Senate colleagues are demanding the Trump administration revoke a proposed rule that would prevent certain non-citizens from being included in census counts, violating the Constitution’s clear direction, and removing questions on race and ethnicity. In a letter to Department of Commerce Under Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs Joyce Meyer and U.S. Census Bureau Deputy Under Secretary George Cook, the lawmakers remind the administration that the Census Bureau was intended to count the “whole number of persons in each state.” Additionally, they warn the rule would erode the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws by eliminating critical compliance data and jeopardize access to federal funding for critical services.

“We write to urge that you rescind your proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from decennial census counts and omit questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census. The proposed rule violates the clear meaning of the Constitution, which requires that the Census Bureau count the ‘whole number of persons in each state.’ The proposed rule would also cause communities across the country to be counted inaccurately, jeopardizing their fair representation in Congress and access to billions of federal dollars for education, health care, and public safety services,” the senators wrote.

“In its attempt to undermine the data used for the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws, the Bureau will degrade the accuracy of all other federal survey data, particularly for small and rural geographic areas. The Bureau writes in its own regulatory filing that the proposed rule ‘deteriorates the accuracy’ of ‘fertility/mortality rates, cancer rates, poverty rates, unemployment rates, [and] labor force participation’ because the Bureau relies on accurate decennial census information to adjust and design other survey estimates,” the senators continued.

“The Bureau also admits in its filing that the proposal would hamper the usability of data for state and local governments who rely on precise and accurate population estimates for small geographic areas. Businesses and local governments that depend on reliable and complete federal data have warned that the Census Bureau’s proposal would increase costs as data is degraded,” the senators concluded.

In addition to King, the letter was signed by U.S. Senators Gary Peters (D-MI), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), John Fetterman (D-PA), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Maggie Hassan (D-NH), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), Patty Murray (D-WA), Jack Reed (D-RI), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and Ron Wyden (D-OR).

The full text of the letter is available here and below.

+++

Dear Under Secretary Meyer and Deputy Under Secretary Cook,

We write to urge that you rescind your proposed rule that would exclude certain noncitizens from decennial census counts and omit questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census (Fed. Reg. Vol. 91, No. 57524, Thursday September 10, 2026). The proposed rule violates the clear meaning of the Constitution, which requires that the Census Bureau count the “whole number of persons in each state.” The proposed rule would also cause communities across the country to be counted inaccurately, jeopardizing their fair representation in Congress and access to billions of federal dollars for education, health care, and public safety services. The proposed rule would also undermine the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws by eliminating the only appropriate data used for compliance. We request that you rescind this proposed rule to ensure the decennial census complies with the Constitution and allows civil and voting rights laws to be enforced.

I. The Bureau’s Proposal to Exclude Certain Non-Citizens from Census Counts Violates the Constitution

The proposal to exclude certain non-citizens, including those who are legal immigrants, from apportionment counts violates the Constitution. The Fourteenth Amendment is clear: the Census Bureau must count the “whole number of persons in each state” in the United States, including non-citizens.

This interpretation of the Constitution has been accepted from the founding of our nation to the present, by our founders, courts, members of Congress, and leaders of the Census Bureau from both parties, including Secretary Howard Lutnick. In 1788, James Madison wrote in

Federalist No. 54 that the apportionment was to be “founded on the aggregate number of inhabitants,” recognizing no distinctions among types of persons to be counted except for those explicitly excluded in the text of the Constitution itself. During consideration of the Fourteenth Amendment, Congress debated and expressly rejected proposals to change the “persons” counted for apportionment to “voters” or “citizens.” During the first half of the twentieth century, Congress considered and rejected proposals to pass statutes to exclude non-citizens from apportionment counts on the basis that it would take a constitutional amendment to change the requirement. In 1929, the Senate’s Legislative Counsel concluded that excluding certain noncitizens from apportionment counts would be unconstitutional. In 1980, a court rejected a lawsuit seeking that the Bureau exclude certain non-citizens from apportionment counts. Even current Secretary of Commerce Lutnick testified to Congress in February that “citizenship is not in the Constitution for the [Census] apportionment... that is not a necessary factor”. This unbroken history of our reading of the Constitution, including courts, Congress, and Census Bureau leaders, is clear: the Census Bureau must count every person.

II. The Bureau’s Proposed Methods to Exclude Certain Non-Citizens Would Cause

Undercounts and Errors in Census Counts

The Bureau has proposed two methods for carrying out its unconstitutional exclusion of certain non-citizens: directly asking every person detailed questions about their immigration status and relying on administrative records. Both proposed methods would cause undercounts of both citizens and non-citizens and errors in the population counts.

First, the Bureau proposes asking each person their legal immigration status so that it can exclude certain non-citizens, but such a question would cause both citizens and non-citizens to not answer the census. This would likely lead to undercounts and errors in census counts. The Bureau has never asked detailed questions about legal immigration status on any nationwide survey before, let alone the decennial census, because of concerns about privacy and accuracy. The Bureau’s own research before the 2020 Census showed that including even a question about citizenship status on the decennial census, itself a less complicated question than immigration status, would cause fewer citizens and non-citizens to complete the census. In addition, the Government Accountability Office previously found that if statistical agencies directly asked about immigration status, they would create invalid, imprecise, and inaccurate estimates. In 2006, the Government Accountability Office recommended that federal agencies should not pursue adding even indirect immigration questions to surveys, and the Census Bureau concurred with that recommendation.

In addition, the Bureau alternatively proposes relying on administrative records acquired from federal agencies, state and local governments, and private data brokers to exclude certain non-citizens from apportionment counts. This approach would also lead to undercounts and inappropriately exclude citizens and non-citizens from census totals. The Bureau previously found that if it relied solely on administrative records the decennial census would misestimate the total population by over 1.3 million people, overcounting non-citizens and undercounting citizens. It also found that relying on administrative records undercounted people in rural areas and group quarters, such as nursing homes and college campuses. The Treasury Department commented on a draft of this very rule warning that using tax records to identify people’s usual address would cause people to be counted in the wrong location. This evidence shows that both of the Bureau’s proposed methods to carry out this unconstitutional effort would cause errors and undercounts, denying people fair representation in Congress and jeopardizing the fair and full allocation of resources.

III. The Bureau’s Proposal to Omit Demographic Questions Would Undermine Enforcement of Civil and Voting Rights Laws and Degrade the Quality of All Census Data

We also express our strong opposition to the Bureau’s proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census, because it would harm the ability to enforce civil and voting rights laws and cause the quality of all census data to deteriorate. Only the decennial census provides the reliable demographic data necessary for compliance with civil and voting rights laws. Congress has made clear that decennial census data should be used to enforce these laws, and the Trump Administration even recognized the legal need to collect this data for enforcing civil rights laws when it published its planned questions for the 2020 Census.

For example, Congress enacted the Fair Housing Act, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Public Health Service Act to ensure that individuals are not discriminated against on the basis of race or ethnicity in housing, employment, and health care, respectively. The Supreme Court has held that statistical evidence using census data can be used to demonstrate violations and ensure compliance with these laws. The Bureau admits in its own regulatory filing that no other federal survey that collects information about race and ethnicity, including the American Community Survey (ACS), can substitute for the decennial census, because other surveys like the ACS cannot create precise population estimates for areas smaller than 65,000 people. This means there is no real alternative for all Americans to bring claims under civil rights laws if the Bureau eliminates collecting information about race and ethnicity on the decennial census. Similarly, Congress enacted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act to prohibit voting practices or procedures that discriminate on the basis of race, including congressional redistricting. While the Supreme Court narrowed the standards to bring a claim under the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais, the Court maintained that the Voting Rights Act is violated “when the evidence supports a strong inference that the State intentionally drew its districts to afford minority voters less opportunity because of their race.” Such evidence requires the availability of decennial census data about race and ethnicity for enforcement, because the Voting Rights Act applies to even small political subdivisions where no other federal data is accurate.

The elimination of data about race and ethnicity would particularly undermine the federal government’s ability to meet its responsibilities and obligations to tribal governments. By eliminating the collection of information about American Indian and Alaska Native identity, the Bureau makes it effectively impossible for the government to administer the Indian Housing Block Grant program, the Indian Community Development Block Grant program, and the Indian Health Service – each of which depend on accurate estimates of American Indian and Alaska Native populations to plan and allocate funding.24 In its own regulatory filing, the Bureau admits that other federal surveys “may not be a suitable substitute for all federally recognized tribes,” because other surveys do not provide accurate and precise estimates of American Indian and Alaska Native populations. The Bureau previously told Congress that relying on alternative options to collect information about American Indian and Alaska Native populations, like asking about tribal enrollment or relying on administrative records, would cause inaccurate estimates and infringe on the private sovereign information of tribes.

In its attempt to undermine the data used for the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws, the Bureau will degrade the accuracy of all other federal survey data, particularly for small and rural geographic areas. The Bureau writes in its own regulatory filing that the proposed rule "deteriorates the accuracy” of “fertility/mortality rates, cancer rates, poverty rates, unemployment rates, [and] labor force participation” because the Bureau relies on accurate decennial census information to adjust and design other survey estimates. The Bureau also admits in its filing that the proposal would hamper the usability of data for state and local governments who rely on precise and accurate population estimates for small geographic areas. Businesses and local governments that depend on reliable and complete federal data have warned that the Census Bureau’s proposal would increase costs as data is degraded.

With these considerations in mind, we urge the Census Bureau to rescind its September 10 proposed regulation.

Sincerely,

###

title: Luján Statement on Vote Against Advancing Permitting Reform Legislation
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) issued the following statement after voting against advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA):

“Making it easier to build clean energy and critical infrastructure projects is important for New Mexico and our nation, and Congress has failed to find a path forward for far too long.

“However, I share the serious concerns raised by New Mexicans across the state, particularly our Pueblo and environmental leaders, and believe they must be addressed. After spending the last month listening to these concerns, I cannot support advancing the bill in its current form.

“I remain committed to working with my colleagues to address these concerns, make meaningful improvements, and get this right.”
